title: VI. For Awhile A Very Obscure One
paragraphs: When Ivan left Alyosha, he headed home to Fyodor Pavlovitch's house. But strangely enough, he was overcome by an unbearable depression that grew heavier with every step he took toward the house. There was nothing strange about being depressed; what was strange was that Ivan couldn't have said what was causing it. He'd been depressed plenty of times before, and it wasn't surprising he'd feel that way now, having broken off with everything that had brought him here, and preparing that very day to start over and step into a new, unknown future. He'd be as alone as ever, and although he had big hopes and big—too big—expectations for life, he couldn't have given any clear account of his hopes, his expectations, or even his wants.

Yet in that moment, though the dread of the new and unknown was certainly there in his heart, what was actually bothering him was something else entirely. "Is it loathing for my father's house?" he wondered. "Quite likely—I'm so sick of it, and even though it's the last time I'll cross that hateful threshold, I still loathe it.... No, that's not it either. Is it the parting with Alyosha, and the conversation we just had? For so many years I've stayed silent with the whole world and not bothered to speak, and then all of a sudden I unload a whole rambling speech like that." It might well have been the youthful irritation of youthful inexperience and vanity—irritation at having failed to express himself properly, especially to someone like Alyosha, on whom his heart had clearly been counting. No doubt that played a part, that irritation, it must have; but still, that wasn't it, that wasn't it either. "I feel sick with depression, and yet I can't say what I want. Maybe it's better not to think about it."

Ivan tried "not to think," but that didn't work either. What made his depression so maddening and irritating was that it had a kind of incidental, external quality to it—he could feel that much. Some person or thing seemed to be lodged somewhere just out of view, the way something sometimes intrudes on your eye, and though you might be so absorbed in work or conversation that for a long time you don't notice it, still it nags and almost torments you until at last you realize what it is and remove the offending object—often something quite trivial and ridiculous, an item left in the wrong place, a handkerchief on the floor, a book not put back on the shelf, and so on.
At last, feeling thoroughly cross and out of sorts, Ivan arrived home, and suddenly, about fifteen paces from the garden gate, he guessed what had been nagging and bothering him.

On a bench by the gate sat the valet Smerdyakov, enjoying the cool of the evening, and the instant Ivan glimpsed him he knew that Smerdyakov had been on his mind, that it was this man his soul recoiled from. It all dawned on him at once and became clear. Just before, when Alyosha had told him about his encounter with Smerdyakov, Ivan had felt a sudden pang of gloom and disgust, which had immediately stirred an answering anger in his heart. Later, as they talked, Smerdyakov had slipped from his mind for a while; but he'd still been there underneath, and as soon as Ivan parted from Alyosha and started walking home, the forgotten sensation began pushing itself forward again. "Is it really possible that a miserable, contemptible creature like that could bother me so much?" he wondered, with unbearable irritation.

It was true that Ivan had lately come to feel an intense dislike for the man, especially over the last few days. He'd even started to notice in himself a growing feeling that was close to hatred for the creature. Maybe this hatred was sharpened by the fact that when Ivan first came to the area, he'd felt quite differently. Back then he'd taken a real interest in Smerdyakov, had even found him rather original. He'd encouraged the man to talk to him, although he'd always been puzzled by a certain incoherence, or rather restlessness, in his mind, and couldn't work out what it was that kept working so persistently on the brain of "the contemplative one." They'd discussed philosophical questions—even the question of how there could have been light on the first day, when the sun, moon, and stars weren't created until the fourth. But Ivan soon saw that, interesting as the sun, moon, and stars might be, they were entirely secondary to Smerdyakov, who was after something quite different. Bit by bit, the man began to reveal a boundless vanity—a wounded vanity, too—and that Ivan disliked. It was what first gave rise to his aversion. Later there'd been trouble in the house. Grushenka had come on the scene, and there'd been the scandals with his brother Dmitri—they discussed that too. But though Smerdyakov always talked about it with great agitation, it was impossible to figure out what he actually wanted to come of it. There was, in fact, something startling in the illogic and incoherence of some of his desires, let slip by accident and always vaguely stated. Smerdyakov kept probing, asking certain roundabout but obviously deliberate questions, without ever explaining what he was after, and usually, at the most important moment, he'd break off and lapse into silence or switch to another subject. But what finally irritated Ivan most, and cemented his dislike for the man, was the peculiar, revolting familiarity Smerdyakov had begun showing more and more openly. Not that he was ever rude or forgot his place—on the contrary, he always spoke very respectfully—yet he'd clearly started to assume, God knows why, that there was some sort of understanding between him and Ivan Fyodorovitch. He always spoke in a tone that implied the two of them had some kind of pact, some secret between them, expressed at some point on both sides, known only to the two of them and beyond the grasp of everyone around them. But for a long time Ivan hadn't recognized the real source of his growing dislike, and had only just recently realized what lay at the root of it.

With a feeling of disgust and irritation, he tried to walk in through the gate without speaking to or even looking at Smerdyakov. But Smerdyakov rose from the bench, and from that gesture alone Ivan knew instantly that he wanted very much to talk to him. Ivan looked at him and stopped, and the fact that he did stop, instead of walking on past as he'd meant to do a moment before, drove him into a fury. With anger and revulsion he looked at Smerdyakov's soft, sickly face, with its little curls combed forward over the forehead. The man's left eye winked, and he grinned, as if to say, "Where are you off to? You won't walk past me—you know perfectly well the two of us, being clever people, have something to say to each other."

Ivan shuddered. "Get out of my way, you miserable idiot. What business do I have with you?" was right on the tip of his tongue, but to his own profound astonishment, what he heard himself say was, "Is my father still asleep, or has he woken up?"

He asked it softly and meekly, to his own surprise, and then, again to his own surprise, sat down on the bench. For a moment he felt almost frightened; he remembered that afterward. Smerdyakov stood facing him, hands behind his back, looking at him with confidence and something close to severity.

"His honor is still asleep," he pronounced deliberately ("You spoke first, not me," he seemed to be saying). "I'm surprised at you, sir," he added after a pause, dropping his eyes with studied modesty, setting his right foot forward, and toying with the tip of his polished boot.

"Why are you surprised at me?" Ivan asked abruptly and sullenly, doing everything he could to hold himself in check, and realizing all at once, with disgust, that he was consumed with curiosity and wouldn't, under any circumstances, leave without satisfying it.

"Why aren't you going to Tchermashnya, sir?" Smerdyakov suddenly raised his eyes and smiled with familiarity. "Why I'm smiling, you can work out for yourself, if you're a clever man," his narrowed left eye seemed to say.
"Why should I go to Tchermashnya?" Ivan asked, surprised.
Smerdyakov fell silent again.

"Fyodor Pavlovitch himself has been begging you to," he said finally, slowly, and apparently attaching no weight to his own answer. "I'm putting you off with a secondary reason," he seemed to be suggesting, "just to have something to say."
"Damn you! Say what you want to say!" Ivan finally cried out in anger, going from meekness straight to violence.
Smerdyakov drew his right foot back up to his left, straightened himself, but kept looking at Ivan with the same composure and the same faint smile.
"Nothing in particular—just talk, is all."

Another silence followed. Neither spoke for nearly a minute. Ivan knew he ought to get up and show his anger, and Smerdyakov stood before him seeming to wait and see whether he would get angry or not. At least that's how it seemed to Ivan. At last he moved to rise. Smerdyakov seized the moment.
"I'm in an awful position, Ivan Fyodorovitch. I don't know how to help myself," he said firmly and clearly, and sighed on the last word. Ivan Fyodorovitch sat back down.

"They're both absolutely out of their minds, no better than little children," Smerdyakov went on. "I mean your father and your brother Dmitri Fyodorovitch. Here's Fyodor Pavlovitch, he'll get up any minute and start pestering me every few minutes, 'Has she come? Why hasn't she come?' and so on, right up until midnight and even past it. And if Agrafena Alexandrovna doesn't come—and very likely she doesn't mean to come at all—then tomorrow morning he'll be at me again, 'Why hasn't she come? When will she come?'—as if I were somehow to blame. And on the other side it's no better. As soon as it gets dark, or even before, your brother turns up with his gun in his hand: 'Watch yourself, you rogue, you soup-maker. If you let her slip past and don't tell me she's been here, I'll kill you before anyone else.' Then once the night's over, in the morning, he too, just like Fyodor Pavlovitch, starts pestering me to death. 'Why hasn't she come? Will she come soon?' And he, too, thinks it's my fault his lady hasn't shown up. Every day and every hour they get angrier and angrier, so that sometimes I think I'll kill myself out of sheer fright. I can't rely on either of them, sir."
"And why have you gotten mixed up in it? Why did you start spying for Dmitri Fyodorovitch?" Ivan said irritably.

"How could I help getting mixed up in it? Though, honestly, if you want the truth of the matter, I haven't gotten mixed up in anything at all. I kept quiet from the very start, not daring to say a word; but he picked me out to be his errand boy. He's had exactly one thing to say ever since: 'I'll kill you, you scoundrel, if you let her slip by,' and I feel certain, sir, that I'll have a long fit tomorrow."
"What do you mean, 'a long fit'?"

"A long fit, lasting a long time—several hours, maybe a day or two. Once it went on for three days. I fell from the garret that time. The convulsions stopped and then started again, and for three days I couldn't come back to my senses. Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Herzenstube, the doctor here, and he put ice on my head and tried something else besides.... I might have died."
"But they say you can't tell with epilepsy when a fit is coming. What makes you say you'll have one tomorrow?" Ivan asked, with a strange, irritable curiosity.
"That's exactly it. You can't tell in advance."
"Besides, you fell from the garret that time."
"I climb up to the garret every single day. I might fall from the garret again tomorrow. And if not that, I might fall down the cellar steps. I have to go down into the cellar every day too."
Ivan gave him a long look.
"You're talking nonsense, I can see that, and I don't quite follow you," he said quietly, but with a kind of menace. "Are you planning to fake being sick tomorrow, for three days?"
Smerdyakov, who was looking down at the ground again, toying with the toe of his right foot, set that foot down, moved the left one forward, and said with a grin:

"If I were able to pull off a trick like that—pretend to have a fit—and it wouldn't be hard for a man who's used to having them—I'd have every right to use a trick like that to save myself from being killed. Because even if Agrafena Alexandrovna does come to see his father while I'm sick, his honor can hardly blame a sick man for not telling him. He'd be ashamed to."

"Damn it all!" Ivan cried, his face contorting with anger, "why are you always in such a panic about your life? All my brother Dmitri's threats are just hasty words and mean nothing. He won't kill you—you're not the one he's going to kill!"
"He'd kill me first of all, like a fly. But what I'm even more afraid of is being taken for his accomplice when he does something crazy to his father."
"Why would you be taken for an accomplice?"
"They'll think I'm an accomplice because I told him the signals as a great secret."
"What signals? Who did you tell? Damn it, speak plainly."

"I'm bound to admit," Smerdyakov drawled with pedantic composure, "that I have a secret arrangement with Fyodor Pavlovitch in this business. As you know yourself—if you even know it—he's kept himself locked in for several days now as soon as night, or even evening, comes on. Lately you've been going up to your room early every evening, and yesterday you didn't come down at all, so maybe you don't know how carefully he's started locking himself in at night, so that even if Grigory Vassilyevitch comes to the door he won't open it until he hears his voice. But Grigory Vassilyevitch doesn't come anymore, because I'm the one who waits on him in his room now, alone. That's the arrangement he made himself, ever since this business with Agrafena Alexandrovna started. But at night, by his orders, I go off to the lodge, and I don't get to sleep until midnight, because I'm on watch, getting up and walking around the yard, waiting for Agrafena Alexandrovna to arrive. These last few days he's been absolutely frantic waiting for her. What he figures is, she's afraid of him, Dmitri Fyodorovitch—Mitya, he calls him—'and so,' he says, 'she'll come by the back way, late at night, to me. You watch for her,' he says, 'until midnight and after; and if she comes, you run up and knock on my door or on the window from the garden. Knock twice first, fairly gently, then three times quicker, and then,' he says, 'I'll know right away she's come, and I'll open the door quietly.' He gave me another signal in case something unexpected happens. First two knocks, then, after a pause, another one much louder. Then he'll understand that something's happened all of a sudden and that I need to see him, and he'll open up so I can go in and speak to him. That's all in case Agrafena Alexandrovna can't come herself but sends word instead. And besides, Dmitri Fyodorovitch might show up too, so I have to be able to let him know he's nearby. His honor is terribly afraid of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, so that even if Agrafena Alexandrovna had already come and were locked in with him, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch turned up anywhere nearby, I'd be bound to let him know at once, knocking three times. So the first signal—five knocks—means Agrafena Alexandrovna has arrived, and the second—three knocks—means 'something important to tell you.' His honor has shown me these several times and explained them. And since not a soul in the whole world knows these signals except me and his honor, he'll open the door without the least hesitation and without calling out—he's terribly afraid of calling out loud. Well, now Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows those signals too."
"How does he know them? Did you tell him? How dare you tell him?"

"It was out of fear that I did it. How could I dare to keep it from him? Dmitri Fyodorovitch kept at me every day, 'You're deceiving me, you're hiding something from me! I'll break both your legs for you.' So I told him the secret signals, so he'd see how loyal I was, and be satisfied I wasn't deceiving him, that I was telling him everything I possibly could."
"If you think he'll use those signals to try to get in, then don't let him in."
"But if I'm laid up with a fit, how am I supposed to stop him getting in, even if I dared to try, knowing how desperate he is?"
"Damn it! How can you be so sure you're going to have a fit? Are you making fun of me?"
"How could I dare make fun of you? I'm in no mood for jokes, with this fear hanging over me. I feel it coming on. I have a premonition. Fright alone will bring it on."
"Damn it all! If you're laid up, Grigory will be keeping watch. Let Grigory know beforehand; he'll be sure not to let him in."

"I'd never dare tell Grigory Vassilyevitch about the signals without my master's orders. And as for Grigory Vassilyevitch hearing him and not letting him in—he's been sick since yesterday, and Marfa Ignatyevna means to give him medicine tomorrow. They've just settled on it. It's a very strange remedy of hers. Marfa Ignatyevna knows how to make a preparation and always keeps some on hand. It's a strong thing, made from some herb. She has the secret of it, and she always gives it to Grigory Vassilyevitch three times a year, when his lumbago gets so bad he's almost paralyzed by it. Then she takes a towel, soaks it in the stuff, and rubs his whole back with it for half an hour, until it's good and red and swollen, and whatever's left in the bottle she gives him to drink, with a special prayer said over it—but not quite all of it, because on those occasions she saves some for herself and drinks it herself. And since neither of them ever touches strong drink otherwise, I promise you they both drop off to sleep at once and sleep very soundly for a long time. And when Grigory Vassilyevitch wakes up he's perfectly fine afterward, but Marfa Ignatyevna always ends up with a headache from it. So if Marfa Ignatyevna carries out her plan tomorrow, they won't hear a thing and won't be able to stop Dmitri Fyodorovitch. They'll be fast asleep."

"What a tangled story! And it's all supposed to happen at once, as if it were arranged. You'll have a fit and they'll both be out cold," Ivan cried. "But aren't you the one arranging it that way?" burst from him suddenly, and he frowned darkly.

"How could I?... And why would I, when it all depends on Dmitri Fyodorovitch and his own plans?... If he means to do something, he'll do it; but if he doesn't, I'm certainly not going to be the one pushing him toward his father."

"And why would he go to father, sneaking in like that, if, as you say yourself, Agrafena Alexandrovna isn't coming at all?" Ivan went on, turning white with anger. "You say so yourself, and this whole time I've been here I've felt sure it was all just the old man's fantasy, and that the woman won't come to him at all. Why would Dmitri break in on him if she doesn't come? Speak up—I want to know what you're thinking!"

"You know perfectly well yourself why he'll come. What good is it what I think? His honor will come simply because he's in a rage, or suspicious on account of my being sick, maybe, and he'll come rushing in, the way he did yesterday, out of impatience, to search the rooms and see whether she hasn't slipped past him on the sly. He's also perfectly well aware that Fyodor Pavlovitch has a big envelope with three thousand roubles in it, tied up with ribbon and sealed with three seals. On it he's written, in his own hand, 'To my angel Grushenka, if she will come,' and three days later he added, 'for my little chicken.' There's no telling what that might lead to."

"Nonsense!" Ivan cried, almost beside himself. "Dmitri isn't going to come to steal money and kill my father to do it. He might have killed him yesterday over Grushenka, being the frantic, savage fool he is, but he won't steal."

"He's in very great need of money right now—the greatest need, Ivan Fyodorovitch. You have no idea how badly he needs it," Smerdyakov explained, with perfect composure and remarkable clarity. "He looks on that three thousand as his own, too, you know. He told me so himself. 'My father still owes me exactly three thousand,' he said. And besides that, consider, Ivan Fyodorovitch, there's something else that's just as true. It's about as certain as anything can be, so to speak, that Agrafena Alexandrovna could force him—if only she wanted to—to marry her—the master himself, I mean, Fyodor Pavlovitch—if only she cared to, and of course she might well care to. All I've said is that she won't come; but maybe she's after something bigger than that—I mean, to become mistress of the whole household. I happen to know that Samsonov, her merchant, was joking with her about it, telling her outright it wouldn't be a stupid move at all. And she's got plenty of sense. She wouldn't marry a beggar like Dmitri Fyodorovitch. So, taking all that into account, Ivan Fyodorovitch, consider that in that case neither Dmitri Fyodorovitch nor you nor your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch would get anything after the master's death, not a rouble, because Agrafena Alexandrovna would marry him purely to get her hands on the whole fortune, every bit of it. But if your father were to die now, there'd be some forty thousand for certain, even for Dmitri Fyodorovitch, whom he hates so much, since he's made no will.... Dmitri Fyodorovitch knows all that perfectly well."
A kind of shudder passed over Ivan's face. He suddenly flushed.
"Then why on earth," he suddenly cut Smerdyakov off, "are you advising me to go to Tchermashnya? What did you mean by that? If I leave, you see what will happen here." Ivan drew a labored breath.
"Exactly so," said Smerdyakov, softly and reasonably, watching Ivan closely all the while.
"What do you mean by 'exactly so'?" Ivan pressed him, a threatening light in his eyes, holding himself back with difficulty.

"I said it because I felt sorry for you. If I were in your place, I'd simply throw the whole thing over... rather than stay on in such a position," Smerdyakov answered, with the most candid look, staring straight into Ivan's blazing eyes. They were both silent for a moment.

"You seem to be a complete idiot, and what's more... a terrible scoundrel too." Ivan rose suddenly from the bench. He meant to walk straight through the gate, but stopped short and turned to Smerdyakov. Something strange followed. Ivan, in a sudden fit, bit his lip, clenched his fists, and, another second, would have thrown himself at Smerdyakov. The other man, at any rate, noticed it in that same instant, flinched, and shrank back. But the moment passed without harm to Smerdyakov, and Ivan turned in silence, seemingly bewildered, toward the gate.

"I'm leaving for Moscow tomorrow, if you want to know—early tomorrow morning. That's all!" he suddenly said aloud, angrily, and wondered afterward himself what need there'd been to say this to Smerdyakov just then.
"That's the best thing you could do," the man replied, as though he'd expected to hear exactly that; "except that you can always be telegraphed for from Moscow, if anything happens here."

Ivan stopped again, and again turned quickly to Smerdyakov. But something had changed in him too. All his familiarity and carelessness had completely vanished. His face showed attention and expectation, intent but timid and cringing.
"Haven't you got something more to say—something to add?" could be read in the intent gaze he fixed on Ivan.
"And couldn't I be sent for from Tchermashnya too—if anything happened?" Ivan suddenly shouted, raising his voice for no reason he could name.
"From Tchermashnya too... you could be sent for," Smerdyakov murmured, almost in a whisper, looking disconcerted, but gazing intently into Ivan's eyes.
"Only Moscow is farther and Tchermashnya is nearer. Is it to save me the cost of the fare, or to save me going so far out of my way, that you're so set on Tchermashnya?"

"Exactly so..." Smerdyakov muttered, his voice breaking. He looked at Ivan with a revolting smile, and again made ready to draw back. But to his own astonishment, Ivan burst out laughing, and walked out through the gate still laughing. Anyone who'd seen his face in that moment would have known he wasn't laughing out of lightheartedness, and he himself couldn't have explained what he was feeling right then. He moved and walked as though caught up in some nervous frenzy.

title: VII. “It’s Always Worth While Speaking To A Clever Man”
paragraphs: And it was in that same nervous frenzy that he spoke, too. Running into Fyodor Pavlovitch in the drawing room the moment he came in, he shouted at him, waving his hands, "I'm going up to my room, not in to see you. Good-bye!" and walked past, trying not even to look at his father. Quite possibly the old man was simply too repulsive to him at that moment; but such a blunt display of hostility took even Fyodor Pavlovitch by surprise. And the old man had clearly wanted to tell him something right away, and had come out to the drawing room on purpose to meet him. Receiving this warm greeting, he stood still in silence, watching his son go upstairs with an ironic look on his face, until Ivan passed out of sight.
"What's the matter with him?" he asked Smerdyakov at once, who had followed Ivan in.
"Angry about something. Who can say?" the valet muttered evasively.
"To hell with him! Let him be angry, then. Bring in the samovar and get moving. Look sharp! No news?"

Then came a string of questions like the ones Smerdyakov had just been complaining to Ivan about, all to do with his expected visitor, and we'll skip over them. Half an hour later the house was locked up, and the crazed old man was wandering through the rooms in a state of excited anticipation, expecting to hear the agreed-upon five knocks at any moment. Every so often he peered out into the darkness and saw nothing.

It was very late, but Ivan was still awake, thinking. He stayed up that night until two o'clock. But we won't give an account of his thoughts, and this isn't the place to look into that particular soul—its turn will come. And even if we tried, it would be hard to give any real account of them, because there weren't really thoughts in his head, but something very vague, and, above all, intense agitation. He felt he'd lost his bearings. He was also plagued by all sorts of strange and nearly startling urges—for instance, after midnight he suddenly felt an intense, irresistible urge to go downstairs, open the door, walk out to the lodge, and beat Smerdyakov. But if he'd been asked why, he couldn't have given any exact reason, except maybe that he loathed the valet as someone who had insulted him more deeply than anyone else on earth. On the other hand, more than once that night he was overcome by a kind of inexplicable, humiliating terror, which he felt actually paralyzed his physical strength. His head ached and he felt dizzy. A feeling of hatred was festering in his heart, as if he meant to get revenge on somebody. He even hated Alyosha, remembering the conversation they'd just had. At moments he hated himself intensely. He almost forgot to think about Katerina Ivanovna at all, and was very surprised by that afterward, especially since he remembered perfectly well that when he'd insisted so forcefully to Katerina Ivanovna that he'd be leaving for Moscow the next day, something had whispered in his heart, "That's nonsense, you're not going, and tearing yourself away won't be as easy as you're boasting right now."

Remembering that night long afterward, Ivan recalled with particular disgust how he'd suddenly gotten up from the sofa and, stealthily, as though afraid of being watched, opened the door, gone out onto the staircase, and listened to Fyodor Pavlovitch moving around down below, had listened a long while—some five minutes—with a strange kind of curiosity, holding his breath while his heart pounded. And why he'd done all this, why he was listening, he couldn't have said. That "act," for the rest of his life, he called "infamous," and deep down he thought of it as the basest act of his life. He felt no hatred for Fyodor Pavlovitch himself in that moment—he was simply intensely curious to know how his father was pacing down there and what he must be doing right then. He wondered and pictured how the old man must be peering out through the dark windows, stopping in the middle of the room, listening, listening—for someone to knock. Ivan went out onto the stairs twice to listen like this.

Around two o'clock, when everything had gone quiet and even Fyodor Pavlovitch had gone to bed, Ivan got into bed himself, firmly resolved to fall asleep at once, since he felt terribly worn out. And he did fall asleep at once, and slept soundly with no dreams, but woke early, at seven, in broad daylight. Opening his eyes, he was surprised to feel unusually full of energy. He jumped straight up and dressed quickly, then dragged out his trunk and started packing immediately. His laundry had come back the previous morning. Ivan actually smiled at the thought that everything seemed to be conspiring to help his sudden departure. And his departure really was sudden. Though Ivan had told everyone the day before—Katerina Ivanovna, Alyosha, and Smerdyakov—that he was leaving the next day, he remembered that he'd had no thought of leaving when he went to bed, hadn't even dreamed that his first act in the morning would be to pack his trunk. At last the trunk and bag were ready. It was about nine o'clock when Marfa Ignatyevna came in with her usual question, "Where will your honor take tea, in your own room or downstairs?" He looked almost cheerful, but there was something rushed and scattered about him, about his words and gestures. Greeting his father affably, and even asking specially after his health, though he didn't wait to hear the answer through to the end, he announced that he was setting off in an hour to return to Moscow for good, and asked him to send for the horses. His father heard the announcement without any sign of surprise, and rudely forgot to express any regret at losing him. Instead, he flew into a great fluster, remembering some important business of his own.

"What a fellow you are! Not telling me yesterday! Never mind, we'll manage it all the same. Do me a great favor, my boy. Go by way of Tchermashnya. You just turn left from the station at Volovya—another twelve versts and you're at Tchermashnya."
"I'm sorry, I can't. It's eighty versts to the railway and the train for Moscow leaves at seven tonight. I can only just make it as it is."

"You'll catch one tomorrow or the day after, but today turn off toward Tchermashnya. It won't set you back much to do your father a favor! If I didn't have something keeping me here, I'd have run over myself long ago, because I've got urgent business there. But as things stand... it's not the time for me to go.... You see, I've got two stretches of woodland there. The Maslovs—an old merchant and his son—will give eight thousand for the timber. But last year I just missed a buyer who'd have given twelve. There's nobody around here you can get to buy it. The Maslovs have it entirely their own way. You have to take whatever they offer, because nobody here dares bid against them. The priest at Ilyinskoe wrote me last Thursday that a merchant named Gorstkin, a man I know, had turned up. What makes him useful is that he's not from these parts, so he's not afraid of the Maslovs. He says he'll give me eleven thousand for the copse. You hear that? But he'll only be there, the priest writes, for a week altogether, so you have to go at once and strike a bargain with him."
"Well, write to the priest, then; let him strike the bargain."

"He can't do it. He has no head for business. He's a perfect treasure—I'd trust him with twenty thousand to hold for me without so much as a receipt—but he has no head for business at all, he's a perfect child, a crow could swindle him. And yet he's a learned man, would you believe it? This Gorstkin looks like a peasant, wears a blue kaftan, but he's a proper rogue. That's the common complaint about him. He's a liar. Sometimes he tells lies so pointless you wonder why he even bothers. He told me the year before last that his wife had died and that he'd remarried, and would you believe it, there wasn't a word of truth in it. His wife never died at all—she's alive to this day and gives him a beating twice a week. So what you need to find out is whether he's lying or telling the truth when he says he wants to buy it and would give eleven thousand."
"I'd be no use in a business like that. I've got no head for it either."

"Wait, hold on a minute! You will be of use, because I'll tell you the signs to judge Gorstkin by. I've done business with him a long time. You see, you have to watch his beard—he's got a nasty, thin, reddish beard. If his beard shakes while he talks and he gets cross, that's a good sign, he's saying what he means, he wants to do the deal. But if he strokes his beard with his left hand and grins, he's trying to swindle you. Don't bother watching his eyes—you won't learn anything from his eyes, he's a deep one, a rogue—but watch the beard! I'll give you a note and you show it to him. His name's Gorstkin, though his real name is Lyagavy—but don't call him that, he'll take offense. If you come to an agreement with him, and it seems solid, write to me here at once. Just write: 'He's not lying.' Hold out for eleven thousand—you can knock off one thousand, but no more. Just think! There's a difference between eight thousand and eleven thousand. It's as good as picking up three thousand off the ground—it's not easy to find a buyer, and I'm in desperate need of money. Just let me know it's serious, and I'll run over and settle it myself. I'll find the time somehow. But what's the use of my galloping over there if it's all just some notion of the priest's? Well, will you go?"
"Oh, I can't spare the time. You'll have to excuse me."

"Come now, you might do your father this favor. I won't forget it. None of you have any heart—that's the truth of it, isn't it? What's a day or two to you? Where are you off to now—Venice? Your Venice will keep another two days. I'd have sent Alyosha, but what use is Alyosha in a thing like this? I'm sending you precisely because you're a clever fellow. Don't think I don't notice that. You don't know the first thing about timber, but you've got an eye. All that's needed is to see whether the man's in earnest. I tell you, watch his beard—if his beard shakes, you'll know he's in earnest."
"So you're forcing me to go to that damned Tchermashnya after all?" Ivan cried, with a spiteful smile.
Fyodor Pavlovitch didn't catch, or chose not to catch, the spite in it, but he caught the smile.
"So you'll go, you'll go? I'll scribble the note for you right now."
"I don't know whether I'll go. I don't know. I'll decide on the way."

"Nonsense! Decide now. My dear boy, decide! If you settle the matter, drop me a line—give it to the priest and he'll send it straight on to me. And I won't hold you up beyond that. You can go on to Venice. The priest will give you horses back to Volovya station."

The old man was thoroughly delighted. He wrote the note and sent for the horses. A light lunch was brought in, with brandy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch was pleased about something, he usually grew expansive, but today he seemed to hold himself in check. About Dmitri, for instance, he didn't say a single word. He seemed entirely unmoved by the parting, and in fact seemed at a loss for what to say. Ivan noticed this in particular. "He must be bored with me," he thought. Only as he walked his son out onto the front steps did the old man start fussing. He would have kissed him, but Ivan hurried to hold out his hand instead, clearly avoiding the kiss. His father saw it at once and pulled himself up short.
"Well, good luck, good luck to you!" he kept saying from the steps. "You'll come back again sometime? Mind you do come back. I'll always be glad to see you. Well, Christ be with you!"
Ivan climbed into the carriage.
"Good-bye, Ivan! Don't be too hard on me!" his father called out one last time.
The whole household came out to say good-bye—Smerdyakov, Marfa, and Grigory. Ivan gave each of them ten roubles. Once he'd settled himself in the carriage, Smerdyakov jumped up to arrange the rug.

"You see... I'm going to Tchermashnya," broke suddenly from Ivan. Again, just as the day before, the words seemed to drop out on their own, and he laughed too, a strange, nervous laugh. He remembered it for a long time afterward.
"So it's true what they say, 'it's always worth talking to a clever man,'" Smerdyakov answered firmly, giving Ivan a meaningful look.

The carriage rolled off. Nothing was clear in Ivan's soul, but he looked eagerly around him—at the fields, at the hills, at the trees, at a flock of geese flying high overhead in the bright sky. And all at once he felt very happy. He tried to make conversation with the driver, and found himself intensely interested in some answer the peasant gave him; but a minute later he realized he hadn't actually caught any of it, hadn't really taken in the peasant's answer at all. He fell silent, and it was pleasant even so. The air was fresh, clean, and cool, the sky bright. The images of Alyosha and Katerina Ivanovna drifted into his mind. But he smiled softly, blew gently on the friendly ghosts, and they flew off. "There's plenty of time for them," he thought. They reached the station quickly, changed horses, and galloped on to Volovya. "Why is it worth talking to a clever man? What did he mean by that?" The thought seemed to suddenly seize hold of his breathing. "And why did I tell him I was going to Tchermashnya?" They reached Volovya station. Ivan got out of the carriage, and the drivers gathered round him bargaining over the twelve-verst trip to Tchermashnya. He told them to harness the horses. He went into the station house, looked around, glanced at the stationmaster's wife, and suddenly turned back toward the entrance.
"I won't go to Tchermashnya. Am I too late to make the seven o'clock train, brothers?"
"We'll just make it. Shall we bring the carriage round?"
"At once. Is any one of you going to town tomorrow?"
"Sure enough. Mitri here will be."
"Can you do me a favor, Mitri? Go to my father's, to Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, and tell him I didn't go to Tchermashnya after all. Can you do that?"
"Of course I can. I've known Fyodor Pavlovitch a long time."
"And here's something for your trouble, since I doubt he'll give you anything," Ivan said, laughing cheerfully.
"You can count on that, he won't." Mitya laughed too. "Thank you, sir. I'll see that it's done."

At seven o'clock Ivan boarded the train and set off for Moscow. "Away with the past. I'm done with the old world for good, and let there be no news, no echo, from it. On to a new life, new places, and no looking back!" But instead of delight, his soul was filled with a gloom so deep, and his heart ached with such anguish, as he had never known before in his life. He sat thinking through the whole night. The train raced on, and only at daybreak, as he was nearing Moscow, did he suddenly rouse himself from his thoughts.
"I'm a scoundrel," he whispered to himself.

Fyodor Pavlovitch was left thoroughly satisfied at having seen his son off. For two hours afterward he felt almost happy, and sat drinking brandy. But suddenly something happened that was very upsetting and unpleasant for everyone in the house, and immediately shattered Fyodor Pavlovitch's peace of mind. Smerdyakov went down to the cellar for something and fell from the top of the steps. Luckily, Marfa Ignatyevna was out in the yard and heard him in time. She didn't see the fall, but heard his scream—that strange, distinctive scream she'd known for years—the scream of an epileptic going into a fit. Nobody could say for sure whether the fit had hit him just as he was going down the steps, so that he must have fallen unconscious, or whether it was the fall and the shock that had brought on the fit in Smerdyakov, who was known to be prone to them. They found him at the bottom of the cellar steps, writhing in convulsions and foaming at the mouth. At first they thought he must have broken something—an arm or a leg—and hurt himself badly, but "God had spared him," as Marfa Ignatyevna put it—nothing of the kind had happened. But it was hard work getting him out of the cellar. They called in the neighbors to help and managed it somehow. Fyodor Pavlovitch himself was present through the whole business. He helped out, clearly alarmed and shaken. The sick man didn't regain consciousness; the convulsions stopped for a while, then started up again, and everyone concluded the same thing would happen as had happened a year before, when he'd accidentally fallen from the garret. They remembered that ice had been put on his head that time. There was still ice down in the cellar, and Marfa Ignatyevna had some brought up. That evening, Fyodor Pavlovitch sent for Doctor Herzenstube, who came at once. He was a most respectable old man, and the most careful and conscientious doctor in the province. After a thorough examination, he concluded that the fit was a very severe one and might have serious consequences; that for the time being he, Herzenstube, didn't fully understand it, but that by the next morning, if the current remedies proved useless, he'd venture to try something else. The sick man was carried to the lodge, to a room next to Grigory's and Marfa Ignatyevna's.

Then Fyodor Pavlovitch had one misfortune after another to put up with that day. Marfa Ignatyevna cooked the dinner, and the soup, next to Smerdyakov's, was "no better than dishwater," and the chicken was so dried out it was impossible to chew. To her master's bitter, though deserved, complaints, Marfa Ignatyevna replied that the chicken had been old to begin with, and that she'd never been trained as a cook. That evening there was yet another trouble in store for Fyodor Pavlovitch: he was told that Grigory, who hadn't been well for the last three days, was now completely laid up by his lumbago. Fyodor Pavlovitch finished his tea as quickly as he could and locked himself up alone in the house. He was in a state of terrible excitement and suspense. That evening he counted on Grushenka's coming almost as a sure thing. He'd gotten word from Smerdyakov that morning assuring him "that she had promised without fail to come." The incorrigible old man's heart pounded with excitement; he paced back and forth through his empty rooms, listening. He had to stay alert. Dmitri might be watching for her somewhere, and the moment she knocked on the window—Smerdyakov had told him two days earlier that he'd shown her where and how to knock—the door had to be opened at once. She mustn't be left standing in the passage even a second, for fear—God forbid!—that she'd get frightened and run off. Fyodor Pavlovitch had a great deal on his mind, but never before had his heart been steeped in such voluptuous hope. This time he could say with near certainty that she would come!

title: I. Father Zossima And His Visitors
paragraphs: When Alyosha went into his elder's cell with an anxious, aching heart, he stopped short, almost astonished. Instead of a dying man at his last gasp, maybe unconscious, as he'd feared to find him, he saw him sitting up in his chair, and though weak and worn out, his face was bright and cheerful; he was surrounded by visitors and taking part in a quiet, joyful conversation. But he'd only gotten up from bed a quarter of an hour before Alyosha arrived; his visitors had gathered in his cell earlier, waiting for him to wake, having received the most confident assurance from Father Païssy that "the teacher would get up, and, as he himself had promised that morning, would talk once more with those dear to his heart." Father Païssy put absolute faith in that promise, indeed in every word of the dying elder. If he'd seen him unconscious, seen him draw his last breath, and yet had his promise that he would rise and say good-bye to him, he probably wouldn't have believed it even in death, but would still have expected the dead man to recover and keep his word. That morning, as he lay down to sleep, Father Zossima had told him plainly: "I won't die without the joy of one more conversation with you, beloved of my heart. I'll look once more on your dear face and pour out my heart to you again." The monks who'd gathered for this probably final conversation with Father Zossima had all been his devoted friends for many years. There were four of them: Father Iosif and Father Païssy, and Father Mihaïl, the warden of the hermitage, a man not very old and far from learned. He was of humble birth, strong-willed and steadfast in faith, austere in appearance but deeply tender at heart, though he clearly hid it, as if almost ashamed of it. The fourth, Father Anfim, was a very old and humble little monk from the poorest peasant stock. He was nearly illiterate, and very quiet, barely speaking to anyone. He was the humblest of the humble, and looked as though he'd been frightened by something great and terrible, beyond the reach of his understanding. Father Zossima had great affection for this timid man, and always treated him with marked respect, though there was perhaps no one he'd known to whom he'd said less, despite having spent years wandering across holy Russia with him. That was very long ago, forty years before, when Father Zossima first began his life as a monk in a small, poor monastery at Kostroma, and when, shortly after, he'd gone with Father Anfim on his pilgrimage to collect alms for their poor monastery.

The whole group was in the bedroom, which, as we mentioned before, was very small, so there was barely room for the four of them—plus Porfiry, the novice, who stood—to sit around Father Zossima on chairs brought in from the sitting room. It was already starting to get dark; the room was lit by the lamps and the candles burning before the icons.
Seeing Alyosha standing self-consciously in the doorway, Father Zossima smiled at him with joy and held out his hand.
"Welcome, my quiet one, welcome, my dear, you're here too. I knew you'd come."
Alyosha went up to him, bowed down to the ground before him, and wept. Something surged up from his heart, his soul trembled, he felt he had to sob.

"Come now, don't cry over me yet," Father Zossima smiled, laying his right hand on his head. "You see, I'm sitting up talking; maybe I'll live another twenty years yet, the way that good woman from Vishegorye, with her little Lizaveta in her arms, wished for me yesterday. God bless the mother and the little girl Lizaveta," he said, crossing himself. "Porfiry, did you take her offering where I told you to?"

He meant the sixty copecks the good-natured woman had brought him the day before, to be given "to someone poorer than me." Such offerings, always of money earned by one's own labor, are given as a form of voluntary penance. The elder had sent Porfiry the evening before to a widow whose house had recently burned down, who after the fire had gone begging alms with her children. Porfiry hurried to answer that he'd given the money, exactly as instructed, "from an unknown benefactress."

"Get up, my dear boy," the elder went on, turning to Alyosha. "Let me look at you. Have you been home and seen your brother?" It struck Alyosha as strange that he asked so confidently and precisely about one particular brother—but which one? Perhaps that was why he'd sent him out both yesterday and today, for that brother's sake.
"I saw one of my brothers," Alyosha answered.
"I mean the elder one, the one I bowed down to."
"I only saw him yesterday, and I couldn't find him today," Alyosha said.

"Hurry and find him, go again tomorrow, and hurry—leave everything and hurry. You may still have time to prevent something terrible. Yesterday I bowed down to the great suffering that's in store for him."

He suddenly fell silent, seeming lost in thought. The words were strange. Father Iosif, who'd witnessed yesterday's scene, exchanged a glance with Father Païssy. Alyosha couldn't stop himself from asking:
"Father, my teacher," he began, deeply moved, "your words are too unclear.... What is this suffering that's in store for him?"

"Don't ask. I seemed to see something terrible yesterday... as though his whole future were written in his eyes. A look came into his eyes—one that struck me with instant horror at what that man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I've seen such a look on a man's face... reflecting, as it were, his coming fate, and that fate, alas, came to pass. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought your brotherly face might help him. But everything, all our fates, come from the Lord. 'Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.' Remember that. You, Alexey, I have many times silently blessed for your face—know that," the elder added with a gentle smile. "Here is what I think of you: you'll go out from these walls, but you'll live in the world like a monk. You'll have many enemies, but even your enemies will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but you'll find your happiness in them, and you'll bless life and lead others to bless it too—which matters most of all. Well, that's your nature. Fathers, teachers," he said, turning to his friends with a tender smile, "until today I've never told even him why this young man's face is so dear to me. Now I'll tell you. His face has been, in a way, both a memory and a prophecy for me. At the dawn of my life, when I was a child, I had an elder brother who died before my eyes at seventeen. Later on, over the course of my life, I gradually became convinced that that brother had been, for me, a form of guidance and a sign sent from above. Because if he hadn't come into my life, I probably would never—or so I like to think, at least—have become a monk and set out on this precious path. He first appeared to me in my childhood, and here, at the end of my pilgrimage, he seems to have come back to me again. It's remarkable, fathers, teachers, that Alexey, who bears some resemblance to him in face, though not a strong one, seems to me so like him in spirit that many times I've mistaken him for that young man, my brother, mysteriously returned to me at the end of my pilgrimage, as a reminder and an inspiration. So much so that I've genuinely marveled at such a strange notion in myself. Do you hear this, Porfiry?" he said, turning to the novice attending him. "Many times I've seen on your face something like a look of hurt, that I love Alexey more than you. Now you know why that is, but I love you too, know that, and I've often grieved over your hurt feelings. I'd like to tell you, dear friends, about that young man, my brother, for there's been no presence in my life more precious, more significant, and more moving. My heart is full of tenderness, and at this moment I'm looking back over my whole life as though living through it all over again."

Here I must note that this last conversation of Father Zossima with the friends who visited him on the final day of his life has been partly preserved in writing. Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov wrote it down from memory, some time after his elder's death. But whether this was only the conversation that took place then, or whether he added notes from earlier conversations with his teacher, I can't say for certain. In his account, Father Zossima's talk runs on without interruption, as though he were telling his friends the story of his life straight through, though there's no doubt, from other accounts of it, that the conversation that evening was a general one. Though the guests didn't interrupt Father Zossima much, they did speak too, and perhaps even told stories of their own. Besides, Father Zossima couldn't have carried on an uninterrupted narrative, since at times he gasped for breath, his voice gave out, and he even lay down on his bed to rest, though he didn't fall asleep, and his visitors didn't leave their seats. Once or twice the conversation was broken up by Father Païssy reading from the Gospel. It's also worth noting that none of them supposed he'd die that very night, since that evening, after his deep sleep during the day, he seemed to have suddenly found new strength, which carried him through this long conversation. It was like a final surge of love that gave him remarkable energy—but only for a short while, since his life was cut short soon after.... But more on that later. I'll only add now that I've chosen to stick to the account given by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. It will be shorter and less exhausting, though of course, as I must repeat, Alyosha drew heavily on earlier conversations and folded them into it.
Notes on the Life of the Departed Priest and Monk, the Elder Zossima, Taken from His Own Words by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov.
BIOGRAPHICAL NOTES
(a) Father Zossima's Brother

Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a distant province in the north, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman by birth, but of no great standing or importance. He died when I was only two, and I don't remember him at all. He left my mother a small wooden house, and a modest fortune—not large, but enough to keep her and her children comfortable. There were two of us, my elder brother Markel and me. He was eight years older than I was, quick-tempered and irritable by nature, but kind-hearted and never sarcastic. He was remarkably quiet, especially at home with me, our mother, and the servants. He did well at school, but didn't get along with his schoolmates, though he never quarreled with them, or so my mother told me at least. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he became friends with a political exile who'd been banished from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and who lived a solitary life there. He was a fine scholar who'd distinguished himself in philosophy at the university. Something made him take a liking to Markel, and he used to invite him over. The young man spent whole evenings with him that winter, until the exile was summoned back to Petersburg to resume his post, at his own request, since he had powerful friends.

It was the start of Lent, and Markel refused to fast; he was rude about it and laughed at it. "That's all foolish nonsense, and there's no God," he said, horrifying my mother, the servants, and me as well. Because even though I was only nine, I too was shaken to hear such words. We had four servants, all serfs. I remember my mother selling one of the four, the cook Afimya, who was lame and elderly, for sixty paper roubles, and hiring a free servant in her place.

In the sixth week of Lent, my brother, who'd never been strong and had a tendency toward consumption, fell ill. He was tall but thin and delicate-looking, with a very pleasant face. I suppose he'd caught cold; in any case, the doctor who came soon whispered to my mother that it was galloping consumption, and that he wouldn't live through the spring. My mother began weeping, and, careful not to frighten my brother, she begged him to go to church, to confess and take the sacrament, since he could still get around. This made him angry, and he said something irreverent about the church. Still, he grew thoughtful; he guessed at once that he was seriously ill, and that that was why our mother was begging him to confess and take communion. In fact, he'd known for some time already that he was far from well, and a year before had coolly remarked at dinner to our mother and me, "My life among you won't be long—I may not live another year," which now seemed like a prophecy.

Three days passed, and Holy Week arrived. On Tuesday morning my brother began going to church. "I'm only doing this for your sake, mother, to please and comfort you," he said. My mother wept with joy and grief both. "His end must be near," she thought, "if there's such a change in him." But he wasn't able to keep going to church for long; he took to his bed, so he had to confess and take the sacrament at home.

It was a late Easter that year, and the days were bright, clear, and full of fragrance. I remember he used to cough all night and sleep badly, but in the morning he'd get dressed and try to sit up in an armchair. That's how I remember him sitting, sweet and gentle, smiling, his face bright and joyful despite his illness. A remarkable change had come over him; his whole spirit seemed transformed. The old nurse would come in and say, "Let me light the lamp before the icon, dear." And there had been a time when he wouldn't have allowed it, would have blown it out himself.
"Light it, light it, dear, I was wretched ever to stop you doing it. You're praying when you light the lamp, and I'm praying when I feel joy watching you. So we're praying to the same God."

Those words struck us as strange, and mother would go off to her room and weep, but when she came back in to him she'd wipe her eyes and put on a cheerful face. "Mother, don't cry, darling," he would say, "I have a long time yet to live, a long time yet to rejoice with you, and life is glad and joyful."
"Ah, dear boy, how can you talk of joy when you lie there feverish at night, coughing as if you'd tear yourself apart?"
"Don't cry, mother," he'd answer, "life is paradise, and we're all in paradise, but we refuse to see it; if we wanted to, we'd have heaven on earth by tomorrow."

Everyone marveled at his words—he spoke so strangely, so firmly; we were all moved and wept. Friends came to visit us. "My dear ones," he would say to them, "what have I done that you should love me so, how can you love someone like me, and how is it I didn't know, didn't appreciate it before?"

When the servants came in to see him, he'd say again and again, "Dear, good people, why are you doing so much for me, do I deserve to be waited on? If it were God's will that I should live, I'd wait on you myself, because everyone should wait on one another."
Mother shook her head listening to this. "My darling, it's your illness making you talk this way."

"Mother, darling," he'd say, "there have to be servants and masters, but if so, I'll be the servant of my servants, just as they are servants to me. And another thing, mother—every one of us has sinned against everyone else, and I more than anyone."

Mother actually smiled at that, smiled through her tears. "Why, how could you have sinned against everyone, more than everyone? Thieves and murderers have done that, but what sin have you committed, that you count yourself guiltier than anyone else?"

"Mother, little heart of mine," he said—he'd started using strange, tender phrases like that around this time—"little heart of mine, my joy, believe me, every person is truly responsible to everyone else for everyone else and for everything. I don't know how to explain it to you, but I feel it's true, painfully even. And how is it we went on living all that time, getting angry and not knowing?"
So each day he'd get up, growing sweeter and more joyful and more full of love. When the doctor, an old German named Eisenschmidt, came to see him, he'd ask, joking:
"Well, doctor, do I have another day left in this world?"
"You'll live many days yet," the doctor would answer, "months and years, too."

"Months and years!" he'd exclaim. "Why count the days? One day is enough for a man to know all of happiness. My dear ones, why do we quarrel, try to outdo each other, and hold grudges against one another? Let's go straight out into the garden, walk and play there, love and appreciate and kiss one another, and glorify life."
"Your son can't last much longer," the doctor told my mother as she walked him to the door. "The illness is affecting his brain."

The windows of his room looked out onto the garden, and ours was a shady garden, full of old trees that were just coming into bud. The first birds of spring flitted among the branches, chirping and singing at the windows. Watching them, admiring them, he suddenly began begging their forgiveness too: "Birds of heaven, happy birds, forgive me, for I've sinned against you too." None of us could make sense of that at the time, but he wept tears of joy over it. "Yes," he said, "there was such a glory of God all around me: birds, trees, meadows, sky; only I lived in shame and dishonored it all, and never noticed the beauty and the glory."
"You're taking too many sins on yourself," mother would say, weeping.

"Mother, darling, it's from joy that I'm crying, not from grief. I can't explain it to you, but I like humbling myself before them, because I don't know how to love them enough. If I've sinned against everyone, well, everyone forgives me too, and that's heaven. Am I not in heaven right now?"

And there was a great deal more that I don't remember. I remember going into his room once when no one else was there. It was a bright evening, the sun was setting, and the whole room was filled with light. He beckoned to me, and I went up to him. He put his hands on my shoulders and looked into my face tenderly, lovingly; he said nothing for a minute, just looked at me like that.
"Well," he said, "run along and play now, enjoy life for me too."

I went out then and ran off to play. And many times afterward, throughout my life, I remembered, even with tears, how he'd told me to enjoy life for him too. He said a great many other remarkable and beautiful things, though we didn't understand them at the time. He died in the third week after Easter. He was fully conscious, though he couldn't speak; right up to his last hour he didn't change. He looked happy, his eyes shone and sought us out, he smiled at us, beckoned to us. There was a good deal of talk about his death even around town. It affected me a great deal at the time, though not excessively, even though I cried plenty at his funeral. I was young then, a child, but a lasting impression, a hidden feeling from it all, stayed in my heart, ready to rise up and answer when the time came. And that's exactly what happened.
(b) On the Holy Scriptures in Father Zossima's Life

I was left alone with my mother. Her friends began urging her to send me to Petersburg, as other parents did. "You have only one son left now," they told her, "and you have a decent income, and you may be denying him a brilliant career if you keep him here." They suggested I be sent to Petersburg to the Cadet Corps, so that I might later join the Imperial Guard. My mother hesitated for a long time—it was dreadful to part with her only remaining child—but she finally made up her mind to it, not without many tears, believing she was acting for my happiness. She brought me to Petersburg and enrolled me in the Cadet Corps, and I never saw her again. For she too died three years later. She spent those three years mourning and grieving for both of us.

From the house of my childhood I've carried nothing but precious memories, since there are no memories more precious than those of early childhood in one's first home. And that's almost always true so long as there's any love and harmony in the family at all. In fact, precious memories can remain even from a bad home, if only the heart knows how to find what's precious in it. Among my memories of home, I count too my memories of the Bible, which, child that I was, I was eager to read at home. I had a book of scripture history back then with wonderful pictures, called A Hundred and Four Stories from the Old and New Testament, and it was from that book I learned to read. I still have it lying on my shelf; I keep it as a precious relic of the past. But even before I learned to read, I remember being moved to devotion for the first time at eight years old. My mother took me alone to Mass—I don't remember where my brother was at the time—on the Monday before Easter. It was a fine day, and even today I remember it as though I were seeing it now: how the incense rose from the censer and drifted gently upward, mingling overhead in the dome, in rising waves, with the sunlight pouring in through the small window. I was moved by the sight, and for the first time in my life I consciously took the seed of God's word into my heart. A young man came out into the middle of the church carrying a large book, so large that at the time I imagined he could barely carry it. He set it on the reading desk, opened it, and began to read, and suddenly, for the first time, I understood something read aloud in the house of God. In the land of Uz there lived a man, righteous and God-fearing, and he had great wealth—so many camels, so many sheep and asses—and his children feasted, and he loved them dearly and prayed for them. 'It may be that my sons have sinned in their feasting.' Then the devil came before the Lord along with the sons of God, and told the Lord that he had been roaming up and down the earth and under it. 'And have you considered my servant Job?' God asked him. And God boasted of him to the devil, pointing to his great and holy servant. And the devil laughed at God's words. 'Hand him over to me and You will see that Your servant will curse You to Your face.' And God handed over the righteous man he loved so much to the devil. And the devil struck down his children and his livestock and scattered his wealth, all at once, like a thunderbolt out of heaven. And Job tore his robe and fell to the ground and cried aloud, 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return to the earth; the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord, forever and ever.'

Fathers and teachers, forgive my tears now, for all my childhood rises up before me again, and I breathe now as I breathed then, with the chest of an eight-year-old child, and I feel now as I felt then—awe, and wonder, and gladness. The camels caught my imagination back then, and Satan, talking to God that way, and God handing over his servant to destruction, and his servant crying out, 'Blessed be Thy name, though Thou dost punish me,' and then the soft, sweet singing in the church, 'Let my prayer rise up before Thee,' and again the incense from the priest's censer, and the kneeling and the prayer. Ever since then—only yesterday I picked it up again—I've never been able to read that sacred story without tears. And how much greatness, mystery, and depth there is in it! Later I heard words of mockery and blame, proud words: 'How could God hand over the most beloved of His saints for the devil's amusement, take away his children, strike him with sores so foul he had to scrape the pus from them with a shard of pottery—and for no reason except to boast to the devil, "See what My saint can suffer for My sake"?' But the greatness of it lies exactly in this—that it's a mystery, that the fleeting earthly show and the eternal truth are brought together in it. In the face of earthly truth, the eternal truth is fulfilled. The Creator, just as on the first days of creation He closed each day with praise—'That is good, which I have made'—looks on Job and again praises His creation. And Job, praising the Lord, serves not only Him but all His creation, for generation after generation, forever and ever, since that was what he was made for. Good heavens, what a book that is, and what lessons are in it! What a book the Bible is, what a miracle, what strength it gives to man! It's like a cast taken of the world and of man and of human nature—everything is in it, a law for everything, for all the ages to come. And what mysteries are solved and revealed there! God raises Job up again, gives him wealth again. Many years pass, and he has other children, and loves them. But how could he love these new ones, when those first children are gone, lost to him forever? Remembering them, how could he be truly happy with the new ones, however dear they might be to him? But he could—he could. That's the great mystery of human life: that old grief passes, little by little, into quiet, tender joy. The gentle calm of old age takes the place of the restless blood of youth. I bless the rising sun every day, and, as before, my heart sings out to meet it, but now I love its setting even more, its long slanting rays, and the soft, tender, gentle memories that come with them—the dear images from the whole of my long, happy life—and over it all, the Divine Truth, softening, reconciling, forgiving! My life is ending, I know that well, but every day that's left to me I can feel how my earthly life is already touching a new, infinite, unknown life approaching, the nearness of which sets my soul trembling with rapture, my mind glowing, and my heart weeping with joy.

Friends and teachers, I've heard more than once, and lately one hears it more and more often, that priests, and village priests above all, complain on every side about their wretched income and their humiliating position. They say plainly, even in print—I've read it myself—that they're unable to teach the people the Scriptures because their means are so small, and that if Lutherans and heretics come and lead the flock astray, they let it happen because they have too little to live on. May the Lord increase the support that's so precious to them, for their complaint is a fair one too. But I say truly, if anyone's to blame in this matter, half the fault is ours. He may be short of time, he may truthfully say he's swamped the whole time with work and services, but still, not every moment—even he has an hour a week to spare to remember God. And he doesn't work every day of the year. Let him gather people around him once a week, some hour in the evening, even if it's only the children at first—the parents will hear of it, and they too will start coming. There's no need to build a hall for it—let him take them into his own cottage. They won't wreck the place, they'll only be there an hour. Let him open the book and start reading it, without grand words or arrogance, without condescension toward them, but gently and kindly, glad that he's reading to them and that they're listening closely, loving the words himself, pausing now and then only to explain words the peasants might not understand. Don't worry, they'll understand everything—the devout heart understands everything! Let him read to them about Abraham and Sarah, about Isaac and Rebecca, about how Jacob went to Laban and wrestled with the Lord in his dream and said, 'This place is holy'—and it will strike the devout mind of the peasant deeply. Let him read to them, especially to the children, how the brothers sold Joseph, the gentle boy, the dreamer and prophet, into slavery, and told their father a wild beast had devoured him, and showed him the boy's blood-stained clothes. Let him read them how the brothers later traveled to Egypt for grain, and how Joseph, by then a great ruler, unrecognized by them, tormented them, accused them, held onto his brother Benjamin, and did it all out of love: 'I love you, and loving you, I torment you.' For he remembered all his life how they had sold him to merchants in the burning desert by the well, and how, wringing his hands, he'd wept and begged his brothers not to sell him as a slave into a strange land. And how, seeing them again after many years, he loved them beyond measure, but harassed and tormented them out of that very love. In the end, unable to bear the suffering in his own heart, he left them, threw himself on his bed, and wept. Then, wiping away his tears, he went out to them, joyful, and told them, 'Brothers, I am your brother Joseph!' Let him go on to read how happy old Jacob was to learn his beloved son was still alive, and how he went to Egypt, leaving his own country behind, and died in a foreign land, leaving behind his great prophecy, which had lain hidden mysteriously in his meek and timid heart his whole life, that from his offspring, from Judah, the world's great hope would come—the Messiah and Savior.

Fathers and teachers, forgive me, and don't be angry, that like a little child I've been babbling on about things you've known for a long time, and could teach me a hundred times more skillfully than I could ever teach you. I only speak out of rapture, and forgive my tears, for I love the Bible. Let him weep too, the priest of God, and be sure that the hearts of his listeners will throb in response. Only the tiniest seed is needed—drop it into the heart of the peasant, and it won't die; it will live in his soul his whole life, hidden in the midst of his darkness and sin, like a bright spot, like a great reminder. And there's no need for much teaching or explaining—he'll understand it all easily, on his own. Do you suppose the peasants don't understand? Try reading them the touching story of the fair Esther and the proud Vashti, or the miraculous story of Jonah in the whale. And don't forget the parables of Our Lord either, choose especially from the Gospel of St. Luke—that's what I did—and then from the Acts of the Apostles the conversion of St. Paul, which you mustn't leave out under any circumstances, and from the Lives of the Saints, for instance, the life of Alexey, the man of God, and, greatest of all, the joyful martyr and God-seer, Mary of Egypt—and you'll reach their hearts with these simple stories. Give one hour a week to it, poor as you are, just one little hour. And you'll see for yourselves that our people are gracious and grateful, and will repay you a hundredfold. Remembering their priest's kindness and the moving words they've heard from him, they'll of their own accord help him in his fields and around his house, and will treat him with more respect than before—so it will even improve his worldly circumstances too. The thing is so simple that sometimes one's almost afraid to say it out loud, for fear of being laughed at, and yet how true it is! Someone who doesn't believe in God won't believe in God's people either. Whoever believes in God's people will come to see His holiness too, even if he hadn't believed in it before. Only the people, and their future spiritual power, will convert our atheists, who've torn themselves away from their native soil.
And what use are Christ's words, unless we set an example by them? The people are lost without the Word of God, for their souls thirst for the Word, and for everything that is good.

In my youth, long ago, nearly forty years back, I traveled all over Russia with Father Anfim, collecting funds for our monastery, and we spent one night on the bank of a great navigable river with some fishermen. A good-looking peasant lad, about eighteen, joined us; he had to hurry back the next morning to help tow a merchant's barge along the bank. I noticed him gazing straight ahead of him with clear, gentle eyes. It was a bright, warm, still July night; a cool mist rose off the broad river, we could hear the splash of a fish, the birds had gone quiet, everything was hushed and beautiful, everything praying to God. Only the two of us weren't asleep, the lad and I, and we talked about the beauty of this world of God's, and about its great mystery. Every blade of grass, every insect, ant, and golden bee, all know their path in some marvelous way, though they have no intelligence—they bear witness to the mystery of God and carry it out themselves, ceaselessly. I could see the dear lad's heart was moved. He told me he loved the forest and the forest birds. He was a bird-catcher, knew each one's call, could summon each bird by name. "I know nothing better than being in the forest," he said, "though everything is good."

"Truly," I answered him, "everything is good and beautiful, because everything is truth. Look," I said, "at the horse, that great creature so close to man; or the humble, thoughtful ox, which feeds him and labors for him; look at their faces, such gentleness, such devotion to man, who often beats them without mercy. What mildness, what trust, what beauty! It's touching to know there's no sin in them, because everything, everything except man, is sinless, and Christ was with them before He was with us."
"Why," the boy asked, "is Christ with them too?"

"It can't be otherwise," I said, "since the Word is for everyone. All creation, all creatures, every leaf, is striving toward the Word, singing glory to God, weeping to Christ, unknowingly fulfilling this through the mystery of their sinless life. Out there," I said, "in the forest wanders the terrible bear, fierce and menacing, and yet innocent even in that." And I told him how once a bear had come to a great saint sheltering in a tiny cell in the woods. And the great saint took pity on him, went up to him without fear, and gave him a piece of bread. "Go on now," he said, "Christ be with you," and the savage beast walked off meekly and obediently, doing no harm to anyone. And the lad was delighted that the bear had walked away without hurting the saint, and that Christ was with him too. "Ah," he said, "how good that is, how good and beautiful is everything God has made!" He sat there thinking, gently and sweetly. I could see he understood. And he slept beside me a light, sinless sleep. God bless the young! And I prayed for him as I drifted off to sleep myself. Lord, send peace and light to Your people!

title: II. The Duel
paragraphs: (c) Recollections of Father Zossima's Youth Before He Became a Monk. The Duel

I spent a long time, almost eight years, at the military cadet school in Petersburg, and amid the novelty of my surroundings there, many of my childhood impressions grew dimmer, though I forgot none of them. I picked up so many new habits and opinions that I turned into a cruel, absurd, almost savage creature. I did pick up a surface polish of courtesy and social manners, along with the French language.

But all of us, myself included, looked on the soldiers under our command as cattle. I was perhaps worse than the rest in that respect, since I was so much more impressionable than my companions. By the time we left the school as officers, we were ready to lay down our lives for the honor of the regiment, but not one of us had any real understanding of what honor actually meant, and if anyone had understood it, he'd have been the first to mock it. Drunkenness, debauchery, and devilry were things we practically took pride in. I don't mean to say we were bad by nature—all these young men were decent fellows—but they behaved badly, and I worst of all. What made it worse for me was that I'd come into my own money, and so I threw myself into a life of pleasure and plunged headlong into every recklessness of youth.

I loved reading, and yet, strange to say, the Bible was the one book I never opened during that time, though I always carried it around with me, never went anywhere without it; in truth I was keeping that book "for the day and the hour, for the month and the year," without even knowing it.

After four years of that life, I happened to be stationed in the town of K., where our regiment was posted at the time. We found the people there hospitable, well-off, and fond of entertaining. I was received warmly everywhere, being of a lively temperament and known to be well off, which always carries weight in the world. And then something happened that was the start of everything.

I became attached to a beautiful and intelligent young woman of noble and elevated character, the daughter of a much-respected family. They were well-to-do people of influence and standing. They always received me warmly and with friendship. I imagined the young lady looked on me with favor, and my heart caught fire at the thought.
