Later on I saw, and fully understood, that I probably wasn't even so passionately in love with her at all, but simply recognized the elevation of her mind and character, which I couldn't really have helped noticing. What kept me from proposing to her at the time, though, was my own selfishness—I was reluctant to give up the pleasures of my free, dissolute bachelor life in the prime of my youth, with my pockets full of money. Still, I did drop some hint of my feelings, though I put off any decisive step for a while. Then, all of a sudden, our regiment was sent off for two months to another district.

When I returned two months later, I found the young lady already married to a wealthy neighboring landowner, a very likable man, still young though older than I was, connected to the best society in Petersburg, which I was not, and excellently educated, which I also was not. I was so thrown by this unexpected turn of events that my mind was genuinely clouded. The worst part of it was that, as I learned then, the young landowner had already been engaged to her for a long while, and I had in fact met him many times at her house, but blinded by my own conceit, I'd noticed nothing at all. And this humiliated me in particular—almost everyone else had known about it, while I knew nothing. I was seized by a sudden, uncontrollable fury. Flushed with anger, I began recalling all the times I'd come close to declaring my love to her, and since she hadn't tried to stop me or warn me off, I concluded she must have been laughing at me the whole time. Later, of course, I thought it over and remembered that she'd been very far from laughing at me; on the contrary, she used to turn aside any attempt at courtship from me with a joke and change the subject; but at that moment I was incapable of thinking straight and was consumed with the desire for revenge. I'm struck, looking back, that this rage and thirst for revenge were deeply out of keeping with my own nature—being an easygoing sort, I found it hard to stay angry at anyone for long, so I had to work myself up into it artificially, and I ended up looking revolting and absurd.

I waited for my chance and managed to insult my "rival" in front of a large gathering. I insulted him over a completely unrelated matter, mocking his opinion on an important public event—it was the year 1826—and my jab was, so people said, clever and effective. Then I forced him to demand an explanation, and behaved so rudely that he accepted my challenge despite the enormous gap between us, since I was younger, of no standing, and inferior in rank. I learned afterward, as a fact, that jealousy on his side had also played a part in his accepting my challenge; he'd been rather jealous of me on account of his wife even before their marriage; he now imagined that if he let himself be insulted by me and declined my challenge, and if she heard of it, she might start to despise him and waver in her love for him. I soon found a second in a fellow officer, an ensign in our regiment. In those days, though dueling was severely punished, it was still something of a fashion among officers—that's how strong and deeply rooted a brutal prejudice can sometimes become.

It was the end of June, and our meeting was set for seven the next morning on the outskirts of town—and then something happened that, in truth, became the turning point of my life. That evening, coming home in a savage and brutal mood, I flew into a rage at my orderly Afanasy and struck him twice in the face with all my strength, so that his face was covered in blood. He hadn't been in my service long, and I'd struck him before, but never with such vicious cruelty. And believe me, though it's forty years ago now, I recall it with shame and pain even today. I went to bed and slept about three hours; when I woke, day was breaking. I got up—I had no wish to sleep any more—went to the window, opened it; it looked out onto the garden. I saw the sun rising; it was warm and lovely, the birds were singing.

"What does this mean?" I thought. "I feel something vile and shameful in my heart. Is it because I'm about to shed blood? No," I thought, "that's not what I feel. Could it be that I'm afraid of death, afraid of being killed? No, that's not it, that's not it at all."... And all at once I knew what it was: it was because I'd beaten Afanasy the evening before! It all rose up before me, played out again as though it were happening once more; he stood in front of me and I was striking him straight in the face while he held his arms rigidly at his sides, his head up, his eyes fixed on me as though standing at attention. He staggered with each blow and didn't even dare raise his hands to shield himself. That is what a man had been reduced to, and that was a man beating a fellow human being! What a crime! It was as if a sharp blade had run straight through me. I stood there as though struck dumb, while the sun shone, the leaves rejoiced, and the birds trilled out their praise of God.... I buried my face in my hands, fell onto my bed, and burst into a storm of tears. And then I remembered my brother Markel, and what he'd said on his deathbed to the servants: "My dear ones, why do you wait on me, why do you love me, am I worth your waiting on me?"

"Yes, am I worth it?" flashed through my mind. "After all, what am I worth, that another man, a fellow creature made in the image and likeness of God, should serve me?" For the first time in my life this question forced itself on me. He had said, "Mother, my little heart, truly we are each responsible to everyone for everything, only people don't know it. If they knew it, the world would become paradise at once."

"God, can that be false too?" I thought as I wept. "In truth, perhaps I'm more responsible than everyone else, for everything, a greater sinner than anyone else in the whole world." And all at once the whole truth appeared before me in its full light: what was I about to do? I was about to kill a good, intelligent, noble man, who'd done me no wrong, and by robbing his wife of happiness for the rest of her life, I'd be torturing and killing her too. I lay there on my bed with my face in the pillow, not caring how the time was passing. Suddenly my second, the ensign, came in with the pistols to fetch me.
"Ah," he said, "good thing you're already up, it's time we were off, come along!"
I didn't know what to do and hurried back and forth, undecided; still, we went out to the carriage.
"Wait here a moment," I said to him. "I'll be right back, I forgot my purse."
And I ran back alone, to Afanasy's little room.
"Afanasy," I said, "I struck you twice in the face yesterday, forgive me," I said.
He flinched as if frightened, and looked at me; and I saw that wasn't enough, and right there, in my full officer's uniform, I dropped to his feet and bowed my head to the ground.
"Forgive me," I said.
Then he was utterly stunned.
"Your honor... sir, what are you doing? Am I worth it?"
And he burst into tears, just as I had before, hid his face in his hands, turned toward the window, and shook all over with sobbing. I rushed out to my comrade and jumped into the carriage.
"Ready," I cried. "Have you ever seen a conqueror?" I asked him. "Here's one standing before you."
I was in ecstasy, laughing and talking the whole way, I don't remember about what.
He looked at me. "Well, brother, you're a plucky fellow, you'll uphold the honor of the uniform, I can see that."

So we reached the spot and found them already waiting for us. We were placed twelve paces apart; he had the first shot. I stood cheerfully, looking him straight in the face; I didn't so much as flinch, I looked at him almost lovingly, because I knew what I was going to do. His shot only grazed my cheek and ear.
"Thank God," I cried, "no man has been killed," and I snatched up my pistol, turned around, and flung it far off into the wood. "That's the place for you," I cried.
I turned to my opponent.

"Forgive me, young fool that I am, sir," I said, "for my unprovoked insult to you and for forcing you to fire at me. I'm ten times worse than you, maybe more. Tell that to whoever it is you hold dearest in the world."
I'd barely gotten the words out before all three of them shouted at me at once.
"Upon my word," cried my opponent, annoyed, "if you didn't want to fight, why didn't you just leave me alone?"
"Yesterday I was a fool, today I know better," I answered cheerfully.
"As for yesterday, I believe you, but as for today, it's hard to agree with your view," he said.
"Bravo," I cried, clapping my hands. "I agree with you there too. I've earned that!"
"Will you fire, sir, or not?"
"No, I won't," I said; "if you like, fire at me again, but it would be better if you didn't."
The seconds, mine especially, were shouting too: "How can you disgrace the regiment like this, standing in front of your opponent begging his forgiveness! If I'd only known this beforehand!"
I stood facing them all, not laughing now.
"Gentlemen," I said, "is it really such a wonder these days to find a man who can repent of his stupidity and publicly admit he was wrong?"
"But not in a duel," my second cried again.

"That's exactly what's strange about it," I said. "Because I should have owned up to my fault the moment I got here, before he'd fired a shot, before leading him into a grave and deadly sin; but we've made our lives so absurd that acting that way would have been almost impossible, since only after I'd faced his shot at twelve paces could my words carry any real weight for him—if I'd spoken before, he'd have said, 'He's a coward, the sight of the pistols has scared him, no point listening to him.' Gentlemen," I cried suddenly, speaking straight from the heart, "look around you at the gifts of God—the clear sky, the pure air, the tender grass, the birds; nature is beautiful and without sin, and only we, only we, are sinful and foolish, and we fail to understand that life is heaven, because all we need is to understand that, and it will be fulfilled at once, in all its beauty—we'll embrace each other and weep."
I would have said more, but I couldn't; my voice broke with the sweetness and youthful gladness of it, and there was a happiness in my heart such as I'd never known before in my life.
"All this is rational and edifying," said my opponent, "and in any case you're an original sort of person."
"You may laugh," I said to him, laughing myself, "but afterward you'll come to approve of me."
"Oh, I'm ready to approve of you right now," he said; "will you shake hands? because I believe you're genuinely sincere."
"No," I said, "not now—later, once I've grown more worthy and earned your respect, then shake hands, and you'll do well to."
We went home, my second scolding me the whole way while I kept kissing him. All my comrades heard of the affair right away and gathered that same day to pass judgment on me.
"He's disgraced the uniform," they said; "let him resign his commission."
Some stood up for me: "He faced the shot," they said.
"Yes, but he was afraid of his own shot and begged forgiveness."

"If he'd been afraid of being shot, he'd have fired his own pistol first, before asking forgiveness, instead of flinging it loaded into the forest. No, there's something else going on here, something original."

I enjoyed listening to them and watching them talk. "My dear friends and comrades," I said, "don't worry about my resigning my commission, because I've already done it. I sent in my papers this morning, and as soon as my discharge comes through, I'm going into a monastery—that's the reason I'm leaving the regiment."
When I said this, every one of them burst out laughing.
"You should have told us that first, that explains everything, you can't judge a monk."

They laughed and couldn't stop, and not scornfully, but warmly and cheerfully. They all became friendly toward me at once, even those who'd been harshest in condemning me, and for the whole following month, until my discharge came through, they couldn't do enough for me. "Ah, you monk," they'd say. And everyone said something kind to me, they began trying to talk me out of it, even pitying me: "What are you doing to yourself?"
"No," others would say, "he's a brave fellow, he faced fire and could have fired his own pistol too, but he had a dream the night before that he'd become a monk, that's why he did it."

It was the same in the town's society. Up till then I'd been well received, but hadn't been the object of any special attention, and now everyone suddenly wanted to know me and invited me everywhere; they laughed at me, but they loved me. I should mention that although everyone spoke openly about our duel, the authorities took no notice of it, because my opponent was a close relative of our general, and since there'd been no bloodshed and no serious consequences, and since I'd resigned my commission, they treated it as a joke. And from then on I began speaking my mind openly and fearlessly, regardless of the laughter, since it was always good-natured laughter, never spiteful. These conversations mostly happened in the evenings, in the company of ladies; women in particular liked listening to me then, and they'd make the men listen too.
"But how can I possibly be responsible for everyone?" people would laugh right in my face. "Can I, for instance, be responsible for you?"

"You may well not know it," I'd answer, "since the whole world has long been running along a different track, since we treat the most bare-faced lies as truth and demand the same lies from others. Here I've acted sincerely, for once in my life, and, well, you all look at me as though I were a madman. Even though you're friendly toward me, still, you see, all of you laugh at me."

"But how can we help being friendly to you?" said my hostess, laughing. The room was full of people. All of a sudden the young lady rose—the one on whose account the duel had been fought, and whom I'd only recently meant to make my future wife. I hadn't even noticed her come into the room. She stood up, came over to me, and held out her hand.
"Let me tell you," she said, "that I'm the first one not to laugh at you—on the contrary, I thank you with tears in my eyes, and I want to express my respect for what you did."

Her husband came up too, and then everyone else gathered around and nearly kissed me. My heart was filled with joy, but my attention was caught in particular by a middle-aged man who came up with the others. I already knew his name, but had never been introduced to him nor exchanged a single word with him before that evening.
(d) The Mysterious Visitor

He'd long held a post in the town; he was in a prominent position, respected by all, wealthy, and known for his charitable works. He gave generously to the almshouse and the orphanage; he was very charitable in secret too, a fact that only came to light after his death. He was a man of about fifty, almost stern in appearance and not one for much conversation. He'd been married about ten years, and his wife, who was still young, had borne him three children. Well, I was sitting alone in my room the following evening when my door suddenly opened and this gentleman walked in.

I should mention, by the way, that I was no longer living in my old quarters. As soon as I'd resigned my commission, I'd taken rooms with an elderly lady, the widow of a government clerk. My landlady's servant waited on me, since I'd moved into her rooms simply because, on returning from the duel, I'd sent Afanasy back to the regiment—I was too ashamed to look him in the face after our last conversation. That's how prone a man of the world is to feel ashamed of even his own righteous actions.

"I have," said my visitor, "listened to you speak in various houses over the last few days with great interest, and I finally wanted to make your personal acquaintance, so as to speak with you more closely. Would you, dear sir, grant me that favor?"

"I would, with the greatest pleasure, and I'll consider it an honor." I said this, though I felt almost uneasy, so strongly had this man's appearance affected me from the very first moment. Because although others had listened to me with interest and attention, no one had ever come to me before with such a serious, stern, and concentrated expression. And now he'd come to see me in my own rooms. He sat down.
"You're, I see, a man of considerable strength of character," he said, "since you dared to serve the truth, even when doing so risked earning you the contempt of everyone."
"Your praise is perhaps a bit much," I replied.

"No, it's not too much," he answered; "believe me, that kind of action is far harder than you think. That's what impressed me, and it's the only reason I've come to see you," he went on. "Tell me, please—if you're not offended by what may be improper curiosity on my part—what exactly were your feelings, if you can recall them, at the moment you decided to ask forgiveness at the duel. Don't think my question is idle; on the contrary, I have a secret motive of my own for asking it, which I may explain to you later, if it's God's will that we grow more closely acquainted."

The whole time he was speaking, I looked him straight in the face, and all at once I felt complete trust in him, along with great curiosity of my own, since I sensed there was some strange secret in his soul.

"You're asking what exactly I felt at the moment I asked my opponent's forgiveness," I answered, "but I'd better tell you from the beginning, something I haven't told anyone else yet." And I described everything that had passed between Afanasy and me, and how I'd bowed to the ground at his feet. "You can see for yourself from that," I concluded, "that by the time of the duel it was easier for me, because I'd already made a start at home, and once I'd set out on that road, going further along it wasn't hard at all—it became a source of joy and happiness instead."
I liked the way he looked at me as he listened. "All of this," he said, "is extremely interesting. I'll come and see you again, and again."

And from that point on he came to see me almost every evening. And we'd have grown even closer friends if only he'd ever talked about himself. But about himself he hardly ever said a word, though he kept constantly asking about me. Despite that, I grew very fond of him and spoke with complete frankness about all my feelings; "for," I thought, "what do I need to know his secrets for, when I can already see he's a good man without that? Besides, serious as he is, and older than me, he still comes to see a youngster like me and treats me as his equal." And I learned a great deal of value from him, for he was a man of lofty mind.

"That life is heaven," he said to me suddenly, "I've long been thinking about that"; and then all at once he added, "In fact I think of nothing else." He looked at me and smiled. "I'm even more convinced of it than you are, I'll tell you why later."
I listened to him and thought he clearly wanted to tell me something.
"Heaven," he went on, "lies hidden within all of us—it lies hidden in me right now, and if I will it, it will be revealed to me tomorrow, and for all time."
I looked at him; he was speaking with great feeling, gazing at me mysteriously, as though questioning me.

"And that we're all responsible to everyone for everything, apart from our own individual sins—you were quite right to think that, and it's remarkable that you were able to grasp its full significance all at once. And in truth, as soon as people understand that, the Kingdom of Heaven will no longer be a dream to them, but a living reality."
"And when," I cried out to him bitterly, "when will that come to pass? And will it ever come to pass at all? Isn't it simply a dream of ours?"

"What, you don't believe it?" he said. "You preach it and don't believe it yourself. Believe me, this dream, as you call it, will come to pass, without a doubt; it will come, but not yet, because every process has its own law. It's a spiritual, psychological process. To transform the world, to remake it from scratch, people must change course psychologically. Until you've become, really and truly, in actual fact, a brother to everyone, brotherhood will never come to pass. No scientific teaching, no kind of shared interest, will ever teach people to divide property and privilege with equal regard for everyone. Everyone will think his own share too small, and they'll always be envying, complaining about, and attacking one another. You ask when it will come to pass; it will come to pass, but first we have to pass through a period of isolation."
"What do you mean by isolation?" I asked him.

"Why, the isolation that's everywhere now, above all in our age—it hasn't fully developed yet, hasn't reached its limit. Because everyone strives to keep his own individuality as separate as possible, wants to secure the fullest possible life for himself; but meanwhile all his efforts end not in fullness of life, but in self-destruction, since instead of self-realization he ends up arriving at complete solitude. All mankind in our age has splintered into units, each keeping to itself, each in its own groove; each person holds himself apart, hides himself and hides what he has from the rest, and ends up repelling others and being repelled by them. He piles up riches on his own and thinks, 'How strong I am now, how secure,' and in his madness he fails to understand that the more he piles up, the deeper he sinks into self-destructive helplessness. Because he's accustomed to relying on himself alone and cutting himself off from the whole; he's trained himself not to believe in the help of others, in people, in humanity, and trembles only for fear of losing his money and the privileges he's won for himself. Everywhere these days, in their mockery, people have stopped understanding that true security is found in social solidarity, not in isolated individual effort. But this terrible individualism must inevitably come to an end, and all at once everyone will understand how unnaturally cut off they've been from one another. It will be the spirit of the age, and people will marvel that they sat so long in darkness without seeing the light. And then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in the heavens.... But until then, we have to keep the banner flying. Sometimes, even if he has to do it alone, and his behavior looks crazy, a man must set an example, and so draw other souls out of their isolation, and spur them toward some act of brotherly love, so that the great idea doesn't die."

Our evenings, one after another, were spent in talk like this, stirring and heartfelt. I gave up society and visited my neighbors far less often. Besides, my popularity had somewhat faded. I say this not as a complaint, since they still loved me and treated me good-humoredly, but there's no denying that fashion is a great power in society. I began to regard my mysterious visitor with real admiration, for besides enjoying his intelligence, I started to sense that he was brooding over some plan in his heart, perhaps preparing himself for some great act. Perhaps he liked that I showed no curiosity about his secret, didn't try to uncover it through direct questions or hints. But at last I noticed that he seemed to be showing signs of wanting to tell me something. This became quite evident, in fact, about a month after he'd first begun visiting me.
"Do you know," he said to me once, "that people in town are very curious about the two of us and wonder why I come to see you so often. But let them wonder, since soon everything will be explained."

Sometimes an extraordinary agitation would come over him, and almost always on those occasions he'd get up and leave. Sometimes he'd fix a long, piercing look on me, and I'd think, "He's about to say something now." But he'd suddenly start talking about something ordinary and familiar instead. He also often complained of headaches.
One day, quite unexpectedly, after he'd been talking with great intensity for a long while, I suddenly saw him go pale, his face working convulsively, while he stared fixedly at me.
"What's the matter?" I said; "do you feel ill?"—he'd just been complaining of a headache.
"I... do you know... I murdered someone."
He said this and smiled, his face white as chalk. "Why is he smiling?" The thought flashed through my mind before I registered anything else. I too went pale.
"What are you saying?" I cried.
"You see," he said, with a pale smile, "how much it's cost me to say that first word. Now that I've said it, I feel I've taken the first step and I'll go on."

For a long while I couldn't believe him, and I didn't believe him at the time, not until he'd come to see me three days running and told me the whole story. I thought he was mad, but ended up convinced, to my great grief and astonishment. His crime was a great and terrible one.

Fourteen years earlier, he'd murdered the widow of a landowner, a wealthy and beautiful young woman who had a house in our town. He'd fallen passionately in love with her, declared his feelings, and tried to convince her to marry him. But she'd already given her heart to another man, an officer of noble birth and high rank in the service, who was at that time away at the front, though she expected him back soon. She turned down his proposal and asked him not to come see her anymore. After he'd stopped visiting her, he made use of his knowledge of the house to slip in at night through the garden and across the roof, at great risk of being discovered. But, as often happens, a crime carried out with extraordinary boldness succeeds more often than others.

Entering the attic through the skylight, he made his way down the ladder, knowing that the door at the bottom was sometimes, through the servants' carelessness, left unlocked. He hoped to find it so, and so it was. He made his way in the dark to her bedroom, where a light was burning. As though by design, both her maids had gone off to a birthday party on the same street, without asking permission. The other servants slept in the servants' quarters or in the kitchen downstairs. His passion flared up at the sight of her sleeping, and then vindictive, jealous rage took hold of his heart, and like a drunken man, beside himself, he drove a knife into her heart, so that she didn't even cry out. Then, with devilish, criminal cunning, he arranged things so suspicion would fall on the servants. He stooped so low as to take her purse, to open her chest with the keys from under her pillow, and to take some things from it, doing it all the way an ignorant servant might have done, leaving valuable papers behind and taking only money. He took some of the larger gold pieces but left smaller items worth ten times as much. He also took a few things for himself, as keepsakes, but more on that later. Having done this dreadful deed, he went back the way he'd come.

Neither the next day, when the alarm was raised, nor at any point afterward in his life, did anyone dream of suspecting him as the criminal. No one, in fact, knew of his love for her, since he'd always been reserved and quiet, and had no friend he'd ever opened his heart to. He was regarded simply as an acquaintance of the murdered woman, and not a particularly close one, since he hadn't even visited her in the previous fortnight. A serf of hers named Pyotr was suspected at once, and every circumstance seemed to confirm it. The man knew—indeed his mistress hadn't concealed the fact—that, having to send one of her serfs off as a military recruit, she'd decided to send him, since he had no family and his conduct had been unsatisfactory. People had heard him drunkenly threatening to kill her in a tavern. Two days before her death, he'd run off, and no one knew where he'd been staying in town. The day after the murder he was found on the road out of town, dead drunk, with a knife in his pocket, his right hand stained with blood. He claimed his nose had been bleeding, but no one believed him. The maids admitted they'd gone to a party and that the street door had been left open until they got back. And a whole string of similar details came to light, casting suspicion on the innocent servant.

They arrested him, and he was tried for the murder; but a week after his arrest, the prisoner fell ill with a fever and died unconscious in the hospital. There the matter ended, and the judges, the authorities, and everyone in town remained convinced that the crime had been committed by no one but the servant who'd died in the hospital. And after that, the punishment began.

My mysterious visitor, my friend by now, told me that at first he wasn't troubled in the least by pangs of conscience. He was miserable for a long time, but not for that reason—only from regret that he'd killed the woman he loved, that she was gone, that in killing her he'd killed his own love as well, while the fire of passion still burned in his veins. But of the innocent blood he'd shed, of the murder of a fellow human being, he scarcely thought at all. The thought that his victim might have become another man's wife was unbearable to him, and so, for a long time, his conscience remained convinced he couldn't have acted otherwise.

At first he was troubled by the servant's arrest, but the man's illness and death soon set his mind at ease, since the death was apparently—so he reasoned to himself at the time—not the result of the arrest or fright, but of a chill the man had caught the day he ran off, when he'd lain all night dead drunk on the damp ground. The theft of the money and other items troubled him little, since he reasoned that the theft hadn't been committed for gain but to divert suspicion. The sum stolen was small, and shortly afterward he donated the whole amount, and far more besides, toward funding an almshouse in town. He did this deliberately to ease his conscience about the theft, and it's a remarkable fact that for a long time he genuinely was at peace—he told me this himself. He then threw himself into a period of intense activity in the service, volunteering for a difficult and demanding assignment that occupied him for two years, and being a strong-willed man, he almost forgot the past. Whenever it came back to him, he tried not to think of it at all. He also became active in philanthropy, founded and helped maintain a number of institutions in town, did a good deal in both capitals, and was elected a member of philanthropic societies in both Moscow and Petersburg.

At last, though, he began brooding over the past, and the strain of it became too much for him. Then he was drawn to a fine, intelligent girl, and soon after married her, hoping marriage would dispel his lonely depression, and that by starting a new life and conscientiously doing his duty by his wife and children, he'd escape the old memories entirely. But exactly the opposite of what he expected happened. He began, even in the first month of his marriage, to be continually gnawed at by the thought, "My wife loves me—but what if she knew?" When she first told him she'd soon bear him a child, he was troubled. "I'm giving life—but I've taken a life." Children came. "How dare I love them, teach them, raise them, how can I speak to them of virtue? I've shed blood." They were wonderful children, he longed to hold them; "and I can't look at their innocent, open faces, I'm unworthy."

At last he began to be bitterly and ominously haunted by the blood of his murdered victim, by the young life he'd destroyed, by blood crying out for vengeance. He began having terrible dreams. But being a man of fortitude, he bore his suffering a long time, thinking, "I'll atone for everything through this secret agony." But that hope, too, proved empty; the longer it went on, the more intense his suffering grew.

He was respected in society for his active charity, though everyone was somewhat awed by his stern, gloomy character. But the more he was respected, the more unbearable it became for him. He confessed to me that he'd thought of killing himself. But he began to be haunted by another idea instead—one he'd at first considered impossible, unthinkable, though in the end it took such a hold on his heart that he couldn't shake it off. He dreamed of standing up, going out, and confessing before all men that he'd committed murder. For three years this dream pursued him, haunting him in different forms. At last he came to believe with his whole heart that if he confessed his crime, he'd heal his soul and find peace forever. But this belief filled his heart with terror, because how could he carry it out? And then came what happened at my duel.
"Watching you, I made up my mind."
I looked at him.
"Is it possible," I cried, clasping my hands, "that such a trivial incident could give rise to such a resolution in you?"

"My resolution has been growing for the last three years," he answered, "and your story only put the finishing touch on it. Watching you, I reproached myself, and envied you." He said this to me almost sullenly.
"But no one will believe you," I pointed out; "it happened fourteen years ago."
"I have proof, solid proof. I'll show it."
Then I cried and kissed him.

"Tell me one thing, just one thing," he said, as though it all depended on me, "my wife, my children! My wife may die of grief, and though my children won't lose their rank or their property, they'll be a convict's children, forever! And what a memory, what a memory of me I'll leave in their hearts!"
I said nothing.
"And to part from them, to leave them forever? It's forever, you understand, forever!"
I sat there in silence, saying a silent prayer. At last I got up, feeling afraid.
"Well?" He looked at me.
"Go," I said. "Confess. Everything passes away, only the truth remains. Your children will understand, once they're grown, the nobility of your decision."

He left me that time as though his mind was made up. And yet for more than two weeks afterward he came to see me every evening, still preparing himself, still unable to bring himself to the point. He made my heart ache. Some days he'd arrive determined and say fervently:

"I know it will be heaven for me, heaven, the instant I confess. Fourteen years I've been in hell. I want to suffer. I'll accept my punishment and begin to live. You can go through the world doing wrong, but there's no turning back. Now I dare not love my neighbor, not even my own children. Good God, my children will understand, perhaps, what my punishment cost me, and won't condemn me! God isn't found in strength, but in truth."
"Everyone will understand your sacrifice," I told him, "if not at once, then later; because you've served the truth, the higher truth, not an earthly one."
And he'd leave seeming comforted, but the next day he'd come again, bitter, pale, sarcastic.

"Every time I come to you, you look at me so inquisitively, as if to say, 'He still hasn't confessed!' Wait a bit, don't despise me too much. It's not such an easy thing to do as you might think. Perhaps I won't do it at all. You won't go and inform on me, will you?"
And far from looking at him with any improper curiosity, I was afraid to even look at him at all. I was quite ill with anxiety, and my heart was full of unshed tears. I couldn't sleep at night.

"I've just come from my wife," he went on. "Do you understand what the word 'wife' means? As I left, the children called after me, 'Good-bye, father, hurry back to read The Children's Magazine with us.' No, you don't understand that! No one grows wise from another man's suffering."

His eyes were glittering, his lips twitching. Suddenly he struck the table with his fist so hard that everything on it jumped—it was the first time he'd ever done such a thing, he was such a mild man.

"But do I have to?" he exclaimed. "Must I? No one's been convicted, no one's been sent to Siberia in my place, the man died of fever. And I've already been punished by my own suffering for the blood I shed. And they won't believe me, they won't believe my proof. Do I need to confess, do I? I'm willing to go on suffering my whole life for the blood I've shed, if only my wife and children can be spared. Would it be just to ruin them along with me? Aren't we making a mistake here? What's the right thing to do in this case? And will people even recognize it, appreciate it, respect it?"

"Good Lord!" I thought to myself, "he's thinking about other people's respect at a moment like this!" And I felt so sorry for him then that I believe I'd have shared his fate if it could have comforted him. I could see he was beside himself. I was appalled, understanding with my heart as much as my mind what a decision like that meant.
"Decide my fate!" he cried out again.

"Go and confess," I whispered to him. My voice failed me, but I whispered it firmly. I picked up the New Testament from the table, the Russian translation, and showed him the Gospel of John, chapter twelve, verse twenty-four:
"Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit."
I'd just been reading that verse when he came in. He read it.

"That's true," he said, but he smiled bitterly. "It's terrible, the things you find in those books," he said, after a pause. "Easy enough to thrust them on someone. And who wrote them? Could men really have written them?"
"The Holy Spirit wrote them," I said.
"Easy for you to say," he smiled again, this time almost with hatred.
I picked up the book again, opened it to another place, and showed him the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter ten, verse thirty-one. He read:
"It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God."
He read it and simply flung the book down. He was trembling all over.

"An awful passage," he said. "No denying you've picked out the right ones." He rose from his chair. "Well!" he said, "good-bye, perhaps I won't come again... we'll meet in heaven. So I've been for fourteen years 'in the hands of the living God'—that's how one must think of those fourteen years. Tomorrow I'll beg those hands to let me go."
I wanted to take him in my arms and kiss him, but I didn't dare—his face was twisted and dark. He left.

"Good God," I thought, "what has he gone off to face!" I fell to my knees before the icon and wept for him before the Holy Mother of God, our swift defender and helper. I prayed in tears for half an hour, and it was late, around midnight. Suddenly I saw the door open, and he came in again. I was startled.
"Where have you been?" I asked him.
"I think," he said, "I forgot something... my handkerchief, I think.... Well, even if I haven't forgotten anything, let me stay a little while."
He sat down. I stood over him.
"You sit down too," he said.
I sat down. We sat in silence for two minutes; he looked at me intently and suddenly smiled—I remember that—then he got up, embraced me warmly, and kissed me.
"Remember," he said, "how I came to you a second time. Do you hear me, remember it!"
And he went out.
"Tomorrow," I thought.

And so it was. I hadn't known that evening that the next day was his birthday. I hadn't been out for the last few days, so I'd had no chance to hear it from anyone. On that day he always held a big gathering, and everyone in town went. This time was no different. After dinner he walked into the middle of the room, a paper in his hand—a formal declaration addressed to the head of his department, who was present. He read this declaration aloud to the whole assembly. It contained a full account of the crime, in every detail.
"I have cut myself off from men as a monster. God has visited me," he said in closing. "I want to suffer for my sin!"

Then he brought out and laid on the table all the things he'd kept for fourteen years, things he believed would prove his crime—the jewels belonging to the murdered woman that he'd stolen to divert suspicion, a cross and a locket taken from her neck, with a portrait of her fiancé inside the locket, her notebook, and two letters: one from her fiancé, telling her he'd soon be with her, and her unfinished reply, left on the table to be sent off the next day. He'd carried off these two letters—for what reason? Why had he kept them for fourteen years afterward instead of destroying them as evidence against himself?

And here's what happened: everyone was astonished and horrified, everyone refused to believe it and assumed he'd lost his mind, though all listened with intense curiosity. A few days later it was fully agreed, in every household in town, that the poor man was insane. The legal authorities couldn't refuse to take up the case, but they too dropped it. Though the jewelry and letters gave them pause, they decided that even if they turned out to be genuine, no charge could be based on those alone. Besides, she might have given him those things as a friend, or asked him to hold onto them for her. I heard afterward, though, that the authenticity of the items was confirmed by the friends and relatives of the murdered woman, and that there was no doubt about them. And yet nothing was ever to come of it, after all.

Five days later, everyone had heard that he was ill and that his life was in danger. I can't say exactly what the illness was; people said it was a heart condition. But it became known that the doctors had been persuaded by his wife to examine his mental state as well, and they'd concluded it was a case of insanity. I gave nothing away, though people rushed to question me about it. But when I wanted to visit him, I was for a long time forbidden to, above all by his wife.

"It's you who caused his illness," she told me; "he was always gloomy, but over the past year people noticed he'd grown strangely agitated and did odd things, and now you've been the ruin of him. Your preaching has brought him to this—he's been with you constantly this past month."

Indeed, not only his wife but the whole town turned against me and blamed me. "It's all your doing," they said. I kept silent, and in truth rejoiced in my heart, because I saw plainly God's mercy toward the man who'd turned against himself and punished himself. I couldn't believe he was insane.

They let me see him at last—he'd insisted on saying good-bye to me. I went in to him and saw at once that not only his days but his hours were numbered. He was weak, yellow-skinned, his hands trembled, he gasped for breath, but his face was full of tender, joyful feeling.
"It is done!" he said. "I've long been longing to see you, why didn't you come?"
I didn't tell him they'd refused to let me see him.

"God has had mercy on me and is calling me to Himself. I know I'm dying, but I feel joy and peace for the first time in so many years. There's been heaven in my heart from the moment I did what I had to do. Now I dare to love my children, to kiss them. Neither my wife, nor the judges, nor anyone has believed it. My children will never believe it either. I see God's mercy toward them in that. I'll die, and my name will stay unstained for them. And now I feel God near, my heart rejoices as if in Heaven... I've done my duty."
He couldn't speak any more, gasping for breath, pressing my hand warmly, gazing at me fervently. We didn't talk for long, his wife kept looking in on us. But he had time to whisper to me:
"Do you remember how I came back to you that second time, at midnight? I told you to remember it. Do you know what I came back for? I came to kill you!"
I flinched.

"I walked out from your rooms that night into the darkness, wandered the streets, wrestling with myself. And suddenly I hated you so much I could barely stand it. Now, I thought, he's the only thing binding me, and he's my judge. I can't refuse to face my punishment tomorrow, since he knows everything. It wasn't that I was afraid you'd betray me—I never even thought of that—but I thought, 'How can I face him if I don't confess?' And even if you'd been at the other end of the earth, but still alive, it would have made no difference—the thought that you were alive, knowing everything, sitting in judgment of me, was unbearable. I hated you as if you were the cause, as if you were to blame for everything. I came back to you then, remembering you had a dagger lying on your table. I sat down and asked you to sit too, and for a whole minute I sat there thinking it over. If I'd killed you, I'd have been ruined by that murder even without ever confessing the first one. But I wasn't thinking about that at all, didn't want to think about it in that moment. I only hated you and longed to take my revenge on you for everything. The Lord defeated the devil in my heart. But let me tell you, you were never closer to death."

A week later he died. The whole town followed him to the grave. The chief priest gave a speech full of feeling. Everyone lamented the terrible illness that had cut short his days. But the whole town turned against me after the funeral, and some people even refused to see me. Some, at first only a few, and later more, did in fact begin to believe the truth of his story, and they came to me and questioned me eagerly and with great interest, because people love to see the downfall and disgrace of a righteous man. But I held my tongue, and very shortly afterward left the town, and five months later, by God's grace, I entered upon the safe and blessed path, praising the unseen hand that had guided me to it so clearly. And to this day I remember in my prayers the servant of God, Mihail, who suffered so greatly.

title: III. Conversations And Exhortations Of Father Zossima
paragraphs: (e) The Russian Monk and His Possible Significance

Fathers and teachers, what is a monk? In educated circles nowadays, some pronounce the word with a sneer, others use it as an insult, and this contempt for the monk keeps growing. It's true, alas, it's true, that there are many sluggards, gluttons, profligates, and shameless beggars among monks. Educated people point to them: "You're idlers, useless to society, you live off the labor of others, you're shameless beggars." And yet how many meek and humble monks there are, yearning for solitude and fervent prayer in peace! These are noticed less, or passed over in silence. And how surprised people would be if I told them that it's from these meek monks, yearning for solitary prayer, that Russia's salvation may come once again! For they are, in truth, being made ready in peace and quiet "for the day and the hour, the month and the year." Meanwhile, in their solitude, they preserve the image of Christ, fair and undefiled, in the purity of God's truth, handed down from the days of the early Fathers, the Apostles, and the martyrs. And when the time comes, they'll hold it up before the world's faltering creeds. That's a great thought. That star will rise out of the East.

That's my view of the monk—is it wrong? Is it too proud a claim? Look at worldly people, and all those who set themselves above God's people—hasn't God's image and His truth been distorted in them? They have science; but in science there's nothing but what falls within the reach of the senses. The spiritual world, the higher part of man's being, is rejected outright, dismissed almost triumphantly, even with hatred. The world has proclaimed the reign of freedom, especially lately, but what do we actually see in this freedom of theirs? Nothing but slavery and self-destruction! Because the world says:

"You have desires, so satisfy them, for you have the same rights as the richest and most powerful. Don't be afraid to satisfy them—multiply them, even." That's the modern doctrine of the world. That's what they call freedom. And what comes of this right to multiply one's desires? In the rich, isolation and spiritual suicide; in the poor, envy and murder; because they've been granted rights, but never shown the means to satisfy their wants. They claim the world is growing more and more united, more and more bound together in brotherly community, as it conquers distance and sends thoughts flying through the air.

Alas, put no faith in such a bond. Treating freedom as the multiplication and quick satisfaction of desires, people distort their own nature, since it breeds in them countless senseless, foolish desires, habits, and absurd fancies. They live only for mutual envy, for luxury and display. Having dinners, visits, carriages, rank, and slaves to wait on you is treated as a necessity, one for which life, honor, and human feeling get sacrificed, and people even kill themselves if they can't satisfy it. We see the same thing among those who aren't rich, while the poor drown their unsatisfied wants and their envy in drink. But soon they'll be drinking blood instead of wine—they're being led toward it. I ask you, is such a man free? I once knew a "champion of freedom" who told me himself that when he was denied tobacco in prison, he was so miserable at the deprivation that he nearly betrayed his own cause just to get tobacco again! And a man like that says, "I'm fighting for the cause of humanity."

How can a man like that fight? What is he fit for? He might manage some quick, isolated act, but he can't hold out for long. And it's no wonder that, instead of gaining freedom, they've sunk into slavery, and instead of serving the cause of brotherly love and human unity, they've fallen instead into discord and isolation, just as my mysterious visitor and teacher told me in my youth. And that's why the idea of serving humanity, of brotherly love and the solidarity of mankind, is dying out more and more in the world, and this idea is even treated with mockery at times. Because how can a man shake off his habits? What's to become of him if he's so enslaved to the habit of satisfying the countless desires he's created for himself? He's isolated, and what does the rest of humanity matter to him? They've succeeded in piling up a greater mass of possessions, but there's less joy in the world.

The monastic way is entirely different. Obedience, fasting, and prayer are laughed at, and yet only through them does the path to real, true freedom lie. I cut off my superfluous, unnecessary desires, I subdue my proud, willful nature and discipline it through obedience, and with God's help I attain freedom of spirit, and with it, spiritual joy. Which is more capable of conceiving a great idea and serving it—the rich man in his isolation, or the man who's freed himself from the tyranny of material things and habits? The monk is reproached for his solitude: "You've shut yourself away within monastery walls for your own salvation, and forgotten the brotherly service of humanity!" But we'll see who turns out to be more devoted to the cause of brotherly love. Because it isn't we who are isolated, but they, even though they don't see it. In the old days, leaders of the people came from among us, so why shouldn't they again? The same meek and humble ascetics will rise up and go out to labor for the great cause. Russia's salvation comes from the people. And the Russian monk has always stood with the people. We're isolated only if the people are isolated. The people believe as we do, and an unbelieving reformer will never accomplish anything in Russia, even if he's sincere at heart and a genius. Remember that! The people will meet the atheist and overcome him, and Russia will be one and orthodox. Take care of the peasant and guard his heart. Keep educating him, quietly. That's your duty as monks, for the peasant carries God in his heart.
(f) On Masters and Servants, and Whether They Can Be Brothers in Spirit

Of course I don't deny that there's sin in the peasants too. And the fire of corruption is spreading visibly, hour by hour, working its way down from above. The spirit of isolation is descending on the people too. Moneylenders and devourers of the village commune are on the rise. Already the merchant grows more and more hungry for rank, strives to appear cultured though he hasn't a trace of it, and toward that end meanly looks down on his own old traditions, even feels ashamed of his fathers' faith. He calls on princes, though he's nothing but a corrupted peasant himself. The peasants are rotting away in drunkenness and can't shake the habit. And what cruelty toward their wives, even toward their children! All from drink! I've seen children of nine in the factories, frail, rickety, stooped, already corrupted. The stifling workshop, the din of machinery, work all day long, foul language, and drink, drink—is that what a small child's heart needs? He needs sunlight, childish play, good examples all around him, and at least a little love. There must be no more of this, monks—no more tormenting children—rise up and preach against it, hurry, hurry!

But God will save Russia, for though the peasants are corrupted and can't renounce their filthy sin, they still know it's accursed by God and that they do wrong in sinning. So our people still believe in righteousness, still have faith in God, and still weep tears of devotion.

It's different with the upper classes. Following science, they want to base justice on reason alone, no longer on Christ as before, and they've already declared that there's no such thing as crime, no such thing as sin. And that's only consistent, because if there's no God, what does crime even mean? In Europe the people are already rising up violently against the rich, and their leaders are everywhere driving them toward bloodshed, teaching them that their rage is righteous. But their "rage is cursed, for it is cruel." But God will save Russia, as He's saved her many times before. Salvation will come from the people, from their faith and their meekness.

Fathers and teachers, watch over the people's faith and this won't remain a dream. All my life I've been struck by the dignity of our great people, their true and fitting dignity. I've seen it myself, I can testify to it, I've seen it and marveled at it, I've seen it despite the degrading sins and poverty-stricken appearance of our peasantry. They aren't servile, and even after two centuries of serfdom they're free in manner and bearing, yet without insolence, without vengefulness, without envy. "You're rich and well-born, you're clever and gifted—fine, be so, God bless you. I respect you, but I know that I too am a man. By respecting you without envy, I prove my own dignity as a man."

In truth, if they don't say this in so many words—since they don't yet know how to put it into words—that's how they act. I've seen it myself, known it myself, and, would you believe it, the poorer our Russian peasant is, the more noticeable that serene goodness becomes, since the richer among them are for the most part already corrupted, and much of that is due to our own carelessness and indifference. But God will save His people, for Russia is great in her humility. I dream of seeing, and seem already to see clearly, our future. It will come to pass that even the most corrupt of our rich will end up feeling ashamed of his riches before the poor, and the poor, seeing his humility, will understand and yield before him, will respond joyfully and kindly to his honorable shame. Believe me, it will end that way; things are already moving toward it. Equality is to be found only in the spiritual dignity of man, and only among us will that be understood. If we were truly brothers, fraternity would exist, but before that, people will never agree on how to divide up wealth. We preserve the image of Christ, and it will shine out like a precious diamond to the whole world. So may it be, so may it be!

Fathers and teachers, a touching thing happened to me once. On my travels I met, in the town of K., my old orderly, Afanasy. It had been eight years since I'd parted from him. He happened to spot me in the marketplace, recognized me, ran up to me—and how delighted he was! He simply pounced on me: "Dear master, is that you? Is it really you I'm seeing?" He took me home with him.

He was no longer in the army; he was married and already had two small children. He and his wife earned their living selling goods in the marketplace. His room was poor, but bright and clean. He made me sit down, put on the samovar, sent for his wife, as though my arrival were a holiday for them. He brought his children to me: "Bless them, Father."

"Is it for me to bless them? I'm only a humble monk. I'll pray for them. And for you, Afanasy Pavlovitch, I've prayed every day since that day, because it all began with you," I said. And I explained that to him as best I could. And what do you think? The man kept staring at me, unable to believe that I, his former master, an officer, now stood before him in this guise and this position; it brought him to tears.
"Why are you crying?" I said, "you should rejoice over me instead, dear friend, whom I can never forget, for my path is a glad and joyful one."
He didn't say much, but kept sighing and shaking his head over me tenderly.
"What became of your fortune?" he asked.
"I gave it to the monastery," I answered; "we live in common there."

After tea I began saying my good-byes, and suddenly he brought out half a rouble as an offering to the monastery, and I saw him hurriedly pressing another half-rouble into my hand as well: "That's for you, for your travels, it may come in useful, Father."

I took his half-rouble, bowed to him and his wife, and went out rejoicing. And on my way I thought: "Here we both are now, he at home and I on the road, sighing and shaking our heads, no doubt, and yet smiling joyfully in the gladness of our hearts, remembering how God brought about our meeting."

I never saw him again after that. I had been his master and he my servant, but now, exchanging a loving kiss with softened hearts, there was a great human bond between us. I've thought a great deal about that, and here's what I think now: is it really so unimaginable that this grand, simple-hearted unity might one day become universal among the Russian people? I believe it will come to pass, and that the time is near.

And about servants I'll add this: in the old days, when I was young, I was often angry with servants—"the cook served something too hot, the orderly didn't brush my clothes properly." But what taught me better then was a thought of my dear brother's, which I'd heard from him in childhood: "Am I worth it, that another person should serve me and be ordered about by me, in his poverty and ignorance?" And I marveled at the time that such simple, self-evident ideas should be so slow to occur to us.

It's impossible for there to be no servants at all in the world, but act so that your servant may be freer in spirit than if he weren't a servant at all. And why couldn't I be a servant to my own servant, and even let him see it, without any pride on my part or mistrust on his? Why shouldn't my servant be like my own family, so that I could take him into my household and rejoice in doing it? Even now this can be done, but it will lead, in the future, to the grand unity of mankind, when a man will no longer seek out servants for himself, or desire to turn his fellow creatures into servants as he does now, but instead will long with his whole heart to be the servant of all, just as the Gospel teaches.

And can it really be a dream that in the end man will find his joy only in deeds of light and mercy, rather than in the cruel pleasures of today—gluttony, lechery, vanity, boasting, and envious rivalry with one another? I firmly believe it isn't, and that the time is near. People laugh and ask, "When will that time come, and does it even look like coming?" I believe that with Christ's help we'll accomplish this great thing. And how many ideas has human history seen that were unthinkable ten years before they came to be! Yet when their appointed hour arrived, they emerged and spread across the whole earth. So it will be with us too, and our people will shine forth before the world, and all men will say: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone of the building."

And we may well ask the scoffers themselves: if our hope is only a dream, when will you build your own edifice and order the world justly through reason alone, without Christ? If they claim they're the ones advancing toward unity, only the most simple-minded among them actually believe it, so much so that one can only marvel at such naïveté. In truth, they have far more far-fetched dreams than we do. They aim at justice, but, denying Christ, they'll end up flooding the earth with blood, for blood cries out for blood, and he who takes up the sword will perish by the sword. And if it weren't for Christ's covenant, they'd slaughter one another down to the last two men left on earth. And even those last two men wouldn't be able to restrain their pride toward each other, and one would kill the other, and then himself. And that is exactly what would happen, were it not for Christ's promise that for the sake of the humble and meek, those days shall be cut short.

While I was still wearing my officer's uniform, after my duel, I talked about servants in polite society, and I remember everyone was amazed at me. "What!" they'd ask, "are we supposed to have our servants sit down on the sofa and offer them tea?" And I answered: "Why not, at least now and then?" Everyone laughed. Their question was frivolous and my answer wasn't very clear, but there was some truth in the thought behind it.
(g) On Prayer, Love, and Contact with Other Worlds

Young man, never forget to pray. Every time you pray, if your prayer is sincere, there will be some new feeling in it, some new meaning, and this will give you fresh courage; you'll come to understand that prayer is itself an education. And remember too, every day, whenever you're able, to repeat to yourself, "Lord, have mercy on all who stand before You today." For every hour, every moment, thousands of people leave this life on earth, and their souls stand before God. And how many of them depart alone, unknown, sad, dejected, with no one to mourn for them or even know whether they lived at all! And behold, from the other end of the earth, perhaps, your prayer for their rest may rise up to God, though you never knew them, nor they you. How moving it must be, for a soul standing in fear before the Lord, to feel in that very instant that someone, somewhere, is praying for him too, that there's still a fellow creature left on earth who loves him! And God will look upon you both more graciously, for if you've had that much pity on him, how much more pity will He have, He who is infinitely more loving and merciful than you! And He will forgive him for your sake.

Brothers, have no fear of men's sin. Love a man even in his sin, for that reflects Divine Love and is the highest form of love on this earth. Love all of God's creation, the whole of it and every grain of sand in it. Love every leaf, every ray of God's light. Love the animals, love the plants, love everything. If you love everything, you'll perceive the divine mystery within things. Once you perceive it, you'll begin to understand it more fully every day. And in the end you'll come to love the whole world with an all-embracing love. Love the animals: God has given them the beginnings of thought and untroubled joy. Don't disturb that, don't torment them, don't deprive them of their happiness, don't work against God's purpose. Man, don't take pride in your superiority to the animals; they are without sin, while you, for all your greatness, defile the earth by your very presence on it, and leave the traces of your corruption behind you—alas, that's true of nearly every one of us! Love children especially, for they too are sinless, like angels; they live to soften and purify our hearts, and, in a sense, to guide us. Woe to anyone who wrongs a child! Father Anfim taught me to love children. That kind, quiet man used to spend, on our travels, the few coins we were given on sweets and cakes for children. He could never pass a child without being moved. That's simply the man's nature.

At certain thoughts one stands baffled, especially at the sight of men's sin, wondering whether to meet it with force or with humble love. Always resolve to use humble love. If you settle on that once and for all, you can subdue the whole world. Loving humility is a marvelously strong thing, the strongest thing there is, and there is nothing else like it.

Every day, every hour, every minute, examine yourself, watch yourself, and make sure your bearing is a fitting one. You pass by a small child—you pass by spiteful, with ugly words, with an angry heart; you may not have even noticed the child, but he's seen you, and your image, unfitting and ignoble, may lodge itself in his defenseless heart. You don't know it, but you may have planted a seed of evil in him, and it may grow, all because you weren't careful in front of the child, because you hadn't cultivated in yourself a careful, actively benevolent love. Brothers, love is a teacher, but one has to know how to acquire it, for it's hard to acquire, it comes at a high price, it's won slowly through long labor. Because we have to love not just occasionally, for a moment, but forever. Anyone can love occasionally—even the wicked can do that.

My brother once asked the birds to forgive him; that sounds senseless, but it's right, because everything is like an ocean, everything flows and blends together; a touch in one place sets off a ripple at the other end of the earth. It may be senseless to beg forgiveness from the birds, but the birds would be happier beside you—a little happier, at least—and so would children, and every animal, if you were nobler than you are now. It's all like an ocean, I tell you. Then you'd pray to the birds too, consumed by an all-embracing love, in a kind of rapture, and pray that they too would forgive you your sin. Treasure that ecstasy, however senseless it may look to others.

My friends, pray to God for gladness. Be glad as children are, as the birds of heaven are. And don't let men's sin throw you off in what you're doing. Don't be afraid that it will wear away your work or keep it from being accomplished. Don't say, "Sin is powerful, wickedness is powerful, our surroundings are corrupting, and we're alone and helpless, and our environment is wearing us down and stopping our good work from being done." Flee from that despair, children! There's only one path to salvation—so take it: make yourself responsible for all men's sins. That's the truth, friends, believe me, for the moment you sincerely make yourself responsible for everything and everyone, you'll see at once that it really is so, that you're to blame for every person and everything. But if you throw your own idleness and weakness onto others, you'll end up sharing Satan's pride, and murmuring against God.

As for the pride of Satan, here's what I think: it's hard for us on earth to grasp it fully, and so it's easy to fall into error and share in it, even imagining we're doing something grand and fine. In fact, many of the strongest feelings and impulses of our nature we simply cannot grasp while on earth. Don't let that be a stumbling block, and don't imagine it can serve as an excuse for anything. For the Eternal Judge asks of you what you're capable of understanding, not what you're not. You'll know that for yourself hereafter, for then you'll see all things truly and won't dispute them. Here on earth, in truth, we walk as if lost, and if it weren't for the precious image of Christ before us, we'd be undone and utterly lost, just as the human race was before the flood. Much on earth is hidden from us, but to make up for it, we've been given a precious, mystical sense of our living bond with the other world, the higher heavenly world, and the roots of our thoughts and feelings lie not here but in other worlds. That's why philosophers say we cannot grasp the true reality of things on earth.

God took seeds from different worlds and sowed them on this earth, and His garden grew up, and everything that could sprout came up, but what grows lives, and stays alive, only through its sense of contact with those other, mysterious worlds. If that feeling weakens or is destroyed in you, the heavenly growth within you will wither away. Then you'll grow indifferent to life, even come to hate it. That's what I believe.
(h) Can a Man Judge His Fellow Creatures? Faith to the End

Remember above all that you cannot be anyone's judge. For no one can judge a criminal until he recognizes that he himself is just as much a criminal as the man standing before him, and that he, perhaps, bears more blame than anyone for that very crime. Once he understands that, he'll be fit to be a judge. Absurd as that may sound, it's true. If I myself had been righteous, perhaps there would have been no criminal standing before me at all. If you can take upon yourself the crime of the person your heart is judging, do it at once—suffer for him yourself, and let him go without a word of reproach. And even if the law itself makes you his judge, act in that same spirit as far as you're able, for he will go away and condemn himself far more bitterly than you ever could. If, after your kiss, he walks away untouched, mocking you, don't let that trip you up. It only means his time hasn't come yet, but it will come in due course. And if it never comes, no matter; if not him, then someone else in his place will come to understand, and suffer, and judge and condemn himself, and the truth will still be fulfilled. Believe that, believe it without a shadow of doubt, for in that belief lies the whole hope and faith of the saints.

Work without ceasing. If, as you're falling asleep at night, you remember, "I haven't done what I ought to have done," get up at once and do it. If the people around you are spiteful and indifferent and won't listen to you, fall down before them and beg their forgiveness, for in truth you are to blame for their unwillingness to listen. And if you can't reach them in their bitterness, serve them in silence and humility, without ever losing hope. If everyone abandons you, even drives you away by force, then, once you're left alone, fall to the earth and kiss it, soak it with your tears, and it will bear fruit even though no one has seen or heard you in your solitude. Believe to the very end, even if every other person has gone astray and you're the only one left faithful; bring your offering even then, and praise God in your loneliness. And if two of you are gathered together, then that is a whole world, a world of living love. Embrace each other tenderly and praise God, for even if His truth has been fulfilled only in the two of you, that is enough.

If you yourself sin, and grieve even unto death over your sins, or over some sudden lapse, then rejoice for others instead—rejoice for the righteous man, rejoice that if you have sinned, he is righteous and has not sinned.

If men's wrongdoing stirs you to indignation and overwhelming distress, even to a desire for vengeance against the wrongdoers, shun that feeling above all else. Go at once and seek out suffering for yourself, as though you yourself were guilty of that wrong. Accept that suffering, bear it, and your heart will find comfort, and you'll come to understand that you too are guilty, since you might have been a light to the wrongdoers, as the one sinless man was, and you were not a light to them. If you had been a light, you'd have lit the way for others too, and the wrongdoer might perhaps have been saved from his sin by your light. And even if your light was shining, and yet you see that others weren't saved by it, stand firm, and don't doubt the power of that heavenly light. Believe that if they weren't saved then, they'll be saved later. And if they're not saved later, their sons will be saved, for your light won't die out even after you're dead. The righteous man passes away, but his light remains. People are always saved after the deliverer's death. People reject their prophets and kill them, but they come to love their martyrs and honor those they've slain. You're working for the whole, you're acting for the future. Don't seek a reward, for your reward on this earth is already great: the spiritual joy granted only to the righteous man. Don't fear the great or the powerful, but be wise and forever serene. Know the measure of things, know the seasons—study that. When you're left alone, pray. Love to throw yourself down on the earth and kiss it. Kiss the earth and love it with an unceasing, consuming love. Love all men, love everything. Seek out that rapture, that ecstasy. Water the earth with the tears of your joy, and love those tears. Don't be ashamed of that rapture, treasure it, for it's a gift from God, and a great one; it isn't given to many, only to the chosen.
(i) On Hell and Hellfire: A Mystical Reflection

Fathers and teachers, I ponder this: "What is hell?" I hold that it's the suffering of being unable to love. Once, in an infinite existence beyond measure in time and space, a spiritual being was granted, on coming into this world, the power to say, "I am, and I love." Once, only once, he was given a moment of active, living love, and for that purpose earthly life was granted him, along with its seasons and its times. And that fortunate being rejected the priceless gift, failed to prize it or love it, scorned it, and remained indifferent. Such a man, having left the earth, sees Abraham's bosom and speaks with Abraham, as we're told in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, and beholds heaven, and can even go up to the Lord. But that is precisely his torment—to rise up to the Lord having never loved, to be brought close to those who did love, after having despised their love. For he sees it clearly and says to himself, "Now I understand, and though I now thirst to love, there'll be nothing great in my love, no sacrifice in it, because my earthly life is over, and Abraham won't come, not even with a single drop of living water"—that being the gift of active earthly life—"to cool the burning thirst of spiritual love now blazing in me, the very love I scorned while on earth; there's no more life left for me, and there will be no more time! Even if I'd gladly give my life for others now, it can never happen, because that life, the one that could have been sacrificed for love, is over, and now a gulf lies fixed between that life and this existence."

They speak of hellfire in the literal, material sense. I won't go into that mystery, and I steer clear of it. But I think that if there really were fire in the material sense, they'd almost be glad of it, since I imagine that in physical agony their still greater spiritual agony would be forgotten, if only for a moment. What's more, that spiritual agony cannot be taken from them, because that suffering isn't external, it lies within them. And if it could somehow be taken away, I think it would only be bitterer still for those unhappy souls. For even if the righteous in Paradise forgave them, watching their torment, and called them up to heaven out of infinite love, that would only multiply their torment, since it would awaken in them, even more sharply, a burning thirst for a responsive, active, grateful love that is now impossible for them. In the timidity of my heart, though, I imagine that the very recognition of this impossibility might in the end serve to console them. For by accepting the love of the righteous alongside the impossibility of ever repaying it, through this submission and the working of this humility, they'll come at last to something like a semblance of that active love they once scorned in life, something resembling its outward form.... I'm sorry, friends and brothers, that I can't put this more clearly. But woe to those who've taken their own lives on earth, woe to suicides! I believe there can be no one more wretched than they are. We're told it's a sin to pray for them, and outwardly the Church, as it were, renounces them, but in the secrecy of my own heart I believe we may pray for them too. Love can never be an offense to Christ. For souls such as these I've prayed silently my whole life, I confess it, fathers and teachers, and even now I pray for them every day.

Oh, there are some who remain proud and fierce even in hell, despite their certain knowledge and contemplation of the absolute truth; there are terrible ones who've given themselves over entirely to Satan and his proud spirit. For these, hell is voluntary and endlessly consuming; they are tormented by their own choice. For they have cursed themselves, cursing God and life itself. They feed on their own vindictive pride like a starving man in the desert sucking blood from his own body. But they're never satisfied, and they refuse forgiveness, curse the God who calls to them. They cannot look upon the living God without hatred, and they cry out that the God of life should be annihilated, that God should destroy Himself and His own creation along with Him. And they will burn forever in the fire of their own wrath, yearning for death and annihilation. But they will never attain death....

Here Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov's manuscript ends. Let me repeat, it's incomplete and fragmentary. The biographical details, for instance, cover only Father Zossima's earliest youth. As for his teachings and opinions, we find sayings gathered together that were clearly spoken on very different occasions. His remarks during the last few hours haven't been kept separate from the rest, but their general character can still be gathered from what we have in Alexey Fyodorovitch's manuscript.

The elder's death came, in the end, quite unexpectedly. Although those gathered around him that last evening realized his death was approaching, it was still hard to imagine it would come so suddenly. On the contrary, his friends, as I mentioned already, seeing him that night so apparently cheerful and talkative, were convinced there'd been at least a temporary turn for the better in his condition. Even five minutes before his death, they said afterward, marveling, it was impossible to foresee it. He seemed to suddenly feel a sharp pain in his chest, went pale, and pressed his hands to his heart. Everyone rose from their seats and hurried to him. But even in his suffering, he still looked at them with a smile, sank slowly from his chair to his knees, then bowed his face to the ground, stretched out his arms, and, as though in joyful rapture, praying and kissing the ground, quietly and joyfully gave up his soul to God.

News of his death spread at once through the hermitage and reached the monastery. The deceased's closest friends, along with those whose position required it, began preparing the body according to the ancient ritual, and all the monks gathered together in the church. And before dawn, news of the death had reached the town. By morning the whole town was talking of the event, and crowds were streaming out from town to the monastery. But that subject will be dealt with in the next book; here I'll only add that before a day had passed, something happened so unexpected, so strange, so upsetting and bewildering in its effect on the monks and the townspeople, that even after all these years, that day of general suspense is still vividly remembered in the town.
PART III

title: I. The Breath Of Corruption
paragraphs: Father Zossima's body was prepared for burial according to the established ritual. As is well known, the bodies of deceased monks and hermits aren't washed.
