In the words of the Church Ritual: "If any of the monks should depart in the Lord, the designated monk (that is, whose duty it is) shall wipe the body with warm water, first making the sign of the cross with a sponge on the forehead of the deceased, on the chest, on the hands and feet, and on the knees, and that is sufficient." All this was carried out by Father Païssy, who then dressed the deceased in his monastic robes and wrapped him in his cloak, slit somewhat, as custom required, so that it could be folded around him in the shape of a cross. On his head he placed a hood bearing an eight-pointed cross. The hood was left open, and the dead man's face was covered with black gauze. In his hands was placed an icon of the Savior. Toward morning he was laid in the coffin, which had been made ready long before. It was decided to leave the coffin in the cell all day, in the larger room where the elder used to receive his visitors and fellow monks. Since the deceased was a priest and a monk under the strictest rule, the Gospel, not the Psalter, had to be read over his body by monks in holy orders. Father Iosif began the reading immediately after the memorial service. Father Païssy meant to read the Gospel over his dead friend all day and night himself, but for now he, along with the Father Superintendent of the hermitage, was kept very busy, since something extraordinary, an unheard-of, even "unseemly" excitement and impatient anticipation had begun to show itself among the monks, and among the visitors staying at the monastery hostels, and the crowds streaming in from town. And as time passed, it only grew more pronounced. Both the Superintendent and Father Païssy did everything they could to calm the general commotion and agitation.

Once it was fully light, some people began bringing their sick—mostly children—with them from town, as though they'd been waiting expressly for this moment, clearly convinced that the dead elder's remains possessed a healing power that would reveal itself at once, in proportion to their faith. Only then did it become clear just how unquestioningly everyone in our town had regarded Father Zossima, during his lifetime, as a great saint. And those who came weren't all from the lower classes, not by any means.

This intense anticipation among believers, displayed so hastily, so openly, even with impatience and something close to insistence, struck Father Païssy as unbecoming. Though he'd long foreseen something of the kind, the actual display of the feeling went beyond anything he'd expected. Whenever he came across monks showing this excitement, Father Païssy began reproving them. "Such immediate expectation of something extraordinary," he said, "betrays a frivolity permissible in worldly people, but unbecoming in us."

But little attention was paid to him, and Father Païssy noticed this with unease. Yet he himself—if the whole truth must be told—secretly, deep in his heart, cherished nearly the same hopes, and couldn't help being aware of it, even as he was indignant at the overly impatient expectation around him and saw in it frivolity and vanity. Nevertheless, it was especially unpleasant for him to encounter certain people whose presence stirred real misgivings in him. In the crowd inside the dead man's cell, he noticed, with an inward distaste he immediately reproached himself for, the presence of Rakitin and of the monk from Obdorsk, who was still staying at the monastery. For some reason Father Païssy felt suddenly suspicious of both of them, though in truth he might well have felt the same about others too.

The monk from Obdorsk stood out as the most restless figure in the excited crowd. He could be seen everywhere; everywhere he was asking questions, everywhere listening, on every side whispering with a peculiar, secretive air. His expression showed the greatest impatience, even something like irritation.

As for Rakitin, it later turned out he'd come to the hermitage so early at the express request of Madame Hohlakov. As soon as that good-hearted but scatterbrained woman, who couldn't have gotten into the hermitage herself, woke and heard of Father Zossima's death, she was seized with such intense curiosity that she immediately dispatched Rakitin to the hermitage, to keep close watch and report back to her by letter roughly every half hour on everything that was happening. She considered Rakitin an exceptionally religious and devout young man. He was particularly skilled at winning people over and playing whatever part he sensed would please them most, the moment he spotted even the slightest advantage to himself in doing so.

It was a bright, clear day, and many of the visitors were crowding around the graves, which were especially numerous near the church and scattered here and there through the hermitage grounds. Walking around the hermitage, Father Païssy remembered Alyosha, and that he hadn't seen him in some time, not since the night before. No sooner had the thought crossed his mind than he spotted him, in the farthest corner of the hermitage garden, sitting on the gravestone of a monk once famed, long ago, for his saintliness. He sat with his back to the hermitage and his face to the wall, seeming to hide behind the gravestone. Coming closer, Father Païssy saw he was weeping quietly but bitterly, his face buried in his hands, his whole body shaking with sobs. Father Païssy stood over him a moment.

"Enough, dear son, enough, my dear," he said at last, with feeling. "Why are you weeping? Rejoice, and do not weep. Don't you know that this is the greatest of his days? Think only of where he is now, at this very moment!"
Alyosha glanced up at him, uncovering his face, swollen from crying like a child's, but turned away again at once without a word and hid his face in his hands once more.
"Perhaps it's for the best," Father Païssy said thoughtfully; "weep, if you must—Christ has sent you these tears."

"Your touching tears are only a relief to your spirit, and will serve to gladden your dear heart," he added to himself, walking away from Alyosha, thinking of him with tenderness. He moved off quickly, though, sensing that he too might weep, looking at him.

Meanwhile time was passing; the monastery services and the memorial prayers for the dead followed one after another in due course. Father Païssy again took Father Iosif's place at the coffin and resumed reading the Gospel. But before three that afternoon, something happened, the very thing I alluded to at the end of the last book—something so unexpected by all of us, so contrary to what everyone had been hoping for, that, I repeat, this trivial incident has been remembered in minute detail to this day in our town and the whole surrounding district. I might add, speaking for myself, that I find it almost distasteful to recall that event, which caused such frivolous agitation and proved such a stumbling block to so many, even though in reality it was the most natural and trivial of matters. I would, of course, have left it out of my story entirely, had it not exerted such a powerful influence on the heart and soul of the chief hero of my story, Alyosha, forming a crisis, a turning point in his spiritual development, delivering a shock to his understanding that ultimately strengthened it for the rest of his life and gave it a fixed purpose.

And so, back to our story. Before dawn, when they laid Father Zossima's body in the coffin and carried it into the front room, someone raised the question, among those gathered around the coffin, of whether to open the windows. But this suggestion, tossed off casually, went unanswered and was almost unnoticed. Some of those present may have privately noted it, only to reflect that expecting decay and corruption from the body of such a saint was itself absurd, deserving of pity, if not an outright smile, for the lack of faith and the frivolity it implied. For they expected something quite different.

And behold, not long after midday, signs of something began to appear—at first only noticed in silence by those coming and going, each apparently afraid to voice the thought in his own mind. But by three o'clock these signs had become so plain, so unmistakable, that word raced through all the monks and visitors at the hermitage, quickly reaching the monastery, throwing every monk into astonishment, and finally, in the shortest possible time, spreading to the town, stirring up everyone there, believers and unbelievers alike. The unbelievers rejoiced, and as for the believers, some of them rejoiced even more than the unbelievers, for "men love the downfall and disgrace of the righteous," as the late elder himself had said in one of his teachings.

The fact was that a smell of decomposition began coming from the coffin, growing gradually stronger, and by three o'clock it was entirely unmistakable. In all the past history of our monastery, no scandal like it could be recalled, and under no other circumstances could such a scandal have been possible, as showed itself, in unseemly disorder, immediately after this discovery, even among the monks themselves. Afterward, even many years afterward, some sensible monks were astonished and appalled, recalling that day, that the scandal could ever have reached such proportions. For in the past, monks of very holy life had died, God-fearing old men whose saintliness everyone acknowledged, and from their humble coffins, too, the breath of decay had come, naturally enough, as it does from every dead body, but that had caused no scandal, not even the slightest stir. Of course there had been, in earlier times, saints in the monastery whose memory was carefully preserved, whose relics, according to tradition, showed no sign of corruption. The monks regarded this as touching and mysterious, and the tradition surrounding it was cherished as something blessed and miraculous, a promise, by God's grace, of still greater glory to come from their tombs in the future.

One such figure, whose memory was especially cherished, was an old monk, Job, who had died seventy years earlier at the age of a hundred and five. He'd been a celebrated ascetic, rigorous in fasting and silence, and his tomb was pointed out to every visitor on arrival with particular reverence, and mysterious hints of great hopes attached to it. (That was the very tomb on which Father Païssy had found Alyosha sitting that morning.) Another memory cherished in the monastery was that of the famous Father Varsonofy, who had died only recently and had preceded Father Zossima as elder. During his lifetime he'd been revered by all the pilgrims to the monastery as a holy fool. Tradition held that both of these men had lain in their coffins as though still alive, that they'd shown no sign of decomposition when buried, and that a holy light had shone in their faces. Some even insisted that a sweet fragrance had risen from their bodies.

And yet, despite these edifying memories, it would be hard to explain the frivolity, absurdity, and malice that showed themselves beside Father Zossima's coffin. My own private opinion is that several different causes were at work simultaneously, one of them being the deep-rooted hostility, hidden in the hearts of many monks, toward the institution of the eldership as a harmful innovation. Even more powerful was jealousy of the dead man's saintliness, so firmly established during his lifetime that questioning it had become almost forbidden. For although the late elder had won over many hearts, more through love than through miracles, and had gathered around him a great mass of devoted followers, that very fact—if anything, all the more because of it—had stirred jealousy, and so he'd come to have bitter enemies, secret and open, not only within the monastery but out in the world too. He'd done no one any harm, and yet: "Why do they think him so saintly?" And that question alone, repeated gradually, gave rise at last to an intense, insatiable hatred of him. That, I believe, is why so many people were positively delighted by the smell of decomposition that came on so quickly, not even a full day after his death. At the same time, there were some among those who'd previously been devoted, reverent followers of the elder who were nearly wounded, personally offended, by this whole business. Here's how it happened.

As soon as signs of decomposition began to appear, the whole bearing of the monks betrayed their secret motives for entering the cell. They'd go in, stay a little while, and hurry out again to confirm the news to the crowd of other monks waiting outside. Some of them shook their heads mournfully, while others didn't even bother concealing the delight plainly gleaming in their spiteful eyes. And now no one reproached them for it, no one raised a voice in protest, which was strange, since the majority of the monks had been devoted to the dead elder. But it seemed as though, in this instance, God had let the minority gain the upper hand for a time.

Visitors from outside, especially the educated ones, soon went into the cell too, with the same prying intent. Few of the peasants went inside the cell, though there were crowds of them at the hermitage gates. After three o'clock the rush of worldly visitors increased sharply, no doubt owing to the shocking news. People came who otherwise wouldn't have, and hadn't meant to come that day at all, and among them were a number of prominent figures. But outward decorum was still preserved for the moment, and Father Païssy, his face stern, went on reading the Gospel aloud, firmly and distinctly, apparently not noticing what was happening around him, though in fact he'd registered something unusual some time before. But at last the murmurs, subdued at first but growing gradually louder and more confident, reached even him. "It just goes to show that God's judgment isn't man's judgment," Father Païssy suddenly heard. The first to give voice to this sentiment was a layman, an elderly town official known for his great piety. But he was only saying out loud what the monks had long been whispering among themselves. They had, in fact, already reached this damning conclusion some time before, and the worst of it was that a kind of triumphant satisfaction at reaching it grew more and more evident by the minute. Soon they began setting aside even outward decorum, almost as if they felt entitled to discard it.

"And for what reason could this have happened," some of the monks said, at first with a show of regret; "he had such a slight frame, his flesh was dried right onto his bones—what was there left to decay?"

"It must be a sign from heaven," others hurried to add, and this view was adopted at once without objection. It was pointed out, too, that if the decomposition had been natural, as with every ordinary sinner, it would only have become apparent later, after at least twenty-four hours; but this premature corruption "exceeded nature," and so the hand of God was plainly at work. It was meant as a sign. This conclusion seemed irresistible.

Gentle Father Iosif, the librarian, a great favorite of the dead man's, tried to answer some of the ill-speakers by pointing out that "this isn't held to be the same everywhere," and that the incorruptibility of the bodies of the righteous wasn't a doctrine of the Orthodox Church at all, only an opinion, and that even in the most Orthodox regions, at Athos for instance, they weren't especially troubled by the smell of decay, and that there the chief sign of a saved soul's glorification wasn't bodily incorruptibility, but the color of the bones once the body had lain many years in the earth and decomposed. "And if the bones turn yellow, like wax, that's the great sign the Lord has glorified the dead saint; if they're not yellow but black, it shows God hasn't judged him worthy of such glory—that's the belief at Athos, a great place, where Orthodox doctrine has been preserved from ancient times, unbroken and in its purest form," Father Iosif concluded.

But the meek Father's words carried little weight, and even provoked a mocking reply. "That's all pedantry and newfangled nonsense, no point listening to it," the monks decided. "We stick to the old teaching, there's all kinds of innovations nowadays, are we supposed to follow every one of them?" others added.

"We've had just as many holy fathers as they have. Look at them, living among the Turks, they've forgotten everything. Their doctrine's been corrupted for ages, they don't even have bells," the most scornful among them added.

Father Iosif walked away, grieving all the more since he'd put forward his own view with little confidence, as though he barely believed it himself. He foresaw, with distress, that something very unseemly was beginning, and that there were unmistakable signs of insubordination. Little by little, all the level-headed monks were reduced to the same silence as Father Iosif. And so it happened that everyone who had loved the elder, and had devoutly accepted the institution of the eldership, was suddenly plunged into gloom, and cast timid glances at one another whenever they met. Those hostile to the eldership as an unwelcome innovation held their heads high. "There was no smell of decay from the late elder Varsonofy, only a sweet fragrance," they recalled spitefully. "But he earned that glory not because he was an elder, but because he was a holy man."

And this was followed by a downpour of criticism, even outright blame, aimed at Father Zossima. "His teaching was false; he taught that life is a great joy and not a vale of tears," said some of the less reasonable among them. "He followed fashionable belief, he wouldn't acknowledge material fire in hell," others, still less reasonable, added. "He wasn't strict about fasting, indulged in sweets, ate cherry jam with his tea, ladies used to send it to him. Is that fitting for a monk under strict rule, drinking tea?" could be heard among the envious. "He sat there in pride," the most spiteful declared vindictively; "he thought himself a saint and took it as his due when people knelt before him." "He abused the sacrament of confession," the fiercest opponents of the eldership added in a malicious whisper. And among these were some of the oldest monks, the strictest in their devotion, genuine ascetics, who had kept silent throughout the elder's life but now suddenly unsealed their lips. And this was terrible, because their words carried great weight with the younger monks, whose convictions weren't yet firm. The monk from Obdorsk listened to all this closely, sighing heavily and nodding his head. "Yes, clearly Father Ferapont was right in what he said yesterday," and at that very moment Father Ferapont himself appeared, as though on purpose to add to the confusion.

I've already mentioned that he rarely left his wooden cell by the apiary. He was seldom even seen at church, and this neglect was excused on account of his eccentricity—he wasn't held to the rules binding on everyone else. But to tell the whole truth, they hardly had any choice in the matter. It would have been shameful to insist on burdening such a great ascetic, who prayed day and night (he even fell asleep on his knees), with the common regulations. If they'd tried to insist, the monks would have said, "He's holier than all the rest of us, and he follows a rule harder than ours. And if he doesn't go to church, it's because he knows when he ought to—he has his own rule." It was to avoid the risk of such sinful murmuring that Father Ferapont was left in peace.

As everyone knew, Father Ferapont particularly disliked Father Zossima. And now the news had reached him in his hut that "God's judgment isn't the same as man's," and that something had happened that "exceeded nature." It's safe to assume that among the first to run to him with the news was the monk from Obdorsk, who'd visited him the evening before and left his cell terror-stricken.

I mentioned above that although Father Païssy, standing firm and unmoving as he read the Gospel over the coffin, couldn't hear or see what was happening outside the cell, he sensed most of it correctly in his heart, since he knew the men around him well. He wasn't shaken by it, but waited without fear to see what would come next, watching with sharp insight for the outcome of the general excitement.

Suddenly an extraordinary uproar broke out in the passage, in open defiance of decorum. The door was flung open, and Father Ferapont appeared in the doorway. Behind him could be seen a crowd of monks accompanying him, along with a good number of townspeople. They didn't come into the cell, though, but stood at the bottom of the steps, waiting to see what Father Ferapont would say or do. For, despite their boldness, they felt a certain awe—he hadn't come for nothing. Standing in the doorway, Father Ferapont raised his arms, and under his right arm the sharp, inquisitive little eyes of the monk from Obdorsk peered in. He alone, in his intense curiosity, hadn't been able to resist running up the steps behind Father Ferapont. The others, by contrast, drew back farther in sudden alarm when the door was thrown open with a bang. Holding his hands aloft, Father Ferapont suddenly bellowed:

"Casting out, I cast out!" and, turning in every direction, he immediately began making the sign of the cross at each of the cell's four walls and four corners in turn. Everyone accompanying Father Ferapont understood the gesture at once. They knew he always did this wherever he went, and that he wouldn't sit down or say a word until he'd driven out the evil spirits.
"Satan, begone! Satan, begone!" he repeated with each sign of the cross. "Casting out, I cast out," he roared again.

He wore his coarse robe, cinched with a rope. Under his hemp shirt, his bare chest, covered in gray hair, could be seen. His feet were bare. The moment he began waving his arms, the harsh iron chains he wore under his robe could be heard clanking.
Father Païssy paused in his reading, stepped forward, and stood before him, waiting.
"What have you come here for, worthy Father? Why do you offend against good order? Why do you disturb the peace of the flock?" he said at last, regarding him sternly.

"What have I come for? You ask why? What is your faith?" Father Ferapont shouted wildly. "I've come to drive out your visitors, the unclean devils. I've come to see how many have gathered here while I've been away. I mean to sweep them out with a birch broom."
"You cast out the evil spirit, but perhaps it's him you're serving," Father Païssy went on, unafraid. "And who can say of himself, 'I am holy'? Can you, Father?"

"I am unclean, not holy. I wouldn't sit in an armchair, and I wouldn't have people bowing down before me like an idol," Father Ferapont thundered. "These days people are destroying the true faith. The dead man, your saint," he said, turning to the crowd and pointing a finger at the coffin, "didn't believe in devils. He gave out medicine to keep the devils off. And so they've become as common as spiders in the corners. And now he's begun to stink himself. In that we see a great sign from God."

The incident he was referring to was this. One of the monks had been haunted, in his dreams and later even while awake, by visions of evil spirits. When, terrified, he confided this to Father Zossima, the elder had advised constant prayer and strict fasting. But when that didn't help, he'd advised him to take a certain medicine as well, while continuing the prayer and fasting. Many people were scandalized at the time and shook their heads over it—none more than Father Ferapont, to whom some of the more censorious monks had hurried to report this "extraordinary" advice from the elder.

"Go away, Father!" said Father Païssy, in a commanding voice. "It's not for man to judge, but for God. Perhaps we're seeing a 'sign' here that neither you, nor I, nor any of us is able to understand. Go, Father, and do not trouble the flock!" he repeated forcefully.

"He didn't keep the fasts according to the rule, and that's why the sign has come. That's plain, and it's a sin to hide it," the fanatic, carried away by a zeal that outran his reason, refused to be calmed. "He was seduced by sweets, ladies brought them to him in their pockets, he sipped tea, he worshiped his own belly, stuffing it with sweet things and his mind with prideful thoughts.... And for that he's been put to shame...."

"You speak carelessly, Father." Father Païssy raised his own voice now too. "I admire your fasting and your austerities, but you're talking like some frivolous youth, fickle and childish. Go away, Father, I command you!" Father Païssy thundered, in conclusion.

"I'll go," said Ferapont, seeming somewhat taken aback but no less bitter. "You learned men! You're so clever you look down on my humble ways. I came here with little learning, and here I've forgotten even what I did know—God Himself has kept me, in my weakness, safe from your cleverness."
Father Païssy stood over him, waiting, resolute. Father Ferapont paused, then, suddenly leaning his cheek despondently on his hand, said in a sing-song voice, gazing at the dead elder's coffin:

"Tomorrow they'll sing over him 'Our Helper and Defender'—a splendid hymn—and over me, when I die, all they'll sing is 'What earthly joy'—a little canticle," he added, with tearful regret. "You are proud and puffed up, this is a place of vanity!" he suddenly shouted, like a madman, and with a wave of his hand he turned sharply and hurried down the steps. The crowd waiting below wavered; some followed him at once, others lingered, since the cell was still open, and Father Païssy, following Father Ferapont out onto the steps, stood watching him go. But the excited old fanatic wasn't quite finished. Walking about twenty paces off, he suddenly turned toward the setting sun, raised both arms, and, as though someone had cut him down, dropped to the ground with a loud cry.

"My God has triumphed! Christ has triumphed over the setting sun!" he shouted frantically, stretching his hands up toward the sun, then fell face down on the ground, sobbing like a small child, shaking with tears, arms spread wide on the earth. Then everyone rushed toward him; there were cries and sympathetic sobs... a kind of frenzy seemed to seize them all.
"This is the one who's a saint! This is the one who's a holy man!" some cried out loudly, their fear forgotten. "This is the one who should be elder," others added spitefully.

"He wouldn't be an elder... he'd refuse... he wouldn't go along with such a cursed innovation... he wouldn't imitate their foolery," other voices chimed in at once. And it's hard to say how far they might have gone, but at that moment the bell rang, calling everyone to service. All at once everyone began crossing themselves. Father Ferapont, too, got up, crossed himself, and went back to his cell without a backward glance, still muttering things that made no sense at all. A few followed him, but most dispersed, hurrying to the service. Father Païssy let Father Iosif take his place reading and went down. The frantic outcries of the zealots hadn't shaken him, but his heart was suddenly filled with a sadness he couldn't quite place, and he was aware of it. He stopped, wondering to himself, "Why am I sad, even downcast?" and immediately, with some surprise, realized that his sudden sadness had a very small, very particular cause. In the crowd gathered at the entrance to the cell, he'd noticed Alyosha, and he remembered feeling a pang in his heart the instant he saw him. "Can that boy really mean so much to my heart now?" he asked himself, wondering.

At that moment Alyosha passed him, hurrying by, though not toward the church. Their eyes met. Alyosha quickly looked away and dropped his eyes to the ground, and from that look alone, Father Païssy guessed at the great change taking place in him at that moment.
"Have you too fallen into temptation?" Father Païssy cried. "Can you really be one of those of little faith?" he added mournfully.

Alyosha stopped and gazed vaguely at Father Païssy, but quickly turned his eyes away again and looked down at the ground once more. He stood at an angle, not turning to face Father Païssy, who watched him closely.
"Where are you hurrying off to? The bell is calling us to service," he asked again, but again Alyosha gave no answer.
"Are you leaving the hermitage? What, without asking leave, without asking a blessing?"

Alyosha suddenly gave a strained smile, cast a strange, very strange look at the Father to whom his former guide, the former ruler of his heart and mind, his beloved elder, had entrusted him as he lay dying. And then, still without a word, he waved his hand, as though he no longer cared even to be respectful, and walked with quick steps toward the gates, away from the hermitage.
"You'll come back again!" Father Païssy murmured, watching him go with sorrowful surprise.

title: II. A Critical Moment
paragraphs: Father Païssy, of course, wasn't wrong to think his "dear boy" would come back. He may well have seen, with real insight, the true meaning of Alyosha's spiritual state. Still, I must honestly admit it would be very hard for me to give a clear account of that strange, hazy moment in the life of the young hero I care about so much. To Father Païssy's sorrowful question, "Are you too among those of little faith?" I could of course answer confidently on Alyosha's behalf, "No, he isn't among those of little faith. Quite the opposite." In fact, all his trouble came from the fact that his faith was so great. But the trouble was real all the same, and so agonizing that even long afterward Alyosha thought of that sorrowful day as one of the bitterest, most fateful days of his life. If someone were to ask, "Could all his grief and turmoil really have come down to nothing more than his elder's body showing signs of premature decay instead of performing miracles on the spot?" I have to answer plainly, without dancing around it: "Yes, that's exactly what it was." I'd only ask the reader not to be too quick to laugh at my young hero's pure heart. I'm not trying to excuse him, or justify his innocent faith on the grounds of his youth, or how little schooling he'd had, or anything of that kind. I want to state, on the contrary, that I have genuine respect for the qualities of his heart. No doubt a young man who took in impressions cautiously, whose love ran lukewarm, whose mind was more prudent than suited his age and so worth little, might well have avoided what happened to my hero—I grant that. But in some cases it's actually more to a person's credit to be swept away by a feeling, however unreasonable, that springs from a great love, than to remain unmoved. And this is even truer in youth, since a young man who's always sensible is a young man to be suspected, and worth little—that's my opinion!
"But," reasonable people will perhaps object, "not every young man can believe in such a superstition, and your hero is no model for the rest."
To which I answer again: "Yes! my hero had faith, a faith both holy and steadfast, but I'm still not going to apologize for him."

Although I said above, perhaps too hastily, that I wouldn't explain or justify my hero, I can see that some explanation is needed if the rest of my story is to make sense. Let me say, then, that it wasn't really a matter of miracles. There was no frivolous, impatient hankering for miracles in his mind. And Alyosha needed no miracles at that moment, no triumphant confirmation of some preconceived notion—oh, no, not at all—what he saw before everything else was one figure: the figure of his beloved elder, the figure of that holy man he revered with such adoration. The fact is that all the love hidden away in his pure young heart, love for everyone and everything, had over the past year become concentrated—perhaps wrongly so—on a single being, his beloved elder. That being had, for so long, been accepted by him as his ideal, that all his youthful strength and energy could hardly help but turn toward that ideal, to the point of forgetting, in the moment, "everyone and everything else." He remembered afterward how, on that terrible day, he'd completely forgotten his brother Dmitri, about whom he'd been so anxious and troubled just the day before; he'd forgotten, too, to bring the two hundred roubles to Ilusha's father, though he'd meant so warmly to do it the evening before. But again, it wasn't miracles he needed, only "the higher justice," which he believed had been violated by the blow that had so suddenly and cruelly wounded his heart. And what does it matter that this "justice" Alyosha was seeking inevitably took the shape, in his mind, of miracles that ought to be worked immediately by the ashes of his beloved teacher? After all, everyone in the monastery cherished the same thought, the same hope—even those whose minds Alyosha revered, Father Païssy himself, for instance. And so Alyosha, untroubled by doubt, gave his own dreams the same shape as everyone else's. A whole year of monastery life had settled this expectation into a habit in his heart. But it was justice, justice, he thirsted for—not simply miracles.

And now the man who, he believed, should have been exalted above everyone in the whole world—that man, instead of receiving the glory owed to him, had suddenly been brought low and dishonored! What for? Who had judged him? Who could have decreed such a thing? Those were the questions that tore at his inexperienced, untested heart. He couldn't bear, without humiliation, without something like resentment even, that the holiest of holy men should be exposed to the jeering, spiteful mockery of a frivolous crowd so far beneath him. Even setting miracles aside, even if there'd been nothing marvelous to justify his hopes, why this indignity, why this humiliation, why this premature decay, "beyond nature," as the spiteful monks put it? Why this "sign from heaven," which they proclaimed so triumphantly alongside Father Ferapont, and what gave them the right, as they believed, to proclaim it? Where was the hand of Providence? Why had Providence hidden its face "at the most critical moment," as Alyosha saw it, as though willingly submitting itself to the blind, mute, pitiless laws of nature?

That was why Alyosha's heart was bleeding, and, as I've already said, the sting of it all was that the man he loved more than anything on earth should be shamed and humiliated! This murmuring against fate may have been shallow and unreasonable in my hero, but I repeat, for the third time—and I'm ready to admit it may be hard to defend the feeling—I'm glad my hero didn't show himself too reasonable in that moment, since any sensible man will always come back around to reason in time; but if love doesn't get the upper hand in a boy's heart at such an extraordinary moment, when will it? I won't, however, pass over something strange that surfaced for a while in Alyosha's mind at this fateful, murky moment. This new element was the disturbing impression left by his conversation with Ivan, which now clung persistently to Alyosha's mind. It haunted him just then. Oh, it wasn't that anything fundamental, elemental, so to speak, in his soul's faith had been shaken. He loved his God and believed in Him steadfastly, even as he suddenly found himself murmuring against Him. And yet a vague but tormenting, unsettling impression left by his talk with Ivan the day before suddenly revived in his soul, seeming to force its way up to the surface of his awareness.

It had begun to grow dark when Rakitin, cutting across the pine grove from the hermitage toward the monastery, suddenly spotted Alyosha lying face down on the ground under a tree, motionless, apparently asleep. He went over and called him by name.
"You, here, Alexey? Can you really have—" he began, wondering, then broke off. He'd meant to say, "Can you really have sunk to this?"
Alyosha didn't look at him, but from a slight movement Rakitin could tell at once that he'd heard and understood.
"What's the matter?" he went on; but the surprise on his face gradually gave way to a smile that grew more and more ironic.
"I say, I've been looking for you the last two hours. You just vanished. What are you doing? What's this foolishness? You might at least look at me...."

Alyosha lifted his head, sat up, and leaned his back against the tree. He wasn't crying, but there was suffering and irritation in his face. Still, he didn't look at Rakitin—he looked off to one side, past him.
"You know your face has changed completely? None of your famous mildness left in it at all. Angry with someone? Has someone been mistreating you?"
"Leave me alone," Alyosha said suddenly, with a tired wave of his hand, still looking away.

"Oho! So that's how it is with us! So you can snap at people like an ordinary mortal, can you. That's a bit of a fall from the angels. I say, Alyosha, you've surprised me, do you hear? I mean it. It's been a long time since anything around here surprised me. I always took you for an educated man...."
Alyosha looked at him at last, but vaguely, as though barely taking in what he was saying.

"Can you really be so upset simply because your old man's started to stink? You don't mean to tell me you seriously believed he was going to work miracles?" Rakitin exclaimed, genuinely surprised again.
"I believed it, I believe it, I want to believe it, and I will believe it—what more do you want?" Alyosha cried, irritated.

"Nothing at all, my boy. Damn it all, no schoolboy of thirteen believes in that sort of thing nowadays. But there you have it.... So now you're furious at your God, rebelling against Him—He hasn't handed out the promotion, hasn't pinned on the medal! Well, aren't you all a fine bunch!"
Alyosha stared at Rakitin a long while, his eyes half closed, and something suddenly flashed in them... but not anger at Rakitin.
"I'm not rebelling against my God—I simply 'don't accept His world.'" Alyosha suddenly gave a strained smile.
"What do you mean, you don't accept the world?" Rakitin thought over the answer for a moment. "What kind of idiocy is that?"
Alyosha didn't answer.
"Come on, enough of this nonsense, down to business. Have you eaten anything today?"
"I don't remember.... I think I have."

"You need feeding up, to judge by your face. It's enough to make a person sorry just looking at you. You didn't sleep all night either, I hear, you had some sort of gathering in there. And then all this uproar afterward. Most likely you've had nothing but a mouthful of holy bread. I've got some sausage in my pocket, brought it from town just in case, though you won't touch sausage, I suppose...."
"Give me some."

"Well, I never! You're really going for it! It's a regular mutiny, barricades and all! All right, my boy, we'd better make the most of it. Come to my place.... I could use a drop of vodka myself, I'm dead tired. Vodka's probably too much for you, I'd guess... or would you like some of that too?"
"Give me some vodka too."
"Well now! You do surprise me, brother!" Rakitin looked at him in amazement. "All right, either way, vodka or sausage, this is a fine bit of luck and shouldn't go to waste. Come along."
Alyosha got up without a word and followed Rakitin.
"If your little brother Ivan could see this, wouldn't he be surprised! By the way, your brother Ivan set off for Moscow this morning, did you know?"

"Yes," Alyosha answered listlessly, and suddenly the image of his brother Dmitri rose before his mind. But only for a moment, and although it reminded him of something that couldn't be put off, some duty, some terrible obligation, even that reminder left no real mark on him, didn't reach his heart, and instantly faded from his mind and was forgotten. But, long afterward, Alyosha remembered this.

"Your brother Ivan once said I was a 'liberal fool with no talent whatsoever.' You yourself once couldn't resist letting me know I was 'dishonorable.' Well! I'd like to see what your talent and your sense of honor do for you now." Rakitin finished this thought to himself, in a whisper.

"Listen!" he said aloud, "let's take the path beyond the monastery, straight to town. Hm! I ought to stop by Madame Hohlakov's on the way, by the by. Just imagine, I wrote and told her everything that happened, and would you believe it, she wrote straight back in pencil—the lady has a passion for writing notes—that 'she would never have expected such conduct from a man of such a reverend character as Father Zossima.' Those were her very words: 'conduct.' She's angry too. Eh, what a bunch you all are! Wait!" he suddenly cried again. He stopped abruptly, and, taking Alyosha by the shoulder, made him stop too.

"Do you know, Alyosha," he peered inquisitively into his eyes, caught up in some sudden new thought that had just struck him, and though he was laughing on the outside, he plainly felt uneasy about saying the new idea out loud, so hard did he still find it to believe in the strange, unexpected mood he now saw in Alyosha. "Alyosha, do you know where we'd better go?" he finally brought out, timidly and with a sly edge.
"I don't care... wherever you like."
"Let's go to Grushenka's, eh? Will you come?" Rakitin finally got out, trembling with nervous suspense.
"Let's go to Grushenka's," Alyosha answered calmly, at once, and this quick, calm agreement caught Rakitin so off guard that he nearly jumped back.
"Well! Would you look at that!" he cried in amazement, but grabbing Alyosha firmly by the arm, he led him off down the path, still afraid he might change his mind.
They walked along in silence; Rakitin was genuinely afraid to talk.

"And how glad she'll be, how delighted!" he muttered, then fell silent again. And in truth it wasn't to please Grushenka that he was bringing Alyosha to her. He was a practical man and never undertook anything without some prospect of gain for himself. His purpose here was twofold: first, a vengeful wish to witness "the downfall of the righteous," Alyosha's fall "from saint to sinner," which he was already savoring in his imagination; and second, he had his eye on a certain material gain for himself, of which more will be said later.
"So the critical moment has arrived," he thought to himself with spiteful glee, "and we'll catch it right as it happens, since that's exactly what we're after."

title: III. An Onion
paragraphs: Grushenka lived in the busiest part of town, near the cathedral square, in a small wooden lodge in the courtyard belonging to the widow Morozov's house. The house itself was a large two-story stone building, old and quite ugly. The widow lived a secluded life with her two unmarried nieces, themselves elderly women. She had no real need to rent out the lodge, but everyone knew she'd taken in Grushenka as a tenant four years earlier, solely to please her relative, the merchant Samsonov, known to be the girl's protector. It was said that the jealous old man's purpose in placing his "favorite" with the widow Morozov was so the old woman could keep a close eye on her new tenant's conduct. But that close eye soon proved unnecessary, and in the end the widow Morozov rarely even saw Grushenka and never bothered her with any kind of oversight. It's true that four years had passed since the old man brought the slim, delicate, shy, timid, dreamy, sad girl of eighteen from the provincial capital, and much had happened since then. Little was known around town about the girl's history, and what little was known was vague. Nothing more had come to light over the past four years, even once a good many people had grown interested in the beautiful young woman Agrafena Alexandrovna had since become. There were rumors that at seventeen she'd been seduced by someone, some sort of officer, and abandoned by him immediately after. The officer had gone away and later married, while Grushenka was left in poverty and disgrace. It was also said, though, that despite having been lifted out of destitution by old Samsonov, she actually came from a respectable family in the clerical class—that she was the daughter of a deacon or something along those lines.

And now, four years on, the sensitive, wounded, pitiable little orphan had become a plump, rosy beauty of the true Russian type, a woman of bold, determined character, proud and insolent. She had a sharp head for business, was acquisitive, thrifty, careful, and had managed, by fair means or foul, so it was said, to amass a modest fortune. There was only one point everyone agreed on. Grushenka wasn't easily approached, and apart from her elderly protector, not a single man could claim to have won her favor over those four years. This was a plain fact, since a good many had tried, especially over the last two years, to win those favors. But all their efforts had come to nothing, and some of these suitors had been forced into an undignified, even comic retreat, driven off by the firm, ironic resistance they met from the strong-willed young woman. It was also known that the young woman had, especially of late, taken up what's called "speculation," and had shown real talent for it, so much so that many people had begun saying she was no better than a Jewish moneylender. It wasn't that she lent money at interest, but it was known, for example, that she'd for some time been buying up bad debts in partnership with old Karamazov, purchasing them for a fraction, a tenth of their face value, and later turning them into ten times their worth.

Old Samsonov, a widower with a large fortune, was stingy and merciless. He ruled over his grown sons like a tyrant, but for the past year, laid up by illness and the swelling in his legs, he'd fallen more and more under the influence of his protégée, whom he'd at first kept on a tight leash, in humble circumstances, "on Lenten fare," as the local wits put it at the time. But Grushenka had managed to free herself from that, all while instilling in him a boundless faith in her loyalty. The old man, long dead now, had run a substantial business in his day and was, in his own right, a remarkable character—miserly and hard as flint. Though Grushenka's hold on him was so strong he couldn't live without her, especially these last two years, he never settled any real fortune on her, and nothing, not even a threat to leave him, would have moved him to. He had given her a small sum, though, and even that came as a surprise to everyone when word got around.

"You're a girl with a good head on her shoulders," he told her, when he handed over eight thousand roubles, "and you'll have to look out for yourself, but understand this: apart from your yearly allowance, as before, you'll get nothing more out of me until the day I die, and you'll get nothing in my will either."

And he kept his word; he died and left everything to his sons, whom he'd treated all his life, along with their wives and children, like servants. Grushenka wasn't even mentioned in the will. All of this came out later. He'd helped Grushenka with advice on growing her capital and steered business her way.

When Fyodor Pavlovitch, who'd first crossed paths with Grushenka over some business speculation, ended up, to his own astonishment, falling madly in love with her, old Samsonov, ill as he was, found it endlessly amusing. It's worth noting that throughout their entire acquaintance, Grushenka was completely and freely open with the old man, and he appears to have been the only person in the world with whom she was. Later, once Dmitri too had come onto the scene with his passion for her, the old man stopped laughing. Instead, he gave Grushenka a stern, serious piece of advice.

"If you have to choose between the two, father or son, better choose the old man, but only if you make sure beforehand that the old scoundrel will actually marry you and settle some money on you. Don't keep stringing along the captain—no good will come of that."
These were the very words of the old libertine, who could already feel that his death wasn't far off, and who did in fact die five months later.

I'll also note in passing that although many people in town knew of the grotesque, monstrous rivalry between the Karamazovs, father and son, both after Grushenka, almost no one really understood what actually lay behind her attitude toward the two of them. Even Grushenka's own two servants—after the catastrophe we'll speak of later—testified in court that she received Dmitri Fyodorovitch out of sheer fear, because "he threatened to kill her." These servants were an elderly cook, sickly and nearly deaf, who'd come with Grushenka from her old home, and the cook's granddaughter, a sharp young woman of twenty who did the work of a maid. Grushenka lived very frugally, and her surroundings were anything but luxurious. Her lodge consisted of three rooms furnished with mahogany pieces in the style of 1820, belonging to her landlady.

It was already quite dark by the time Rakitin and Alyosha entered her rooms, and yet no lamps were lit. Grushenka was lying in her drawing room on the big, hard, ungainly sofa with its mahogany back. The sofa was upholstered in worn, cracked leather. Under her head lay two white down pillows taken from her own bed. She lay stretched out on her back, perfectly still, her hands behind her head. She was dressed as though expecting someone: a black silk dress, a delicate lace scarf over her head, which suited her beautifully. A lace shawl was thrown over her shoulders, pinned with a heavy gold brooch. She really was expecting someone. She lay there as if impatient and worn out, her face rather pale, her lips and eyes burning, restlessly tapping the arm of the sofa with the tip of her right foot. Rakitin and Alyosha's arrival caused a brief stir. From the hall they could hear Grushenka spring up off the sofa and cry out in a frightened voice, "Who's there?" But the maid met the visitors and called back at once to her mistress.
"It's not him, it's nothing, just some other visitors."
"What on earth is going on?" Rakitin muttered, leading Alyosha into the drawing room.

Grushenka stood by the sofa, still looking alarmed. A thick coil of her dark brown hair had slipped loose from its lace covering and fallen over her right shoulder, but she didn't notice it, didn't tuck it back, until she'd looked her visitors over and recognized them.
"Ah, it's you, Rakitin? You gave me quite a fright. Who have you brought? Who's this with you? Good heavens, you've brought him!" she exclaimed, recognizing Alyosha.
"Send for some candles!" said Rakitin, with the easy familiarity of a man privileged to give orders in the house.

"Candles... yes, of course, candles.... Fenya, bring him a candle.... Well, you've certainly picked your moment to bring him!" she exclaimed again, nodding toward Alyosha, and turning to the mirror, she began quickly pinning up her hair with both hands. She seemed put out.
"Haven't I managed to please you?" Rakitin asked, instantly almost offended.

"You gave me a fright, Rakitin, that's all it is." Grushenka turned to Alyosha with a smile. "Don't be afraid of me, dear Alyosha, you can't imagine how glad I am to see you, my unexpected guest. But you frightened me, Rakitin, I thought it was Mitya breaking in. You see, I deceived him just now—I made him promise to believe me, and I told him a lie. I told him I'd be spending the evening with my old man, Kuzma Kuzmitch, going through his money till late. I spend a whole evening with him every week, going over his accounts. We lock ourselves in and he counts on his abacus while I sit and write it all down in the book. I'm the only one he trusts. Mitya believes I'm there, but I slipped back and have been sitting here with the door locked, waiting for news. How did Fenya even let you in? Fenya, Fenya, run out to the gate, open it, see if the captain's anywhere about! Maybe he's hiding, spying on the place—I'm terribly frightened."
"There's no one there, Agrafena Alexandrovna, I just looked, I keep running out to peek through the gap, I'm shaking in my own boots."

"Are the shutters fastened, Fenya? And we ought to draw the curtains too—there, that's better!" She drew the heavy curtains herself. "He'd come rushing straight in if he saw a light. I'm terribly afraid of your brother Mitya today, Alyosha."
Grushenka spoke this out loud, and though she was clearly alarmed, she also seemed happy about something.
"Why are you so afraid of Mitya today?" Rakitin asked. "I'd have thought you weren't shy with him at all—you twist him round your little finger."

"I'm telling you, I'm expecting news, priceless news, so I don't want Mitya anywhere near me right now. And he didn't believe me, I could tell he didn't, that I'd be staying at Kuzma Kuzmitch's. He must be lying in wait right now, behind Fyodor Pavlovitch's place, in the garden, watching for me. And if he's there, he won't come here, so much the better! But I really was at Kuzma Kuzmitch's, Mitya walked me there himself. I told him I'd stay till midnight and asked him to be sure to come fetch me home at midnight. He went off, and I sat with Kuzma Kuzmitch for ten minutes and slipped back here again. Oof, I was so afraid, I ran the whole way for fear of running into him."
"And why are you all dressed up like that? What a strange little cap you've got on."

"Aren't you the curious one, Rakitin! I told you, I'm expecting a message. If the message comes, I'll fly out of here, I'll gallop off, and you won't see me again. That's why I'm dressed up, so I'll be ready."
"And where will you be flying off to?"
"Know too much too young, and you'll grow old too fast."
"Well, well! You're in high spirits... I've never seen you quite like this before. Dressed up like you're off to a ball." Rakitin looked her up and down.
"Much you know about balls."
"And do you know so much more about them?"

"I've seen a ball. The year before last, Kuzma Kuzmitch's son got married, and I watched from the gallery. Do you really think I want to sit here talking to you, Rakitin, when a prince like this is standing right here? What a visitor! Alyosha, my dear boy, I can hardly believe my eyes, looking at you. Good heavens, that you'd actually come here to see me! To tell you the truth, it never once crossed my mind that I'd see you, I never thought you'd ever come to see me. Though this isn't really the moment, I'm still terribly glad to see you. Sit down here on the sofa, that's it, my bright young moon. I still can't quite take it in.... Eh, Rakitin, if only you'd brought him yesterday, or the day before! But I'm glad even now! Maybe it's better he's come just now, at a moment like this, rather than the day before yesterday."

She sat down cheerfully beside Alyosha on the sofa, gazing at him with real delight. And she really was delighted—she wasn't lying about that. Her eyes glowed, her lips laughed, but it was a good-natured, merry laugh. Alyosha hadn't expected to see such a kind expression on her face.... He'd barely met her before the day before, had formed a frightening picture of her in his mind, and had been horribly upset the day before by the spiteful, treacherous trick she'd played on Katerina Ivanovna. He was greatly surprised now to find her so entirely different from what he'd expected. And, crushed as he was by his own grief, his eyes rested on her, unable to help themselves, taking her in with real attention. Her whole manner seemed to have changed for the better since the day before; there was hardly any trace of that cloying sweetness in her speech, that voluptuous softness in her movements. Everything about her was simple and good-natured, her gestures quick, direct, trusting—but she was greatly worked up.
"Goodness, how everything's coming together today!" she chattered on. "And why I'm so glad to see you, Alyosha, I couldn't even say myself! If you asked me, I couldn't tell you."
"Come now, don't you know why you're glad?" Rakitin said, grinning. "You used to keep pestering me to bring him around, you must have had some reason."

"I had a different reason once, but that's over now, this isn't the moment for it. I only want to give you something nice right now. I'm feeling so good-natured today. Sit down too, Rakitin—why are you standing? Oh, you've already sat down. No fear of Rakitin ever forgetting to look after himself. Look, Alyosha, there he sits across from us, so offended I didn't ask him to sit down before you. Ugh, Rakitin's such a one for taking offense!" Grushenka laughed. "Don't be angry, Rakitin, I'm feeling kind today. Why are you so downcast, Alyosha? Afraid of me?" She peered into his eyes with merry mockery.
"He's sad. No promotion came through," Rakitin boomed.
"What promotion?"
"His elder's started to stink."

"What? You're talking nonsense, you just want to say something nasty. Be quiet, you fool! Let me sit on your knee, Alyosha, like this." She suddenly hopped forward and jumped, laughing, onto his knee, like a little bird settling in, her right arm around his neck. "I'll cheer you up, my pious boy. Really, will you let me sit on your knee? You won't be angry? Just say the word and I'll get up."

Alyosha said nothing. He sat there, afraid to move; he heard her say, "Just say the word and I'll get up," but gave no answer. But there was nothing in his heart of the sort Rakitin, watching him spitefully from his corner, might have expected or imagined. The great grief in his heart swallowed up every other feeling that might otherwise have been stirred, and if he could only have thought clearly in that moment, he'd have realized he now carried the strongest possible armor against every lust and every temptation. And yet, despite the vague numbness of his spiritual state and the sorrow weighing him down, he couldn't help marveling at a new, strange sensation in his heart. This woman, this "terrible" woman, held no terror for him now, none of the fear that used to stir in his soul at even the passing thought of a woman. On the contrary, this woman, dreaded above all women, sitting now on his knee, her arms around him, stirred in him a wholly different, unexpected, peculiar feeling—a feeling of the purest, most intense interest, without a trace of fear, of his old dread. That was what struck him, almost instinctively, with surprise.
"You've talked enough nonsense," Rakitin cried, "you'd do better to bring us some champagne. You owe it to me, you know you do!"

"Yes, I really do. Do you know, Alyosha, I promised him champagne on top of everything else, if he'd bring you? I'll have some too! Fenya, Fenya, bring us the bottle Mitya left behind! Look sharp! Stingy as I am, I'll stand a bottle—not for you, Rakitin, you're a toadstool—but for him, because he's a falcon! And though my heart's full of something else entirely, so be it, I'll drink with you. I'm longing for a little wildness."
"But what's the matter with you? And what's this message, may I ask, or is it a secret?" Rakitin put in, curious, doing his best to pretend not to notice the jabs constantly aimed his way.

"Ech, it's no secret, and you know it too," Grushenka said, her voice suddenly anxious, turning her head toward Rakitin and pulling back a little from Alyosha, though she still sat on his knee with her arm around his neck. "My officer's coming, Rakitin, my officer's coming."
"I heard he was on his way, but is he that close now?"
"He's at Mokroe right now; he'll send a messenger from there, so he wrote—I got a letter from him today. I'm expecting the messenger any minute."
"You don't say! Why Mokroe, of all places?"
"That's a long story, I've told you as much as I'm going to."
"Mitya's going to be up to something now, I tell you. Does he know, or doesn't he?"

"Him know! Of course not. If he knew, there'd be murder. But I'm not afraid of that right now, I'm not afraid of his knife. Hush, Rakitin, don't remind me of Dmitri Fyodorovitch, he's bruised my heart badly enough already. And I don't want to think about that right now. I want to think about Alyosha here, I want to look at Alyosha... smile at me, dear, cheer up, smile at my foolishness, at my happiness.... Ah, he's smiling, he's smiling! How kindly he looks at me! And you know, Alyosha, I've been thinking all this time that you were angry with me, over what happened the day before yesterday, over that young lady. I was a wretch, that's the truth of it.... But it's a good thing it happened the way it did. A nasty business, but a good thing too." Grushenka smiled dreamily, and a faint cruel line showed in that smile. "Mitya told me she screamed out that I 'ought to be flogged.' I really did insult her terribly. She sent for me, she wanted to win me over, charm me with her chocolate.... No, it's a good thing it ended the way it did." She smiled again. "But I'm still afraid you're angry with me."
"Yes, that's actually true," Rakitin put in suddenly, genuinely surprised. "Alyosha, she's actually afraid of a chick like you."

"He's a chick to you, Rakitin... because you've got no conscience, that's the whole of it! You see, I love him with my whole soul, that's how it is! Alyosha, do you believe I love you with my whole soul?"
"Ah, you shameless woman! She's declaring herself to you, Alexey!"
"Well, and what of it, I love him!"
"And what about your officer? And that priceless message from Mokroe?"
"That's a completely different thing."
"That's just how a woman looks at it!"

"Don't you go making me angry, Rakitin." Grushenka cut him off sharply. "This is entirely different. I love Alyosha differently. It's true, Alyosha, I once had sly designs on you. Because I'm a nasty, violent creature. But other times I've looked at you, Alyosha, as my conscience. I've kept thinking, 'How someone like that must despise a wretched thing like me.' I thought that the day before yesterday, running home from that young lady's. I've thought of you that way for a long time now, Alyosha, and Mitya knows it, I've talked to him about it. Mitya understands. Would you believe it, sometimes I look at you and feel ashamed, utterly ashamed of myself.... And how it started, and when I began thinking of you that way, I couldn't say, I don't remember...."
Fenya came in and set a tray with an uncorked bottle and three champagne glasses on the table.

"Here's the champagne!" Rakitin cried. "You're all worked up, Agrafena Alexandrovna, not yourself at all. Once you've had a glass of champagne, you'll be ready to dance. Eh, they can't even manage this properly," he added, eyeing the bottle. "The old woman poured it out in the kitchen and the bottle's come in warm, with no cork on it. Well, give it here anyway."
He went up to the table, took a glass, emptied it in one gulp, and poured himself another.

"Champagne doesn't come round every day," he said, licking his lips. "Now, Alyosha, take a glass, show us what you can do! What shall we drink to? The gates of paradise? Take a glass, Grushenka, you drink to the gates of paradise too."
"What gates of paradise?"
She took a glass, Alyosha took his, tasted it, and set it back down.
"No, I'd better not," he said, smiling gently.
"And you were bragging!" Rakitin cried.
"Well, if that's how it is, I won't either," Grushenka chimed in, "I don't really want any, truth be told. You can drink the whole bottle yourself, Rakitin. If Alyosha drinks, I'll drink."

"What touching sentimentality!" said Rakitin, mocking. "And she's sitting on his knee, too! He's got something to grieve over, but what's got into you? He's rebelling against his God and ready to eat sausage...."
"How's that?"
"His elder died today. Father Zossima, the saint."

"So Father Zossima's dead," Grushenka cried. "Good God, I didn't know!" She crossed herself devoutly. "Heavens, what have I been doing, sitting on his knee like this at a moment like this!" She jumped up as though startled, slid off his lap at once, and sat down on the sofa.
Alyosha fixed her with a long, wondering look, and something like light seemed to dawn on his face.

"Rakitin," he said suddenly, in a firm, loud voice, "don't taunt me with rebelling against God. I don't want to feel angry at you, so you'll have to be kinder too—I've lost a treasure such as you've never had, and you're not in a position to judge me right now. You'd do much better to look at her—do you see how she's taken pity on me? I came here looking for my own ruin—I felt drawn to evil, because I was base and evil myself—and instead I've found a true sister, I've found a treasure, a loving heart. She had pity on me, just now.... Agrafena Alexandrovna, I'm talking about you. You've lifted my soul up out of the depths."
Alyosha's lips trembled and he caught his breath.
"She's saved you, it seems," Rakitin laughed spitefully. "And here she was meaning to get you in her clutches, do you realize that?"

"Stop, Rakitin." Grushenka jumped to her feet. "Hush, both of you. Now I'll tell you the whole thing. Hush, Alyosha, your words make me ashamed, because I'm bad, not good—that's what I am. And you hush too, Rakitin, because you're lying now. I did have the low idea of trying to get him in my clutches, but that was before, now everything's different. And I don't want to hear another word out of you, Rakitin."
Grushenka said all of this with intense feeling.
"They're both out of their minds," said Rakitin, staring at them in amazement. "I feel like I've wandered into a madhouse. They're both getting so weepy they'll start crying any minute."
"I will start crying, I will," Grushenka repeated. "He called me his sister and I'll never forget that. Only let me tell you, Rakitin—bad as I am, I did give away an onion once."
"An onion? What the devil, you really have gone mad."

Rakitin marveled at their sudden fervor. He was hurt and irritated, though he might have reflected that each of them was passing through a spiritual crisis of the kind that doesn't come often in a lifetime. But while Rakitin was extremely sensitive about anything touching himself, he was quite obtuse when it came to other people's feelings and experiences—partly from youth and inexperience, partly from sheer self-regard.

"You see, Alyosha," Grushenka turned to him with a nervous laugh, "I was bragging when I told Rakitin I'd given away an onion, but I'm not telling you this to boast. It's just a story, but it's a good one. I used to hear it as a child from Matryona, my cook, who's still with me. It goes like this. Once upon a time there was a peasant woman, and a very wicked woman she was. And she died, and left not a single good deed behind her. The devils caught her and threw her into the lake of fire. So her guardian angel stood there, wondering if there was any good deed of hers at all he could bring up to God. 'She once pulled up an onion from her garden,' he said, 'and gave it to a beggar woman.' And God answered: 'Take that onion, then, hold it out to her in the lake, and let her grab hold, and you can pull her out by it. And if you manage to pull her out of the lake, let her come into Paradise, but if the onion breaks, then the woman has to stay right where she is.' The angel ran to the woman and held the onion out to her. 'Here,' he said, 'grab hold, and I'll pull you out.' And he began carefully pulling her up. He'd very nearly pulled her all the way out when the other sinners in the lake, seeing her being drawn up, started grabbing hold of her too, so they could be pulled out along with her. But she was a very wicked woman, and she started kicking them off. 'It's me being pulled out, not you. It's my onion, not yours.' The moment she said that, the onion snapped. And the woman fell back into the lake, and she's burning there to this day. So the angel wept and went away. That's the story, Alyosha; I know it by heart, because I'm that wicked woman myself. I bragged to Rakitin that I gave away an onion, but to you I'll say: 'I've done nothing in my whole life but give away that one onion, that's the only good deed I've ever done.' So don't you praise me, Alyosha, don't think me good, I'm bad, I'm a wicked woman, and it shames me if you praise me. Eh, I might as well confess everything. Listen, Alyosha. I wanted so badly to get hold of you that I promised Rakitin twenty-five roubles if he'd bring you to me. Wait, Rakitin, hold on!"
She went with quick steps to the table, opened a drawer, pulled out a purse, and took out a twenty-five rouble note.
"What nonsense! What nonsense!" Rakitin cried, thrown off balance.
"Take it. Rakitin, I owe it to you, don't even think of refusing, you asked for it yourself." And she tossed the note to him.
"As if I'd refuse it," Rakitin boomed, clearly embarrassed but covering his confusion with bravado. "That'll come in handy—fools were made for wise men's profit."
"Now hold your tongue, Rakitin, what I'm about to say isn't for your ears. Go sit in that corner and stay quiet. You don't even like us, so hush."

"Why should I like you?" Rakitin snapped, not bothering to hide his sour mood. He tucked the twenty-five rouble note into his pocket and felt ashamed that Alyosha had seen it. He'd counted on being paid later, without Alyosha's knowledge, and now, embarrassed, he lost his temper entirely. Up to that moment he'd thought it wise not to contradict Grushenka too directly, despite her snubs, since he still had something to get out of her. But now he was angry too:
"People love each other for some reason or other, but what have either of you ever done for me?"
"You're supposed to love people without a reason, the way Alyosha does."
"How does he love you? What's he done to prove it, that you're making such a fuss over it?"
Grushenka was standing in the middle of the room; she spoke heatedly, and there was something hysterical in her voice.

"Hush, Rakitin, you know nothing about the two of us! And don't you dare talk to me like that again. How dare you take such liberties! Sit in that corner and be quiet, like you were my footman! And now, Alyosha, I'm going to tell you the whole truth, so you can see what a wretch I am! I'm not talking to Rakitin, I'm talking to you. I wanted to ruin you, Alyosha, that's the plain truth; I fully meant to. I wanted it so badly that I bribed Rakitin to bring you here. And why did I want to do such a thing? You knew nothing about it, Alyosha, you turned away from me; if you passed me on the street, you dropped your eyes. And I'd looked at you a hundred times before today; I started asking everyone about you. Your face wouldn't leave me alone. 'He despises me,' I thought, 'he won't even look at me.' And I felt it so keenly in the end that I marveled at myself for being so frightened of a boy. I'll get him in my clutches, I thought, and I'll laugh at him. I was full of spite and anger. Would you believe it, nobody around here dares even think of coming to Agrafena Alexandrovna with any evil intent. Old Kuzma is the only man I have any dealings with here; I was bound to him, sold to him, the devil brought us together, but there's been no one else. But looking at you, I thought, I'll get him in my clutches and laugh at him. See what a spiteful cur I am, and you called me your sister! And now that man who wronged me has come back; I'm sitting here waiting for a message from him. And do you know what that man has meant to me? Five years ago, when Kuzma brought me here, I used to shut myself up so no one could see or hear anything of me. I was a silly young slip of a girl; I used to sit here sobbing; I used to lie awake whole nights, thinking, 'Where is he now, the man who wronged me? Laughing at me with some other woman, most likely. If only I could see him, if I could just meet him again, I'd pay him back, I'd pay him back!' At night I'd lie sobbing into my pillow in the dark, brooding over it, tearing my own heart apart on purpose and gloating over my own anger. 'I'll pay him back, I'll pay him back!' That's what I used to cry out into the dark. And then, when it suddenly struck me that I'd really do nothing to him at all, that he was probably laughing at me right then, or had forgotten me entirely, I'd throw myself on the floor, dissolve into helpless tears, and lie there shaking until dawn. In the morning I'd get up nastier than a dog, ready to tear the whole world apart. And then what do you suppose happened? I started saving money, grew hard-hearted, put on weight—grew wiser, would you say? No, no one in the whole world sees it, no one knows it, but when night falls I sometimes still lie there just as I did five years ago, a foolish girl, clenching my teeth, crying the whole night through, thinking, 'I'll pay him back, I'll pay him back!' Do you hear me? Well, now you understand me. A month ago a letter came—he was on his way, a widower now, he wanted to see me. It took my breath clean away; and then it suddenly struck me: 'If he comes and whistles for me, I'll go crawling back to him like a beaten dog.' I couldn't believe it of myself. Am I really that low? Will I run to him or won't I? And I've been so furious with myself this whole month that I'm worse than I was five years ago. Do you see now, Alyosha, what a violent, vindictive creature I am? I've shown you the whole truth! I played with Mitya just to keep myself from running to that other man. Hush, Rakitin, it's not for you to judge me, I'm not talking to you. Before you two came in, I was lying here waiting, brooding, deciding the whole rest of my life, and you can never know what was going on in my heart. Yes, Alyosha, tell your young lady not to be angry with me over what happened the day before yesterday.... Nobody in the whole world knows what I'm going through right now, and no one ever will.... Because maybe I'll take a knife with me today, I can't make up my mind..."
And at this "tragic" declaration, Grushenka broke down, buried her face in her hands, flung herself onto the sofa cushions, and sobbed like a small child.
Alyosha got up and went over to Rakitin.
"Misha," he said, "don't be angry. She wounded you, but don't hold it against her. Did you hear what she just said? You can't ask too much of human endurance—one has to be merciful."

Alyosha said this on the instinctive prompting of his heart. He felt he had to say something, and he turned to Rakitin. If Rakitin hadn't been there, he'd have spoken to the empty air. But Rakitin looked at him with an ironic expression, and Alyosha stopped short.
"You were so wound up with your elder's teaching last night that now you have to let it off on me, Alexey, man of God!" said Rakitin, with a hateful smile.

"Don't laugh, Rakitin, don't smile, don't talk about the dead—he was better than anyone in the world!" Alyosha cried, tears in his voice. "I wasn't speaking to you as a judge, but as the lowest of the judged. What am I, next to her? I came here looking for my own ruin, telling myself, 'What does it matter,' out of pure cowardice—but she, after five years of torment, the moment someone speaks a single word from the heart to her, forgets everything, forgives everything, in her tears! The man who wronged her has come back, he sends for her, and she forgives him everything, and hurries off joyfully to meet him, and she won't take a knife along. She won't! No, I'm not like that. I don't know about you, Misha, but I'm not like that. It's a lesson to me.... She has more love in her than we do.... Have you ever heard her speak before about what she just told us? No, you haven't; if you had, you'd have understood her long ago... and the person she insulted the day before yesterday will have to forgive her too! She will, once she knows... and she will know.... This soul isn't at peace with itself yet, one has to be gentle with it... there may be a treasure hidden in that soul...."
Alyosha stopped, out of breath. Despite his sour mood, Rakitin looked at him in astonishment. He'd never expected such a speech from the gentle Alyosha.
"She's found herself a defender! Why, are you in love with her? Agrafena Alexandrovna, our monk here's really fallen for you, you've made a conquest!" he cried, with a coarse laugh.
Grushenka lifted her head from the pillow and looked at Alyosha with a tender smile on her tear-streaked face.

"Leave him be, Alyosha, my little angel, you see what he is, he's not someone worth talking to. Mihail Osipovitch," she turned to Rakitin, "I meant to apologize for being rude to you, but now I don't feel like it. Alyosha, come here, sit down." She beckoned to him with a happy smile. "That's it, sit here. Tell me," she took his hand and peered into his face, smiling, "tell me, do I love that man or not—the one who wronged me, do I love him or not? Before you came, I was lying here in the dark, asking my own heart whether I loved him. You decide for me, Alyosha, the time's come, whatever you say, so it'll be. Should I forgive him or not?"
"But you've already forgiven him," Alyosha said, smiling.

"Yes, I really have forgiven him," Grushenka murmured, thoughtfully. "What a wretched heart! To my own wretched heart!" She snatched a glass off the table, drained it in one gulp, lifted it in the air, and flung it to the floor. The glass shattered with a crash. A faint cruel line crept into her smile.

"Or maybe I haven't forgiven him, though," she said, a kind of menace in her voice, dropping her eyes to the floor as though talking to herself. "Maybe my heart's only just getting ready to forgive. I'll have to fight it out with my own heart. You see, Alyosha, I've grown fond of my tears, over these five years.... Maybe it's my resentment I love, and not him at all..."
"Well, I shouldn't much like to be in his shoes," Rakitin hissed.
"Well, you won't be, Rakitin, you'll never be in his shoes. You can black my shoes, Rakitin, that's about your speed. You'll never get a woman like me... and maybe he won't either..."
"Won't he? Then why get all dressed up like that?" Rakitin said, with a venomous sneer.

"Don't you taunt me about dressing up, Rakitin, you don't know everything in my heart! If I wanted to tear off all this finery, I'd tear it off right now, this very minute," she cried, in a ringing voice. "You don't know what this finery is for, Rakitin! Maybe I'll see him and say: 'Have you ever seen me look like this before?' He left me a thin, sickly little crybaby of seventeen. I'll sit next to him, I'll charm him, work him up into a state. 'See what I look like now?' I'll say to him; 'well, that's all you're getting, my dear sir, there's many a slip between the cup and the lip!' That may be exactly what this finery's for, Rakitin." Grushenka finished with a spiteful laugh. "I'm a violent, vengeful creature, Alyosha, I'll tear off my finery, I'll ruin my own looks, scorch my own face, slash it with a knife, and go begging in the streets. If I wanted to, I wouldn't go see anyone at all now. If I wanted to, I'd send Kuzma back everything he's ever given me, tomorrow, every last rouble of it, and go out scrubbing floors for the rest of my life. You think I wouldn't do it, Rakitin, that I wouldn't dare? I would, I would, I could do it this instant, only don't push me too far... and I'll send him packing, I'll snap my fingers right in his face, he'll never lay eyes on me again!"
She hurled the last words out in a hysterical scream, then broke down again, hid her face in her hands, buried it in the pillow, and shook with sobs.
Rakitin got up.
"Time we were off," he said, "it's late, they'll lock us out of the monastery."
Grushenka sprang up from her seat.

"Surely you're not leaving, Alyosha!" she cried, in mournful astonishment. "What have you done to me? You've stirred up my feelings, tormented me, and now you're going to leave me to face this night alone!"
"He can hardly spend the night with you! Though if he wants to, let him! I'm off on my own," Rakitin scoffed, jeering.
