"Hush, you spiteful tongue!" Grushenka snapped at him angrily; "you've never once said the kind of words to me that he's come here to say."
"What's he said to you that's so special?" Rakitin asked, irritated.

"I can't say, I don't know. I don't know what he said to me, it went straight to my heart, he's wrung my very heart.... He's the first person, the only one, who's ever pitied me, that's what it is. Why didn't you come sooner, you angel?" She dropped to her knees before him, in a sudden fit of feeling. "I've been waiting my whole life for someone like you, I knew that someone like you would come and forgive me. I believed that, wretched as I am, someone would really love me, not just with a shameful kind of love!"
"What have I done for you?" Alyosha answered, bending over her with a tender smile and gently taking her hands. "I only gave you an onion, nothing but a tiny little onion, that's all!"

He was moved to tears himself, saying it. At that moment there was a sudden noise in the hallway, someone came into the entryway. Grushenka jumped up, looking thoroughly alarmed. Fenya burst noisily into the room, crying out:

"Mistress, mistress darling, a messenger's ridden up!" she cried, breathless and overjoyed. "A carriage from Mokroe for you, Timofey driving, with three horses, they're putting in fresh ones right now.... A letter, here's the letter, mistress."

A letter was in her hand and she waved it in the air the whole time she talked. Grushenka snatched the letter from her and carried it to the candle. It was only a note, a few lines. She read it in an instant.
"He's sent for me," she cried, her face white and twisted, a wan smile on it; "he's whistling for me! Crawl back, little dog!"
But she stood there hesitating only for an instant; then all at once the blood rushed to her head, flooding her cheeks with color.

"I'll go," she cried; "five years of my life! Good-bye! Good-bye, Alyosha, my fate is sealed. Go, go, all of you, leave me be, don't let me see you again! Grushenka is flying off to a new life.... And you, Rakitin, don't hold any of this against me either. I may be going to my death! Ugh! I feel like I'm drunk!"
She suddenly left them and ran into her bedroom.
"Well, she's got no thought for us now!" Rakitin grumbled. "Let's go, or we'll hear that woman's shriek again. I've had enough of all this crying and carrying on."

Alyosha let himself be led out without a word, moving mechanically. In the yard stood a covered cart. The horses were being unhitched from the shafts, men were running back and forth with a lantern. Three fresh horses were being led in through the open gate. But as Alyosha and Rakitin reached the bottom of the steps, Grushenka's bedroom window suddenly flew open, and she called after Alyosha in a ringing voice:

"Alyosha, give my greetings to your brother Mitya, and tell him not to hold any of this against me, even though I've brought him such misery. And tell him too, in my own words: 'Grushenka has fallen for a scoundrel, and not for you, noble heart.' And add this too: that Grushenka loved him for just one hour, only one short hour did she love him—so let him remember that hour for the rest of his life—say, 'Grushenka tells you to!'"
She finished in a voice full of sobs. The window slammed shut.
"Hm, hm!" Rakitin growled, laughing. "She murders your brother Mitya and then tells him to remember it his whole life! What ferocity!"

Alyosha made no reply, seemed not even to have heard. He walked fast alongside Rakitin, as though in a tremendous hurry. He was lost in thought, moving mechanically. Rakitin felt a sudden pang, as though someone had pressed on an open wound. He'd expected something quite different from bringing Grushenka and Alyosha together. Something very different from what he'd hoped for had happened instead.

"He's a Pole, that officer of hers," he began again, restraining himself; "and honestly he's not even an officer any more. Worked in customs somewhere in Siberia, on the Chinese border, some puny little beggar of a Pole, I'd guess. Lost his post, they say. He's heard now that Grushenka's put a bit of money aside, so he's turned up again—that's the whole mystery explained."
Once again Alyosha seemed not to hear. Rakitin couldn't hold himself back any longer.

"So, you've saved the sinner, then?" he laughed spitefully. "Turned the Magdalene onto the true path? Driven out the seven devils, eh? So there you are, those miracles you were looking for earlier have come to pass after all!"
"Hush, Rakitin," Alyosha answered, his heart aching.
"So now you despise me over that twenty-five roubles? Sold out a friend, is that what you think? But you're not Christ, you know, and I'm no Judas."
"Oh, Rakitin, I swear to you I'd already forgotten about it," Alyosha cried, "you're the one reminding me of it now...."
But this was the last straw for Rakitin.
"To hell with the lot of you!" he suddenly cried. "Why the devil did I ever take you up? I don't want anything more to do with you from now on. Go on alone, there's your road!"
And he turned abruptly down another street, leaving Alyosha alone in the dark. Alyosha came out of the town and walked across the fields toward the monastery.

title: IV. Cana Of Galilee
paragraphs: It was very late, by monastery standards, when Alyosha returned to the hermitage; the gatekeeper let him in through a side entrance. It had already struck nine—the hour of rest after a day of such upheaval for everyone. Alyosha timidly opened the door and went into the elder's cell, where the coffin now stood. There was no one in the cell but Father Païssy, reading the Gospel alone over the coffin, and the young novice Porfiry, who, worn out by the previous night's conversation and the day's unsettling events, was sleeping the deep, sound sleep of youth on the floor of the other room. Though Father Païssy heard Alyosha come in, he didn't even glance his way. Alyosha turned right from the door, toward the corner, dropped to his knees, and began to pray.

His soul was overflowing, but with mixed feelings; no single sensation stood out clearly; instead, one drove out another in a slow, continuous rotation. But there was a sweetness in his heart, and, strange to say, Alyosha wasn't surprised by it. Once again he saw the coffin before him, the hidden dead figure so precious to him, but the weeping and piercing grief of the morning no longer ached inside him. The moment he came in he'd fallen before the coffin as before a holy shrine, but joy, joy, was glowing in his mind and in his heart. The cell's one window stood open, the air fresh and cool. "So the smell must have gotten stronger, if they've opened the window," Alyosha thought. But even this thought of the smell of decay, which had struck him as so dreadful and humiliating just hours before, no longer made him feel wretched or indignant. He began praying quietly, but soon felt he was praying almost mechanically. Fragments of thought drifted through his mind, flashed like stars and went out again at once, replaced by others. And yet a sense of wholeness reigned in his soul—something steady and comforting—and he was aware of it himself. At moments he began praying fervently, longing to pour out his gratitude and love....

But once he'd begun to pray, he'd suddenly drift off into something else, sink into thought, forgetting both the prayer and whatever had interrupted it. He started listening to what Father Païssy was reading, but, worn out with exhaustion, gradually began to doze.
"And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee," Father Païssy read. "And the mother of Jesus was there: And both Jesus was called, and his disciples, to the marriage."

"Marriage? What's that?... A marriage!" floated whirling through Alyosha's mind. "There's happiness for her too.... She's gone to the feast.... No, she didn't take the knife.... That was just a tragic turn of phrase.... Well... tragic phrases should be forgiven, they have to be. Tragic phrases comfort the heart.... Without them, sorrow would be too heavy for people to bear. Rakitin's gone off down some back alley. As long as Rakitin keeps brooding over his grievances, he'll always end up down some back alley.... But the high road... The road is wide and straight and bright as crystal, and the sun is waiting at the end of it.... Ah!... What's being read?"...
"And when they wanted wine, the mother of Jesus saith unto him, They have no wine"... Alyosha heard.

"Ah, yes, I was missing that part, and I didn't want to miss it, I love this passage: it's Cana of Galilee, the first miracle.... Ah, that miracle! Ah, that sweet miracle! It wasn't people's grief but their joy Christ came to visit—He worked His first miracle to add to people's happiness.... 'Whoever loves people loves their happiness too'—he kept repeating that, it was one of his central ideas.... 'There's no living without joy,' Mitya says.... Yes, Mitya.... 'Everything true and good is always full of forgiveness,' he used to say that too"...
"Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come.
"His mother saith unto the servants, Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it"...

"Do it.... Joy, the joy of some poor, very poor people.... Of course they were poor, since they didn't even have enough wine at a wedding.... Historians write that, in those days, the people living around the Sea of Galilee were about as poor as anyone could possibly be... and another great heart, that other great being, His Mother, knew He'd come not only to make His great, terrible sacrifice. She knew His heart was open even to the plain, artless merrymaking of a handful of obscure, unlearned people, who had warmly invited Him to their humble wedding. 'Mine hour is not yet come,' He said, with a gentle smile—He must have smiled gently at her. And really, was it to keep the wine flowing at poor people's weddings that He'd come down to earth? And yet He went and did just as she asked.... Ah, he's reading again"...
"Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.
"And he saith unto them, Draw out now, and bear unto the governor of the feast. And they bare it.
"When the ruler of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and knew not whence it was: (but the servants which drew the water knew;) the governor of the feast called the bridegroom,
"And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now."

"But what's this, what's this? Why is the room growing wider?... Ah, yes... It's the marriage, the wedding... yes, of course. Here are the guests, here sit the young couple, and the merry crowd, and... Where's the wise governor of the feast? But who is this? Who? The walls are receding again.... Who's that, rising from the great table? What!... Him too? But he's in the coffin... and yet he's here too. He's stood up, he sees me, he's coming this way.... God!"...

Yes, he was coming toward him, toward him, that little, thin old man, with the fine wrinkles on his face, joyful, laughing softly. There was no coffin now, and he wore the same clothes he'd worn the day before, sitting among them, when the visitors had gathered around him. His face was uncovered, his eyes were shining. How could this be? He too had been called to the feast. He too, to the marriage at Cana in Galilee....
"Yes, my dear, I'm called too, called and invited," he heard a soft voice say over him. "Why have you hidden yourself away here, out of sight? Come and join us too."
It was his voice, Father Zossima's voice. And it had to be him, since he was the one calling!
The elder took Alyosha by the hand and lifted him, and he rose from his knees.

"We're rejoicing," the little, thin old man went on. "We're drinking the new wine, the wine of a new, great gladness; do you see how many guests there are? Here are the bride and bridegroom, here's the wise governor of the feast, tasting the new wine. Why are you so amazed at me? I gave an onion to a beggar woman once, and so I'm here too. And many here have given only an onion each—only one little onion.... What are any of our deeds worth, really? And you, my gentle one, you, my kind boy, you too knew how to give a starving woman an onion today. Begin your work, dear one, begin it, gentle one!... Do you see our Sun, do you see Him?"
"I'm afraid... I don't dare look," Alyosha whispered.

"Don't be afraid of Him. He's terrible in His greatness, awesome in His majesty, but infinitely merciful. He has made Himself like us out of love, and rejoices with us. He's turning the water into wine so the guests' gladness won't be cut short. He's waiting for new guests, calling new ones ceaselessly, forever and ever.... There, they're bringing new wine. Do you see, they're carrying in the vessels...."
Something glowed in Alyosha's heart, something filled it until it ached, tears of rapture rose up from his soul.... He stretched out his hands, cried out, and woke up.

Again the coffin, the open window, the soft, solemn, measured reading of the Gospel. But Alyosha wasn't listening to the reading now. It was strange—he'd fallen asleep on his knees, but now he was on his feet, and suddenly, as though propelled forward, he crossed to the coffin in three firm, quick strides. His shoulder brushed against Father Païssy without his even noticing. Father Païssy lifted his eyes from his book for a moment, but looked away again at once, seeing that something strange was happening to the boy. Alyosha gazed for half a minute at the coffin, at the shrouded, motionless dead man lying inside it, the icon on his chest, the peaked cap with its eight-pointed cross on his head. He'd only just been hearing his voice, and that voice was still ringing in his ears. He stood listening, still expecting more words, but suddenly turned sharply and walked out of the cell.

He didn't pause on the steps either, but went quickly down; his soul, overflowing with rapture, craved freedom, space, open air. The vault of heaven, full of soft, shining stars, stretched vast and fathomless above him. The Milky Way ran in two pale streams from the zenith to the horizon. The cool, motionless, still night wrapped itself around the earth. The white towers and golden domes of the cathedral gleamed out against the sapphire sky. The gorgeous autumn flowers in the beds around the house lay sleeping until morning. The silence of earth seemed to melt into the silence of the heavens. The mystery of the earth touched the mystery of the stars....

Alyosha stood, gazed, and suddenly threw himself down onto the earth. He didn't know why he embraced it. He couldn't have said why he longed so irresistibly to kiss it, to kiss all of it. But he kissed it, weeping, sobbing, soaking it with his tears, and vowed passionately to love it, to love it forever and ever. "Water the earth with the tears of your joy, and love those tears," echoed through his soul.
What was he weeping over?

Oh! In his rapture he was weeping even over those stars shining down at him from the depths of space, and "he wasn't ashamed of that ecstasy." It seemed as though threads ran from all those countless worlds of God, linking his soul to them, and it trembled all over, "in contact with other worlds." He longed to forgive everyone, for everything, and to beg forgiveness in return. Oh, not for himself, but for all men, for everyone and everything. "And others are praying for me too," echoed again through his soul. But with every passing instant he felt, clearly and almost tangibly, that something firm and unshakable, like that vault of heaven itself, had entered his soul. It was as though some idea had taken hold of the very center of his mind—and it was for his whole life, forever and ever. He'd fallen to the earth a weak boy, but he rose a resolute champion, and he knew it, felt it, suddenly, in that very moment of ecstasy. And never, never, for the rest of his life, could Alyosha forget that moment.
"Someone visited my soul in that hour," he used to say afterward, with unshakable faith in his own words.
Within three days he left the monastery, in keeping with his elder's words, who had bidden him "go out and sojourn in the world."

title: I. Kuzma Samsonov
paragraphs: But Dmitri, to whom Grushenka, flying off toward a new life, had left her final greetings, telling him to remember the hour of her love forever, knew nothing of what had happened to her, and was at that very moment in a state of feverish agitation and activity. For the past two days he'd been in such an unimaginable state of mind that he might easily have come down with brain fever, as he said himself afterward. Alyosha hadn't been able to find him the morning before, and Ivan hadn't managed to meet him at the tavern that same day. The people at his lodgings, on his orders, kept his movements hidden.

He'd spent those two days literally tearing around in every direction, "wrestling with his fate and trying to save himself," as he put it himself afterward, and for a few hours he'd even dashed out of town on urgent business, terrible as it was for him to lose sight of Grushenka even for a moment. All of this was explained in detail later, and confirmed by documentary evidence; but for now we'll note only the most essential events of those two terrible days that immediately preceded the awful catastrophe that broke over him so suddenly.

Though Grushenka had, it's true, loved him genuinely and sincerely for an hour, she also tormented him at times cruelly, mercilessly. The worst of it was that he could never tell what she meant to do. There was no way to win her over, whether by force or by kindness: she'd yield to nothing. She'd only grow angry and turn away from him entirely—he already knew that well. He suspected, and quite rightly, that she too was going through some inner struggle, that she was in a state of extraordinary indecision, that she was trying to make up her mind about something and couldn't settle on it. And so, not without good reason, he guessed, with a sinking heart, that at times she must simply hate him and his passion for her. And perhaps that was so, but what exactly was tormenting Grushenka, he didn't understand. For him the whole agonizing question came down to the struggle between him and Fyodor Pavlovitch.

Here we should note, in passing, one particular fact: he was firmly convinced that Fyodor Pavlovitch would offer, or perhaps already had offered, Grushenka lawful marriage, and never for a moment believed that the old lecher hoped to win her over for three thousand roubles. Mitya had reached this conclusion from what he knew of Grushenka and her character. That's how it was that at times he could believe all of Grushenka's unease came from not knowing which of the two to choose, which one was more to her advantage.

Strange to say, during all this time it never once occurred to him to think about the impending return of the "officer"—the man who'd had such a fateful influence on Grushenka's life, and whose arrival she awaited with such emotion and dread. It's true that lately Grushenka had said very little about it. And yet he was perfectly aware of a letter she'd received a month earlier from the man who'd seduced her, and had heard of it from her own lips. He partly knew, too, what the letter contained. In a moment of spite, Grushenka had shown him that letter, but to his own surprise, he'd hardly attached any importance to it. It would be hard to say why. Perhaps, weighed down as he was by the whole hideous horror of his struggle with his own father over this woman, he simply couldn't picture any threat more terrible—at least not at the time. He simply didn't believe in a suitor who'd suddenly resurface after five years' absence, and believed even less in his prompt arrival. Besides, in the "officer's" first letter, which had been shown to Mitya, the possibility of this new rival's visit had been only very vaguely hinted at. The letter was vague, overwrought, and full of sentimentality. It should be noted that Grushenka had kept from him the last lines of that letter, where his return was mentioned more plainly. He'd noticed, too, he remembered afterward, a certain involuntary, proud contempt on Grushenka's face for this letter from Siberia, at the time. Grushenka told him nothing of what had passed later between her and this rival, so that little by little he'd forgotten the officer even existed.

He felt that whatever might come afterward, whatever turn things might take, his final showdown with Fyodor Pavlovitch was closing in on him, and would have to be settled before anything else. With a sinking heart, he waited from moment to moment for Grushenka's decision, always believing it would come suddenly, on some impulse of the moment. All at once she'd say to him: "Take me, I'm yours forever," and it would all be over. He'd seize her and carry her off at once to the ends of the earth. Oh, then he'd carry her away at once, as far, far away as possible; to the farthest reaches of Russia, if not the earth itself; he'd marry her and settle down with her under a false name, so no one would ever know anything about them, there, here, anywhere. Then, oh, then, a new life would begin at once!

He dreamed feverishly, every waking moment, of this different, reformed, "virtuous" life—"it has to be virtuous, it has to"—thirsting for that reform and renewal. The filthy swamp he'd sunk into of his own free will disgusted him, and like a great many men in such situations, he put his faith above all in a change of scene. If only it weren't for these people, if only it weren't for these circumstances, if only he could fly away from this cursed place—he'd be an entirely different man, would set out on a new path. That was what he believed, what he longed for.

But all of this depended on one thing: the first, the happy resolution of the question. There was another possibility, too, a different and terrible ending. Suddenly she might say to him: "Go away. I've just come to an understanding with Fyodor Pavlovitch. I'm going to marry him, and I don't want you"—and then... but then.... But Mitya didn't know what would happen then. Right up to the last hour, he didn't know. That much should be said in his favor. He had no fixed intentions, had plotted no crime. He was simply watching, spying, in agony, all while preparing himself for the first, happy resolution of his fate. He pushed every other thought away, in fact. But that other ending brought with it a quite different worry, a new, secondary, but no less fatal and unsolvable difficulty.

If she were to say to him, "I'm yours, take me away," how was he supposed to take her away? Where would he find the means, the money to do it? It was right at this time that every source of income from Fyodor Pavlovitch, the handouts that had gone on without a break for so many years, dried up completely. Grushenka had money, of course, but on this point Mitya suddenly showed an extraordinary streak of pride; he wanted to carry her off and start their new life at his own expense, not hers. He couldn't bear the thought of taking her money, and the very idea filled him with intense revulsion. I won't dwell on this fact or dig into it here, but will simply note that this was his attitude at the time. All of it may have sprung, indirectly and without his even realizing it, from the secret stings of his conscience over Katerina Ivanovna's money, which he'd dishonestly kept for himself. "I've been a scoundrel to one of them, and I'll be a scoundrel to the other right away too," was how he felt at the time, as he explained afterward: "and once Grushenka finds out, she won't want a scoundrel like that."
So where was he to get the means, where was he to find that fateful money? Without it, everything would be lost, nothing could be done—"and all because I didn't have the money. Oh, the shame of it!"

To get ahead of the story: he did, perhaps, know where to get the money, perhaps even knew where it was sitting at that very moment. I won't say more about that here, since it will all become clear later. But his chief trouble, however murkily I have to put it, was that to lay hands on that sum he knew of, to have the right to take it, he first had to pay back Katerina Ivanovna's three thousand—otherwise, "I'm nothing but a common pickpocket, a scoundrel, and I refuse to start a new life as a scoundrel," Mitya decided. And so he made up his mind to move heaven and earth to return that three thousand to Katerina Ivanovna, and to do that first of all. This final stage of his decision, so to speak, had only been reached in the last few hours, that is, after his last meeting with Alyosha, two days before, on the highway, the evening Grushenka had insulted Katerina Ivanovna, and Mitya, after hearing Alyosha's account of it, had admitted he was a scoundrel and told him to say so to Katerina Ivanovna, if it would bring her any comfort. After parting from his brother that night, he'd felt, in his frenzy, that it would be better "to murder and rob someone than fail to repay my debt to Katya. I'd rather have everyone think me a robber and a murderer, I'd rather go to Siberia, than have Katya have the right to say I deceived her, stole her money, and used it to run off with Grushenka and start a new life! I can't do that!" That's how Mitya decided it, grinding his teeth, and there were moments when he could well imagine his mind giving way entirely. But meanwhile he kept struggling on....

Strange to say, though one might suppose there was nothing left for him but despair—since what chance did he have, penniless as he was, of raising such a sum?—he nonetheless kept hoping, right up to the very end, that he'd somehow get that three thousand, that the money would find its own way to him, almost as though it might drop from the sky. That's just how it is with people who, like Dmitri, have never had to do anything with money except squander what came to them through inheritance, without any effort of their own, and have no notion of how money is actually earned. A whirlwind of the most fantastic notions took hold of his brain right after he parted from Alyosha two days before, throwing his thoughts into a tangle of confusion. That's how he landed on a thoroughly wild scheme first of all. And perhaps for men like him, in circumstances like his, it's precisely the most impossible, far-fetched schemes that occur first, and seem the most practical.

He suddenly decided to go to Samsonov, the merchant who was Grushenka's protector, and put a "scheme" to him, and through it get the whole sum he needed from him at once. He had no doubts whatsoever about the commercial soundness of his scheme, not the slightest; the only thing he wasn't sure of was how Samsonov would view his impulsive plan, supposing he looked at it from any angle other than the purely commercial one. Though Mitya knew the merchant by sight, he wasn't acquainted with him and had never exchanged a word with him. But for some reason he'd long held the conviction that the old reprobate, now lying at death's door, might not at all object to Grushenka securing a respectable position, marrying a man "who could be depended on." And he believed not only that the old man wouldn't object, but that this was exactly what he wanted, and that if the chance arose, he'd be ready to help. From some rumor, or perhaps some stray word of Grushenka's, he'd further gathered that the old man might even prefer him to Fyodor Pavlovitch as a match for Grushenka.

Quite a few readers of my novel will probably feel that in counting on this kind of assistance, and being ready to take his bride, so to speak, straight out of the hands of her protector, Dmitri showed real coarseness and a lack of tact. I'll only note that Mitya looked on Grushenka's past as something entirely finished. He viewed that past with boundless pity, and resolved, with all the fervor of his passion, that the moment Grushenka told him she loved him and would marry him, it would mark the start of a new Grushenka and a new Dmitri, free of every vice. They would forgive each other and start their lives over. As for Kuzma Samsonov, Dmitri regarded him as a man who'd exercised a fateful influence in Grushenka's distant past, even though she'd never loved him, and who was now himself a thing of the past, entirely finished, practically nonexistent. Besides, Mitya hardly thought of him as a man at all, since it was known throughout town that he was nothing but a broken wreck, whose relations with Grushenka had long since changed in character and become purely paternal.

In any case, there was a good deal of simplicity in all this on Mitya's part, since, for all his vices, he was at heart a very simple-hearted man. One sign of that simplicity was that Mitya was seriously convinced that, standing on the threshold of the next world, old Kuzma must genuinely repent of his past relations with Grushenka, and that she had no more devoted friend and protector in the whole world than this now-harmless old man.

After his conversation with Alyosha at the crossroads, he barely slept all night, and by ten o'clock the next morning he was already at Samsonov's house, telling the servant to announce him. It was a very large, gloomy old two-story house, with a lodge and outbuildings. On the ground floor lived Samsonov's two married sons with their families, his elderly sister, and his unmarried daughter. In the lodge lived two of his clerks, one of them with a large family of his own. Both the lodge and the ground floor were badly overcrowded, but the old man kept the upper floor entirely for himself, and wouldn't even let his daughter live up there with him, although she waited on him, and, despite her asthma, was obliged, at set hours and any time he might call for her, to run up to him from below.

This upper floor held a number of large rooms kept purely for show, furnished in the old merchant style, with long, monotonous rows of clumsy mahogany chairs lined up along the walls, glass chandeliers hung with shades, and gloomy mirrors on the walls. All these rooms sat entirely empty and unused, since the old man kept to a single room, a small, out-of-the-way bedroom, where an old servant in a headscarf waited on him, along with a young man who usually sat on the chest in the hallway. Because of his swollen legs, the old man could barely walk at all, and was only rarely helped up out of his leather armchair, when the old woman would support him and walk him up and down the room once or twice. He was gloomy and tight-lipped even with her.

When he was told of the "captain's" arrival, he refused outright to see him. But Mitya persisted and sent his name up again. Samsonov questioned the young man closely: What did he look like? Was he drunk? Was he going to make trouble? The answer came back that he was sober, but wouldn't leave. The old man again refused to see him. Then Mitya, who'd foreseen this and had deliberately brought pencil and paper with him, wrote out clearly on the paper the words: "On business of the utmost importance, closely concerning Agrafena Alexandrovna," and sent it up to the old man.

After thinking it over for a moment, Samsonov told the young man to show the visitor into the drawing room, and sent the old woman downstairs with orders for his younger son to come up to him at once. This younger son, a man over six feet tall and of unusual physical strength, clean-shaven and dressed in European style, though his father still wore a kaftan and a beard, came at once without a word of comment. The whole family trembled before the father. The old man had sent for this giant not out of any fear of the "captain"—he wasn't a timid man by any means—but in order to have a witness on hand, in case anything went wrong. Supported by his son and the servant boy, he shuffled at last into the drawing room. One can assume he felt a good deal of curiosity. The drawing room where Mitya waited for him was a vast, dreary room that pressed a weight of gloom onto the heart. It had a double row of windows, a gallery, marbled walls, and three enormous chandeliers with glass pendants covered in shades.

Mitya sat on a small chair by the entrance, waiting for his fate with nervous impatience. When the old man appeared at the far door, some seventy feet away, Mitya jumped up at once and, with his long, military stride, walked to meet him. Mitya was well dressed, in a buttoned-up frock coat, a round hat and black gloves in hand, exactly as he'd been three days before at the elder's, at the family gathering with his father and brothers. The old man waited for him, standing dignified and unbending, and Mitya sensed at once that he'd been looked through and through as he approached. Mitya was also struck by the extreme swelling of Samsonov's face. His lower lip, always thick, now hung down, looking like a bun. He bowed to his guest in dignified silence, motioned him to a low chair by the sofa, and, leaning on his son's arm, began lowering himself painfully onto the sofa across from him, groaning the whole time, so that Mitya, watching his painful effort, immediately felt a stab of remorse and a keen sense of his own insignificance in the presence of this dignified man he'd taken it upon himself to disturb.
"What is it you want from me, sir?" the old man said at last, once he was seated, deliberately, distinctly, sternly, but courteously.

Mitya started, sprang up, then sat back down. Then he launched at once into speech, loud, nervous, and hurried, gesturing wildly, in a state of genuine frenzy. He was unmistakably a man backed into a corner, on the brink of ruin, grasping at the last straw, ready to go under if it failed him. Old Samsonov probably took all this in at a glance, though his face stayed as cold and fixed as a statue's.

"Most honored sir, Kuzma Kuzmitch, you've no doubt heard more than once about my disputes with my father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, who robbed me of my inheritance from my mother... seeing as the whole town's been gossiping about it... everyone here gossips about things they shouldn't... and besides, it may well have reached you through Grushenka... I beg your pardon, through Agrafena Alexandrovna... Agrafena Alexandrovna, a lady for whom I hold the highest respect and esteem..."

So Mitya began, and stumbled at the very first sentence. We won't reproduce his speech word for word, only summarize the gist of it. Three months earlier, he said, he'd made a point of consulting (Mitya deliberately used those words rather than "consulted") a lawyer in the provincial capital, "a distinguished lawyer, Kuzma Kuzmitch, Pavel Pavlovitch Korneplodov. You've perhaps heard of him? A man of tremendous intellect, the mind of a statesman... he knows you too... spoke of you in the highest terms..." Mitya faltered again. But these stumbles didn't stop him. He leapt over the gaps each time and pressed on and on.

This Korneplodov, after questioning him closely and examining what documents he could bring him (Mitya referred to these documents somewhat vaguely, hurrying past the subject), had concluded that legal action could certainly be brought over the village of Tchermashnya, which, he said, should by rights have come to him, Mitya, through his mother, and so outmaneuver the old scoundrel, his father... "because not every door is shut, and justice may yet find a loophole." In fact, he might reasonably expect an additional six or even seven thousand roubles from Fyodor Pavlovitch, since Tchermashnya was worth, at the very least, twenty-five thousand, or even twenty-eight thousand, in fact, "thirty, thirty, Kuzma Kuzmitch, and would you believe it, I never got even seventeen out of that heartless man!" So he, Mitya, had set the matter aside for the time being, knowing nothing about the law, but on arriving here had been stunned by a counterclaim brought against him (here Mitya wandered off track again and again leapt ahead), "so wouldn't you, most excellent and honored Kuzma Kuzmitch, be willing to take over all my claims against that unnatural monster, and pay me a lump sum of just three thousand?... You see, there's no way you could possibly lose on it. On my honor, my honor, I swear it. Quite the opposite—you could make six or seven thousand instead of three." Above all, he wanted the whole thing settled that very day.

"I'll do the business with you before a notary, or whatever's needed... in fact, I'm ready to do anything.... I'll hand over all the papers... sign whatever you like... and we could draw up the agreement right away... and if possible, if it were only possible, this very morning.... You could pay me the three thousand, since there's no financier in this whole town to match you, and so save me from... save me, in fact... for the sake of a good deed, I might even say an honorable one.... Because I hold the most honorable feelings toward a certain person, whom you know well, and care for as a father would. I wouldn't have come at all, in fact, if it weren't in that spirit, as a father would. And really, this is a struggle between three people, because it's fate—a terrible thing, Kuzma Kuzmitch! A tragedy, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a tragedy! And since you dropped out of it long ago, it's really a tug-of-war between two. I may be putting this clumsily, I'm no man of letters. But you see, I'm on one side, and that monster is on the other. So you have to choose. It's either me or the monster. The whole thing rests in your hands—the fate of three lives, and the happiness of two.... Forgive me, I'm making a mess of this, but you understand... I can see in your venerable eyes that you understand... and if you don't understand, I'm finished... so there it is!"

Mitya broke off his clumsy speech with that, "so there it is!" and, jumping up from his seat, waited for the answer to his foolish proposal. On that last phrase he'd suddenly become hopelessly aware that the whole thing had fallen completely flat, and worse, that he'd been talking absolute nonsense.

"How strange—on the way here it all seemed to make perfect sense, and now it's nothing but nonsense." The thought suddenly dawned on his despairing mind. The whole time he'd been talking, the old man had sat motionless, watching him with an icy look in his eyes. After leaving him hanging a moment longer, Kuzma Kuzmitch finally pronounced, in the most flat, chilling tone:
"Forgive me, we don't take on business of that sort."
Mitya suddenly felt his legs go weak under him.
"What am I to do now, Kuzma Kuzmitch?" he muttered, with a pale smile. "I suppose it's all over for me—what do you think?"
"Forgive me...."
Mitya stood there, frozen, staring. He suddenly caught a flicker of movement in the old man's face. He started.
"You see, sir, business of that kind simply isn't our line," the old man said slowly. "There's the courts, the lawyers—it's a perfect headache. But if you like, there's a man here you might try."
"Good heavens! Who is it? You're my salvation, Kuzma Kuzmitch," Mitya stammered.

"He doesn't live here, and he's not here just now. A peasant, does business in timber. Goes by the name Lyagavy. He's been haggling with Fyodor Pavlovitch for the past year over your copse at Tchermashnya. They can't agree on a price, you may have heard? Now he's come back and is staying with the priest at Ilyinskoe, about twelve versts from Volovya station. He wrote to me too, about the copse business, asking my advice. Fyodor Pavlovitch means to go see him himself. So if you were to get to Fyodor Pavlovitch first, and put the same proposal to Lyagavy that you put to me, he might just—"

"A brilliant idea!" Mitya broke in, ecstatic. "He's exactly the man, it would suit him perfectly. He's haggling with him now, being asked too much for it, and here he'd have all the papers giving him a claim to the property itself. Ha ha ha!"
And Mitya suddenly burst into his short, wooden laugh, startling Samsonov.
"How can I ever thank you, Kuzma Kuzmitch?" Mitya cried, effusive.
"Don't mention it," said Samsonov, inclining his head.
"But you don't know, you've saved me. Oh, it was a true premonition that brought me to you.... So now, off to this priest!"
"No need for thanks."
"I'll hurry, I'll fly straight there. I'm afraid I've worn you out. I'll never forget this. That's a Russian speaking, Kuzma Kuzmitch, a R-r-russian!"
"Indeed!"
Mitya grabbed his hand to shake it, but there was a spiteful gleam in the old man's eye. Mitya pulled his hand back, then immediately blamed himself for his own suspicion.
"It's just that he's tired," he thought.

"For her sake! For her sake, Kuzma Kuzmitch! You understand it's all for her," he cried, his voice ringing through the room. He bowed, turned sharply, and, with the same long stride, walked to the door without looking back. He was trembling with delight.

"Everything was right on the edge of ruin, and my guardian angel saved me," he thought. And if a businessman like Samsonov—a most worthy old man, and what dignity!—had suggested this course, then... then success was as good as guaranteed. He'd fly straight off. "I'll be back before nightfall, I'll be back tonight and the whole thing will be settled. Could the old man have been laughing at me?" Mitya exclaimed, striding toward his lodgings. He could, of course, imagine nothing except that the advice was sound, coming "from such a businessman," who understood the business, who understood this Lyagavy—curious surname!—or else the old man had been laughing at him.

Alas! It was the second explanation that turned out to be true. Long afterward, once the catastrophe had happened, old Samsonov himself admitted, laughing, that he'd made a fool of the "captain." He was a cold, spiteful, sarcastic man, prone to sudden, violent aversions. Whether it was the "captain's" excited face, or the foolish conviction of this "rake and spendthrift" that he, Samsonov, could be taken in by such a cock-and-bull scheme, or jealousy over Grushenka, in whose name this "scapegrace" had come barreling in at him with such a story to squeeze money out of him—which of these it was that worked on the old man, I couldn't say. But in the moment when Mitya stood before him, feeling his legs give way under him, frantically crying that he was ruined, at that very moment the old man looked at him with intense spite and decided to make a laughingstock of him. Once Mitya had gone, Kuzma Kuzmitch, white with rage, turned to his son and ordered him to see to it that that beggar was never seen again, never let so much as onto the property, or else he'd—

He never finished the threat. But even his son, who'd often seen him enraged before, trembled with fear. For a whole hour afterward the old man shook with anger, and by evening he was worse still, and sent for the doctor.

title: II. Lyagavy
paragraphs: So he had to drive at full speed, and he had no money for horses. He had forty kopecks, and that was all—all that remained of so many years of prosperity! But he still had, at home, an old silver watch that had long since stopped running. He grabbed it and carried it to a Jewish watchmaker with a shop on the market square. The Jew gave him six roubles for it.

"And I wasn't even expecting that," Mitya cried, ecstatic. He was still in a state of pure elation. He snatched up his six roubles and ran home. There he borrowed three roubles from the people who ran the house, who were so fond of him that they were glad to give it to him, even though it was all they had. Mitya, in his excitement, told them on the spot that his fate would be decided that very day, and described, in a desperate rush, the whole scheme he'd laid out for Samsonov, Samsonov's answer, his own hopes for the future, and so on. These people had already heard plenty of their lodger's secrets before, and so regarded him as a gentleman without a shred of pride, almost one of their own. Having scraped together nine roubles this way, Mitya sent for post-horses to take him to Volovya station. That's how it came to be remembered and established that "at midday, the day before the event, Mitya didn't have a farthing to his name, and had sold his watch to get money, and had borrowed three roubles from his landlord, all in front of witnesses."
I note this fact here; later it will become clear why.

Though he glowed with joyful anticipation that he'd finally solve all his troubles, still, as he drew near Volovya station, he trembled at the thought of what Grushenka might be doing while he was away. What if she decided today, of all days, to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch? That was exactly why he'd left without telling her, and why he'd instructed his landlady not to reveal where he'd gone if anyone came asking for him.

"I must, I must get back tonight," he kept repeating, jolting along in the cart, "and I daresay I'll have to bring this Lyagavy back here with me... to draw up the deed." So Mitya mused, his heart pounding, but alas, his dreams weren't destined to come true.

To begin with, he was late, having taken a shortcut from Volovya station that turned out to be eighteen versts instead of twelve. Second, he didn't find the priest at home in Ilyinskoe; he'd gone off to a neighboring village. By the time Mitya, setting off after him with the same worn-out horses, tracked him down, it was nearly dark.

The priest, a shy, pleasant-looking little man, told him at once that although Lyagavy had been staying with him at first, he was now at Suhoy Possyolok, spending the night at the forester's cottage, since he was buying timber there too. At Mitya's urgent request that he take him to Lyagavy right away, and so, as it were, "save him," the priest agreed, after a bit of hesitation, to guide him to Suhoy Possyolok; his curiosity was clearly aroused. But unfortunately he suggested they go on foot, since it wasn't "much more than" a verst. Mitya, naturally, agreed, and set off with his long, yard-wide strides, so that the poor priest could barely keep pace, practically running after him. He was a very cautious man, though not old.

Mitya launched at once into telling him about his plans too, nervously and excitedly asking for advice about Lyagavy, talking the whole way. The priest listened closely but offered little advice. He deflected Mitya's questions with "I don't know. Ah, I couldn't say. How would I know?" and so on. When Mitya began telling him about his quarrel with his father over the inheritance, the priest grew genuinely alarmed, since he depended on Fyodor Pavlovitch in some way himself. He did ask, with some surprise, though, why Mitya called the peasant trader Gorstkin "Lyagavy," and obligingly explained that although the man's real name was indeed Lyagavy, no one ever called him that, since it deeply offended him, and that Mitya must be sure to call him Gorstkin instead, "or you won't get anywhere with him, he won't even listen to you," the priest concluded.

Mitya was somewhat taken aback for a moment, and explained that this was what Samsonov had called him. On hearing this, the priest dropped the matter, though he would have done well to voice his suspicion that if Samsonov had sent him to that peasant calling him Lyagavy, there might be something off about it, that he might be making a fool of him. But Mitya had no time to dwell on such trifles. He hurried along, striding fast, and only when they finally reached Suhoy Possyolok did he realize they'd covered not one verst, not even one and a half, but at least three. This irritated him, but he held himself in check.

They went into the hut. The forester lived in one half of it, and Gorstkin was lodging in the other, the better room across the passage. They went into that room and lit a tallow candle. The hut was stiflingly overheated. On the table stood a samovar that had gone cold, a tray with cups, an empty rum bottle, a partly full bottle of vodka, and a few half-eaten crusts of wheat bread. The visitor himself lay stretched out full length on the bench, his coat balled up under his head as a pillow, snoring heavily. Mitya stood there, at a loss.

"Of course I have to wake him. My business is too important. I've come in such a rush. I'm in a hurry to get back today," he said, deeply agitated. But the priest and the forester stood there in silence, offering no opinion. Mitya went up and tried to wake him himself; he tried vigorously, but the sleeper wouldn't budge.

"He's drunk," Mitya decided. "Good Lord! What am I to do? What am I to do?" And, in a fit of impatience, he began pulling at his arms, his legs, shaking his head, lifting him up and trying to sit him upright on the bench. Yet after a long, exhausting effort, all he managed to get out of the drunken man were absurd grunts and violent but incoherent curses.
"No, you'd better wait a bit," the priest finally said, "since he's clearly not in a fit state."
"He's been drinking all day," the forester chimed in.
"Good heavens!" Mitya cried. "If only you knew how important this is to me, how desperate I am!"
"No, better wait till morning," the priest repeated.
"Till morning? Mercy, that's impossible!"

And in his despair he was on the point of attacking the sleeping man again, but stopped himself short, realizing the futility of it. The priest said nothing, and the drowsy forester looked on gloomily.

"What terrible tragedies real life comes up with for people," Mitya said, in utter despair. Sweat streamed down his face. The priest took the moment to point out, quite reasonably, that even if he succeeded in waking the man, he'd still be too drunk for any real conversation. "And since your business is important," he said, "you'd really be better off putting it off until morning." With a gesture of despair, Mitya agreed.

"Father, I'll stay here with a light and wait for the right moment. The second he wakes, I'll begin. I'll pay you for the candle," he said to the forester, "for the night's lodging too—you'll remember Dmitri Karamazov. Only, Father, I don't know what to do about you. Where will you sleep?"
"No, I'm heading home. I'll take his horse and get back," he said, gesturing at the forester. "And now I'll say good-bye. I wish you every success."

And so it was settled. The priest rode off on the forester's horse, glad to be free of it all, though he shook his head uneasily, wondering whether he oughtn't, the next day, to tell his benefactor Fyodor Pavlovitch about this odd incident, "or he might hear of it at some unlucky moment, get angry, and withdraw his favor."

The forester scratched himself and went back to his own room without a word, and Mitya sat down on the bench to "catch the right moment," as he put it. A deep despondency clung to his soul like a heavy fog. A deep, intense despondency! He sat there thinking, but reached no conclusion. The candle burned dimly, a cricket chirped; the overheated room grew unbearably stuffy. He suddenly pictured the garden, the path behind it, the door to his father's house mysteriously swinging open, Grushenka running in. He leapt up off the bench.

"It's a tragedy!" he said, grinding his teeth. Mechanically he went over to the sleeping man and looked into his face. He was a lean, middle-aged peasant, with a very long face, flaxen curls, and a long, thin, reddish beard, wearing a blue cotton shirt and a black waistcoat, from whose pocket peeked the chain of a silver watch. Mitya looked at his face with intense hatred, and for some inexplicable reason his curly hair irritated him more than anything else.

What was unbearably humiliating was that, after abandoning matters of such importance and making such sacrifices, he, Mitya, utterly worn to the bone, with business of such urgency at stake, should be standing over this dolt on whom his entire fate depended, while the man snored away as though nothing were the matter, as though he'd dropped in from another planet.

"Oh, the irony of fate!" Mitya cried, and, completely losing his head, threw himself back into rousing the drunken peasant. He roused him with something close to savagery, pulled at him, shoved him, even struck him; but after five minutes of fruitless effort, he went back to the bench in helpless despair and sat down.

"Stupid! Stupid!" Mitya cried. "And how dishonorable this whole thing is!" something made him add. His head had begun to ache terribly. Should he give up and just leave altogether? he wondered. "No, wait until morning now. I'll stay on purpose. What else did I come for? Besides, I've no way to leave. How would I even get away from here now? Oh, the idiocy of it all!"

But his head kept aching worse and worse. He sat motionless, and without meaning to, dozed off and fell asleep right where he sat. He seemed to have slept two hours or more. He was woken by a headache so unbearable he could have screamed. His temples pounded, the top of his head ached. It took him a long while to fully wake up and understand what had happened to him.

At last he realized the room was filled with charcoal fumes from the stove, and that he might suffocate. And the drunken peasant was still lying there, snoring. The candle guttered, about to go out. Mitya cried out and stumbled, staggering, across the passage into the forester's room. The forester woke at once, but on hearing the other room was full of fumes, to Mitya's astonishment and irritation, took it with strange indifference, though he did go to check on it.
"But he's dead, he's dead! And... what am I supposed to do then?" Mitya cried, frantic.

They threw open the doors, opened a window and the chimney flue. Mitya fetched a pail of water from the passage. First he soaked his own head, then, finding some kind of rag, dipped it in the water and laid it on Lyagavy's head. The forester still treated the whole affair with contempt, and, opening the window, muttered grumpily:
"It'll be all right now."

He went back to sleep, leaving Mitya a lit lantern. Mitya fussed over the drunken peasant for half an hour, wetting his head, and solemnly resolved not to sleep at all that night. But he was so worn out that when he sat down for a moment to catch his breath, his eyes closed, and without meaning to, he stretched full length on the bench and slept like the dead.

It was dreadfully late when he woke. Somewhere around nine o'clock. The sun was shining brightly through the hut's two little windows. The curly-headed peasant was sitting on the bench, already in his coat. He had a fresh samovar in front of him, and a new bottle. Yesterday's bottle was already finished, and the new one was more than half empty. Mitya jumped up and saw at once that the cursed peasant was drunk again, hopelessly, incurably drunk. He stared at him a moment, wide-eyed. The peasant sat watching him back, silent and sly, with an insulting calm, even, Mitya thought, a kind of contemptuous condescension. He rushed up to him.
"Excuse me, you see... I... you've most likely heard from the forester here at the hut. I'm Lieutenant Dmitri Karamazov, son of old Karamazov, whose copse you're buying."
"That's a lie!" said the peasant, calm and confident.
"A lie? You know Fyodor Pavlovitch, don't you?"
"I don't know any of your Fyodor Pavlovitches," the peasant said, his speech thick.

"You're bargaining with him over the copse, the copse. Come on, wake up, pull yourself together. Father Pavel of Ilyinskoe brought me here. You wrote to Samsonov, and he's sent me to you," Mitya gasped, out of breath.
"You're l-lying!" Lyagavy blurted out again. Mitya's legs went cold.
"For mercy's sake! This isn't a joke! You're drunk, maybe, but you can still talk, still understand... or else... I don't understand anything anymore!"
"You're a painter!"
"For mercy's sake! I'm Karamazov, Dmitri Karamazov. I have a proposal for you, an advantageous proposal... a very advantageous proposal, about the copse!"
The peasant stroked his beard, self-important.
"No, you took on the job and it turned out you're a swindler. You're a scoundrel!"
"I assure you, you're mistaken," Mitya cried, wringing his hands in despair. The peasant kept stroking his beard, then suddenly narrowed his eyes cunningly.
"No, you show me this: show me the law that allows for swindling. You hear? You're a scoundrel! Do you understand that?"

Mitya stepped back, gloomy, and suddenly "something seemed to strike him on the head," as he said afterward. In an instant a light seemed to dawn in his mind—"a light went on, and I understood it all." He stood there, dumbfounded, wondering how he, a man of intelligence after all, could have given himself over to such foolishness, been led into such a misadventure, and kept it up for nearly twenty-four hours, fussing around this Lyagavy, wetting his head with water.
"Why, the man's drunk, dead drunk, and he'll go on drinking for a week now—what's the use waiting around here? And what if Samsonov sent me here on purpose? What if she—? Oh, God, what have I done?"

The peasant sat watching him, grinning. At any other time Mitya might have flown into a rage and struck the fool down, but now he felt as weak as a child. He walked quietly to the bench, picked up his overcoat, put it on without a word, and left the hut. He didn't find the forester in the next room; there was no one there. He took fifty kopecks in small change out of his pocket and left it on the table for the night's lodging, the candle, and the trouble he'd caused. Coming out of the hut, he saw nothing but forest all around him. He walked at random, not knowing which way to go from the hut, right or left. Hurrying there the evening before with the priest, he hadn't paid attention to the road. He felt no vengeful feeling toward anyone, not even Samsonov, in his heart. He strode along a narrow forest path, aimless, dazed, oblivious to where he was going. A child could have knocked him over, so weak was he, body and soul. He made it out of the forest somehow, though, and a view of fields, bare after the harvest, stretched out as far as the eye could see.
"What despair! What death all around!" he repeated, striding on and on.

He was saved by running into an old merchant being driven across the country in a hired cart. When he caught up with him, Mitya asked the way, and it turned out the old merchant was also headed to Volovya. After a bit of back and forth, Mitya climbed into the cart. Three hours later they arrived. At Volovya, Mitya immediately ordered post-horses to drive him to town, and suddenly realized he was appallingly hungry. While the horses were being harnessed, an omelet was made for him. He ate the whole thing in an instant, wolfed down a huge hunk of bread, ate a sausage, and downed three glasses of vodka. After eating, his mood and his heart both lifted. He flew toward town, urging the driver on, and suddenly hit on a new and "unshakable" plan to get hold of that "accursed money" before evening. "And to think, just to think, that a man's whole life could be wrecked over a paltry three thousand!" he cried, contemptuous. "I'll settle it today." And if it hadn't been for the thought of Grushenka, and of what might have happened to her, which never once left him, he might have grown almost cheerful again.... But the thought of her kept stabbing at his heart, over and over, like a sharp knife.
At last they arrived, and Mitya ran straight to Grushenka's.

title: III. Gold-Mines
paragraphs: This was the visit from Mitya that Grushenka had described to Rakitin with such horror. She'd been expecting the "message" right then, and had been much relieved that Mitya hadn't come to see her that day or the day before. She'd been hoping "please God he won't come until I've already gone," and then he'd suddenly burst in on her. The rest we already know. To get him off her hands, she'd suggested right away that he walk with her to Samsonov's, where she said she absolutely had to go "to settle his accounts," and when Mitya offered to walk her there at once, she'd said good-bye to him at the gate, making him promise to come back at midnight to walk her home again. Mitya, too, was delighted with this arrangement. If she was sitting at Samsonov's, she couldn't be off at Fyodor Pavlovitch's—"assuming she's not lying," he added at once. But from what he'd seen, he didn't think she was lying.

He was the kind of jealous man who, whenever the woman he loved was out of sight, immediately invents every sort of terrible fantasy about what she might be doing, how she might be betraying him—but the moment he's shaken, heartbroken, convinced beyond doubt of her unfaithfulness, he runs straight back to her; at the very first glance at her face, her cheerful, laughing, affectionate face, he revives instantly, casts off every suspicion, and with joyful shame curses himself for his own jealousy.
After leaving Grushenka at the gate, he raced home. Oh, he still had so much to do that day! But at least a weight had lifted off his heart.
"Now I just have to hurry and find out from Smerdyakov whether anything happened there last night, whether by any chance she went to Fyodor Pavlovitch's; ugh!" drifted through his mind.
Before he'd even reached his lodgings, jealousy had surged up again in his restless heart.

Jealousy! "Othello wasn't jealous, he was trusting," Pushkin once observed. And that remark alone shows the depth of our great poet's insight. Othello's soul was shattered, his whole view of the world clouded, simply because his ideal had been destroyed. But Othello never took to hiding, spying, peering through cracks. He was trusting, in fact quite the opposite. He had to be led on, pushed, worked up with tremendous effort before he could even entertain the idea of betrayal. That's not what a truly jealous man is like. It's impossible to picture the shame and moral degradation a jealous man can sink to without the slightest twinge of conscience. And yet it isn't as though jealous men are all vulgar, base souls. On the contrary, a man of lofty feeling, whose love is pure and full of self-sacrifice, can still hide under tables, bribe the vilest people, and grow perfectly comfortable with the lowest depths of spying and eavesdropping.

Othello was incapable of resigning himself to unfaithfulness—not incapable of forgiving it, but of accepting it as fact—even though his soul was as innocent and free of malice as a child's. It's not that way with the truly jealous man. It's hard to imagine what some jealous men can bring themselves to accept, to overlook, and what they're capable of forgiving! The jealous are the quickest of all to forgive, and every woman knows it. A jealous man can forgive with astonishing speed, though of course only after a violent scene, and he can forgive infidelity that's been all but proven, the very kisses and embraces he's witnessed with his own eyes, so long as he can somehow convince himself it's all happened "for the last time," that his rival will vanish from that day on, will go off to the ends of the earth, or that he himself will carry her away somewhere that dreaded rival can never reach. Of course, the reconciliation lasts only an hour. Because even if the rival really did vanish the next day, he'd invent another one and be jealous of him instead. And one might well wonder what kind of love needs watching over so closely, what a love could really be worth if it required such exhausting vigilance. But the jealous will never understand that. And yet there are men of noble hearts among them. It's remarkable, too, that those very men of noble hearts, crouched hidden in some closet, listening and spying, feel no sting of conscience in that moment at least, even though, with their "noble hearts," they understand perfectly well the shameful depths they've willingly sunk to.

At the sight of Grushenka, Mitya's jealousy vanished, and for an instant he became trusting and generous, genuinely disgusted with himself for his ugly feelings. But that only proved that his love for this woman held within it something far higher than he himself realized, that it wasn't merely sensual passion, wasn't just the "curve of her body," as he'd once put it to Alyosha. But the moment Grushenka was gone, Mitya began suspecting her of every low form of cunning and deceit, and felt no sting of conscience over it at all.

And so jealousy surged up in him again. In any case, he had to hurry. The first thing to do was scrape together even a small, temporary loan. The nine roubles had nearly all gone on his expedition. And, as everyone knows, you can't take a single step without money. But he'd already worked out, in the cart, where he might get a loan. He owned a fine pair of dueling pistols in a case, which he hadn't pawned until now only because he prized them above all his other possessions.

At the Metropolis tavern he'd made the acquaintance, some time back, of a young official, and had learned that this very well-off bachelor had a passion for weapons. He liked to buy pistols, revolvers, daggers, hang them on his wall, and show them off to visitors. He took great pride in them, and was quite the expert on how a revolver worked. Mitya, without a second thought, went straight to him and offered to pawn his pistols for ten roubles. The official, delighted, tried to talk him into selling them outright instead. But Mitya wouldn't agree to that, so the young man gave him the ten roubles, insisting nothing would induce him to take interest on it. They parted as friends.

Mitya was in a rush; he hurried toward Fyodor Pavlovitch's by the back way, toward the arbor, to catch hold of Smerdyakov as soon as he could. It was in this way that it later came to be established that three or four hours before a certain event, which I'll speak of later, Mitya hadn't had a farthing to his name, and had pawned an object he valued for just ten roubles, even though, three hours after that, he was in possession of thousands.... But I'm getting ahead of the story. From Marya Kondratyevna, the woman who lived near Fyodor Pavlovitch's, he learned the very unsettling news of Smerdyakov's illness. He heard the story of his fall in the cellar, his fit, the doctor's visit, Fyodor Pavlovitch's anxiety; he also heard, with some interest, that his brother Ivan had set off that morning for Moscow.

"Then he must have driven through Volovya ahead of me," Dmitri thought, but he was terribly troubled about Smerdyakov. "What's going to happen now? Who'll keep watch for me? Who'll bring me word?" he wondered. He began eagerly questioning the women about whether they'd seen anything the evening before. They understood at once what he was fishing for and reassured him completely. No one had been there. Ivan Fyodorovitch had been there in the evening; everything had gone exactly as usual. Mitya grew thoughtful. He'd definitely need to keep watch today, but where? Here, or at Samsonov's gate? He decided he'd have to keep an eye on both places, and meanwhile... meanwhile.... The trouble was he still had to carry out the new plan he'd worked out on the journey back. He was sure it would work, but he couldn't afford to delay acting on it. Mitya resolved to give it a single hour: "In an hour I'll know everything, I'll settle everything, and then, then, straight to Samsonov's first of all. I'll find out whether Grushenka's there and come straight back here, stay until eleven, then off to Samsonov's again to bring her home." That was his plan.

He flew home, washed, combed his hair, brushed off his clothes, got dressed, and went to Madame Hohlakov's. Alas, he'd pinned his hopes on her. He'd resolved to borrow three thousand from that lady. And what's more, he suddenly felt entirely convinced she wouldn't refuse him. One might wonder why, feeling so certain, he hadn't gone to her first, someone of his own sort, so to speak, rather than to Samsonov, a man he didn't even know, not of his class at all, whom he'd barely known how to address.

But the fact was that he'd never really known Madame Hohlakov well, had seen nothing of her over the past month, and knew she couldn't stand him. She'd disliked him from the start because he was engaged to Katerina Ivanovna, while for some reason she'd suddenly gotten it into her head that Katerina Ivanovna ought to throw him over and marry the "charming, chivalrously refined Ivan, with such excellent manners" instead. Mitya's manners she despised. Mitya had actually laughed at her once, and had remarked about her that she was every bit as lively and easygoing as she was uncultured. But that morning, riding in the cart, a brilliant idea had struck him: "If she's so eager for me not to marry Katerina Ivanovna"—and he knew she was practically hysterical on the subject—"then why would she refuse me the three thousand now, when it would let me leave Katya and be rid of her forever. These pampered fine ladies, once they've set their hearts on something, will spare no expense to satisfy the whim. Besides, she's rich," Mitya reasoned.

As for his "plan," it was essentially the same as before: offering his rights to Tchermashnya, though not with any commercial angle this time, as it had been with Samsonov, not trying to tempt the lady with the prospect of a six or seven thousand rouble profit, but simply offering it as security for the loan. As he worked out this new idea, Mitya was thrilled with it, though that was always how it went with him, with every new undertaking, every sudden decision. He threw himself into every new idea with passionate enthusiasm. Yet, climbing the steps of Madame Hohlakov's house, he felt a shiver of fear run down his spine. In that moment he saw, with the certainty of a mathematical proof, that this was his last hope, that if it fell through, there was nothing left for him in the world but to "rob and kill someone for the three thousand." It was half past seven when he rang the bell.

At first, fortune seemed to smile on him. The moment he was announced, he was received with remarkable speed. "As if she'd been waiting for me," Mitya thought, and no sooner had he been shown into the drawing room than the lady of the house herself came running in, announcing at once that she'd been expecting him.

"I was expecting you! I was expecting you! Though I had no reason at all to think you'd come see me, you'll admit that yourself. And yet, I did expect you. You may marvel at my intuition, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but I was convinced all morning that you'd come."

"That really is remarkable, madam," Mitya remarked, sinking limply into a chair, "but I've come to you on a matter of great importance.... A matter of the utmost importance to me, that is, madam... only to me... and I'm in a hurry—"

"I know you've come on the most important business, Dmitri Fyodorovitch; it's not some premonition, not some backward reach toward the miraculous—have you heard about Father Zossima? No, this is a matter of pure mathematics: you couldn't possibly not have come, after everything that's happened with Katerina Ivanovna; you couldn't, you couldn't, it's a mathematical certainty."
"The plain realism of everyday life, madam, that's what it is. But allow me to explain—"
"Realism indeed, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I'm entirely for realism now. I've seen quite enough of miracles. Have you heard that Father Zossima has died?"
"No, madam, this is the first I'm hearing of it." Mitya was a bit surprised. The image of Alyosha rose in his mind.
"Last night, and just imagine—"

"Madam," Mitya said, "I can't imagine anything except that I'm in a desperate position, and that if you don't help me, everything will come crashing down, me most of all. Forgive me for the crudeness of the phrase, but I'm in a fever—"

"I know, I know you're in a fever. How could you not be, and whatever you're about to tell me, I already know it in advance. I've been thinking over your fate for a long time now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I've been watching it closely, studying it.... Oh, believe me, I'm an experienced physician of the soul, Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

"Madam, if you're an experienced physician, then I'm certainly an experienced patient," Mitya said, making an effort to be polite, "and I feel that, since you're watching over my fate this closely, you'll come to my aid now that I'm ruined, and so allow me at least to lay out for you the plan I've come here hoping to propose... and what I'm hoping to get from you.... I've come, madam—"

"Don't explain it. That's secondary. But as for help, you're not the first person I've helped, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You've most likely heard of my cousin, Madame Belmesov. Her husband was ruined, 'come to grief,' as you so characteristically put it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I advised him to go into horse breeding, and now he's doing splendidly. Do you know anything about horse breeding, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?"

"Not the faintest idea, madam; ah, madam, not the faintest!" Mitya cried, in nervous impatience, all but leaping out of his seat. "I'm simply begging you, madam, to listen to me. Just give me two minutes to speak freely, so I can explain the whole plan I've come here with. Besides, I'm short on time. I'm in a dreadful hurry," Mitya cried, half hysterical, sensing she was about to launch into another speech and hoping to head her off. "I've come in despair... in the very last gasp of despair, to beg you to lend me the sum of three thousand, a loan, but on the safest possible security, madam, with the most trustworthy guarantees! Just let me explain—"

"You can tell me all that afterward, afterward!" Madame Hohlakov, with a gesture, demanded silence in her turn. "And whatever you're about to tell me, I already know it all in advance; I've told you that already. You're asking for a certain sum, three thousand, but I can give you more, immeasurably more, I'll save you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but you must listen to me."
Mitya sprang up from his seat again.
"Madam, would you really be so kind!" he cried, overcome with feeling. "Good God, you've saved me! You've saved a man from a violent death, from a bullet.... My eternal gratitude—"
"I'll give you more, infinitely more than three thousand!" cried Madame Hohlakov, gazing with a radiant smile at Mitya's rapture.
"Infinitely more? But I don't need that much. I only need that fateful three thousand, and for my part I can offer security for that sum with infinite gratitude, and I propose a plan which—"

"Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it's settled, it's done." Madame Hohlakov cut him off, with the quiet triumph of someone doing good: "I've promised to save you, and I will save you. I'll save you the way I saved Belmesov. What do you think of gold mines, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?"
"Gold mines, madam? I've never given them a thought."

"But I have, on your behalf. I've thought about it, over and over. I've been watching you this past month. I've watched you a hundred times as you walked by, telling myself: there's a man of energy who ought to be out at the gold mines. I've studied your walk, and I've come to a conclusion: that's a man who would strike gold."
"From my walk, madam?" Mitya said, smiling.

"Yes, from your walk. You surely can't deny that character shows itself in the way a man walks, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Science backs this up. I'm entirely for science and realism now. After this whole business with Father Zossima, which has upset me so terribly, from this very day I'm a realist, and I want to devote myself to practical usefulness. I'm cured. 'Enough,' as Turgenev says."
"But, madam, the three thousand you so generously promised to lend me—"

"It's yours, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Madame Hohlakov cut in at once. "The money's as good as in your pocket already—not three thousand, but three million, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, in no time at all. I'll make you a gift of the idea: you'll go find gold mines, make millions, come back and become a leading man, and wake the rest of us up and lead us all toward something better. Are we supposed to just leave it all to the Jews? You'll found institutions, enterprises of every kind. You'll help the poor, and they'll bless your name. This is the age of railways, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You'll become famous, indispensable to the Ministry of Finance, which is in such a sorry state right now. The falling value of the rouble keeps me up at night, Dmitri Fyodorovitch; people don't know that side of me—"

"Madam, madam!" Dmitri broke in, with an uneasy sense of foreboding. "I shall, indeed, perhaps, follow your advice, your wise advice, madam.... I'll perhaps set off... for the gold mines.... I'll come see you about it again... many times, in fact... but right now, that three thousand you so generously... oh, that would set me free, and if you could, today... you see, I haven't a moment, not a moment to spare today—"
"Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, enough!" Madame Hohlakov cut in firmly. "The question is, will you go to the gold mines or won't you—have you fully made up your mind? Answer yes or no."
"I'll go, madam, afterward.... I'll go wherever you like... but right now—"

"Wait!" cried Madame Hohlakov. And, jumping up, she ran to a handsome writing desk with a great many small drawers and began pulling them open one after another, searching for something with desperate haste.

"The three thousand," Mitya thought, his heart nearly stopping, "and right this instant... no papers, no formalities... that's how a real gentlewoman does things! What a splendid woman she is, if only she didn't talk quite so much!"
"Here!" Madame Hohlakov cried, running back to Mitya, overjoyed, "here's what I was looking for!"
It was a tiny silver icon on a cord, of the kind sometimes worn against the skin along with a cross.

"This is from Kiev, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," she went on, reverently, "from the relics of the Holy Martyr Varvara. Let me hang it round your neck myself, and with it dedicate you to a new life, a new calling."

And she actually looped the cord around his neck and began arranging it. Deeply embarrassed, Mitya bent down and helped her, and finally managed to tuck it beneath his necktie and collar, down through his shirt to his chest.
"Now you can set off," Madame Hohlakov announced, sitting back down triumphantly in her place.

"Madam, I'm so touched. I don't know how to thank you, truly... for such kindness, but... if only you knew how precious every minute is to me right now.... That sum of money, which I'll owe to your generosity.... Oh, madam, since you're being so kind, so movingly generous with me," Mitya burst out impulsively, "then let me confess to you... though, of course, you've known it for some time already... that I love someone else here.... I've been unfaithful to Katya... Katerina Ivanovna, I mean.... Oh, I've treated her cruelly, dishonorably, but I've fallen in love here with another woman... a woman you, madam, perhaps look down on, since you already know everything, but one I cannot leave under any circumstances, and so that three thousand right now—"

"Leave everything, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Madame Hohlakov interrupted, in the most decisive tone. "Leave everything, especially women. Gold mines are your destiny, and there's no room for women there. Later, when you come back rich and famous, you'll find the girl of your heart in the very best society. She'll be a modern girl, educated, with advanced ideas. By then the dawning woman question will have gained real ground, and the new woman will have arrived."
"Madam, that's not the point, not at all...." Mitya clasped his hands, pleading.

"Yes, it is, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it's exactly what you need, precisely what you're longing for, even if you don't realize it yourself.
